problems.title: Problem 1: Physics of tsunamis
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (80 points)

Physics of tsunamis

In our country, tsunamis caused by changes in the crustal structure of the sea floor due to earthquakes, or by the collapse of mountain bodies and the like, have occurred in the past. In the case of an earthquake, the deformation of the crust of the sea floor is transmitted to the sea surface, which becomes the wave source and causes the propagation of large waves in the ocean. The damage to the Sanriku coast of Tōhoku and to Fukushima caused by the tsunami due to the crustal movement of the sea floor accompanying the 2011 off the Pacific coast of Tōhoku Earthquake in March 2011 is still fresh in our memory. The structure of a tsunami has properties different from those of the ordinary waves, caused by wind and the like, that we are used to seeing. The aim of this problem is to deepen our understanding of the structure of tsunamis from a physical point of view.

The simplest example of a wave that comes to mind is probably a wave propagating along the string of a stringed instrument. The medium transmitting the wave is the string, and its displacement is perpendicular to the direction of propagation; it is classified as a transverse wave. Another example is a sound wave in air. Here the air moves in the direction of propagation, and condensations and rarefactions of density are transmitted; it is classified as a longitudinal wave. Electromagnetic waves (including light) propagating in vacuum are transverse waves in which the electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

On the other hand, the propagation of wave motion of sea water is more complicated than these. In the case of sea water, the water surface moves up and down, and the displacement of the sea water clearly has components both parallel and perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Therefore the classification into transverse and longitudinal waves described above cannot be applied. For water, a classification from a somewhat different point of view is made. It focuses on the relative size of the wavelength of the wave and the depth of the sea water.

Here we consider the propagation of waves of "small amplitude" generated on the surface of water whose "depth is shallow". Let us make clear the definitions of the words "the depth is shallow" and "small amplitude". Let the wavelength of the wave be $\lambda$, the height of the wave $h$, and the depth of the sea water $d$. We consider the propagation of waves under the condition

$$\lambda\gg d\gg h \qquad (1)$$

Such waves are called shallow-water waves. The sea is deep. The average depth of the Pacific Ocean is $4000\,\mathrm{m}$. It may seem strange to study shallow-water waves in order to consider a tsunami that propagated across this sea and caused a tragic disaster. However, the wavelength of a tsunami accompanying a huge earthquake is $\lambda>100\,\mathrm{km}$, while the depth of the sea is $d<11\,\mathrm{km}$ and the height of the wave is $h<100\,\mathrm{m}$, so condition (1) is satisfied for large-scale tsunamis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1. The wave in the rest frame. The sea floor is at depth $-d$, and the solid line represents the water surface. Note that this is a conceptual figure for explanation and is not drawn according to condition (1).

The motion of the sea water in a shallow-water wave is a back-and-forth motion almost parallel to the direction of propagation; the water moves all together with the same speed from the sea surface to the sea floor, but the average position of the sea water does not move. As shown in Fig. 1, at the position of the crest of the wave the sea water moves in the direction of propagation of the wave with speed $V$, and at the trough of the wave it moves opposite to the direction of propagation with $-V$. The crests and troughs of the wave advance with speed $c$ ($c\gg V$). These facts should really be shown on the basis of the equations of motion of the sea water, but we shall accept them as correct and examine the speed at which the wave propagates, the energy carried by the wave, and so on. Note that for waves occurring in a liquid with a free surface, changes of the density of the liquid can be neglected.

Note: In the case where the relation between the wavelength and the depth is reversed ($\lambda\ll d$), the motion of the sea water depends on the depth below the sea surface. The amplitude of the motion becomes smaller with increasing depth below the sea surface. Water waves in such a case are called deep-water waves.

As shown in Fig. 1, the sea water moves in the $x$ direction, the direction of propagation of the wave, and does not move in the horizontal direction perpendicular to it ($y$ direction). In the vertical direction ($z$ direction), the mean water surface is $z=0$ and the sea floor is $z=-d$. Although the propagation of the wave is one-dimensional in its direction of propagation, strictly speaking the motion of the sea water is not one-dimensional but takes place in two dimensions in the vertical $xz$ plane; below we shall call this a one-dimensional model. Here we adopt this one-dimensional model to simplify the problem.

Let us consider the problem in a coordinate system moving together with the wave with speed $c$, as in Fig. 2. In this coordinate system the position and the shape of the wave do not move, but the sea water flows backward (in the negative $x$ direction). Let the $x$ coordinate of a trough of the wave be $x_1$ and the $x$ coordinate of a crest be $x_2$. At $x_1$ the sea water flows backward with $-V-c$, and at $x_2$ it flows backward with $V-c$. The height of the sea surface at $x_1$ is $-h$, and the height at $x_2$ is $h$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2. The wave in the coordinate system moving with the wave

Consider a small lump of sea water just below the sea surface at the crest of the wave. Let its mass be $\varDelta m$. The mechanical energy of this part in the coordinate system moving with the wave can be written as

$$\frac{1}{2}\varDelta m(c-V)^2+\varDelta m gh \qquad (2)$$

This part flows backward and eventually reaches the trough. Here $g$ is the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration.

Q1. (a) Write down the mechanical energy of $\varDelta m$ when it has reached the trough.

(b) In this process the mechanical energy of the part under consideration is constant. From this condition, find the relation between $V$, $h$ and $c$.

Note: The argument here may be regarded as an application of Bernoulli's theorem to the sea water flowing along the sea surface. The same result is obtained by applying Bernoulli's theorem to the sea water flowing along the sea floor.

Consider the cross-section $x=x_2$ in Fig. 2. Let its thickness in the $y$ direction be $\delta y$. The amount of sea water flowing in per unit time from the front through this surface is $(d+h)(c-V)\,\delta y$.

Q2. (a) What is the amount of sea water flowing out backward per unit time through the cross-section of thickness $\delta y$ at $x=x_1$?

The amount of sea water in the region between $x_1$ and $x_2$ must be constant because of the law of conservation of mass (known in fluid dynamics as the equation of continuity).

(b) Using the law of conservation of mass, express $V$ in terms of $c$, $d$, $h$.

Q3. From the answers to Q1 and Q2, show that the propagation speed $c$ of the wave is given by

$$c=\sqrt{gd} \qquad (3)$$

Now let us represent a wave travelling in the positive $x$ direction concretely by a sine wave. The dependence on $x$, $t$ of the flow velocity $u$ of the sea water in the rest frame is given by the following equation.

$$u(x,t)=V\sin[k(x-ct)]=V\sin(kx-\omega t) \qquad (4)$$

Below, this expression is used as needed. Here $V$ is the magnitude of the flow velocity at the crests and troughs, $k$ is the wave number, and $\omega=kc$ is the angular frequency. If the period of this wave motion is $T$, then $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, the frequency is $\nu=\dfrac{1}{T}$, and the wavelength is $\lambda=cT$. Here, under condition (1), the speed $c$ of the wave is given by equation (3). That is, in the case of shallow-water waves the speed of the wave does not depend on the wave number, and hence it is constant independently of the angular frequency; this is called non-dispersive wave motion. In general, the speed of a wave depends on the wave number $k$. This gives rise to dispersion effects, but we shall not go further into them here. In non-dispersive wave motion, low-frequency components and high-frequency components propagate with the same speed, so the wave propagates without changing its waveform.

Q4. (a) Let the dependence of the wave height on $x$, $t$ be $f(x,t)$; it is known that $f(x,t)$ is proportional to $u(x,t)$. Derive the relation

$$f(x,t)=\left(\frac{d}{g}\right)^{1/2}u(x,t) \qquad (5)$$

(b) Consider a small lump $\varDelta m$ of sea water just below the sea surface. Let its $(x,z)$ coordinates when there is no wave be $(x_0,0)$. In this sub-question, $x_0$, which can be chosen arbitrarily, is a label giving the coordinate of $\varDelta m$ when there is no wave, and is not a variable. When there is a wave, using the displacement $X$ in the $x$ direction, the coordinates of $\varDelta m$ are expressed as $(x_0+X(x_0,t),\,f(x_0,t))$. Using

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}X(x_0,t)}{\mathrm{d}t}=u(x_0,t),$$

show that the displacement $(X,f)$ of $\varDelta m$ satisfies the equation of an elliptic orbit

$$\frac{X(x_0,t)^2}{a^2}+\frac{f(x_0,t)^2}{b^2}=1,$$

and express the semi-axes $a$ and $b$ in terms of $V$, $\omega$, $d$, $g$.

In May 1960 (Shōwa 35), the largest earthquake in the history of observation, of magnitude 9.5, occurred off Chile, and the tsunami with its source there crossed the Pacific Ocean, reached the sea off Sanriku in the Tōhoku region of Japan about 23 hours later, and caused great damage to this region. The period of this tsunami over the Pacific Ocean was observed to be more than 1 hour. Furthermore, if the Earth is regarded as a perfect sphere, Japan is geographically located on the side opposite to the epicentre with respect to the centre of the Earth. This is called the antipodal point. It has been pointed out theoretically that a tsunami generated at an epicentre on a spherical surface tends to converge at this antipodal point if there are no obstacles on the sphere. This is also considered to be one of the reasons why the damage on the Sanriku coast became large. Furthermore, simulations by numerical computation have confirmed that the waves passing south of the Hawaiian Islands and those passing north of them tend to converge near Japan, the antipodal point.

Q5. Our one-dimensional model cannot treat a problem on a spherical surface strictly correctly, but if the radius of the sphere is sufficiently large, as in the case of the Earth ($R=6378\,\mathrm{km}$), an approximate treatment by this model is considered possible.

(a) If the Earth is a perfect sphere, the length of its equator is 40 thousand km. The distance from off Chile to off Sanriku, close to the antipodal point on the Earth, is then about 20 thousand km. According to the observational data, the time it took the tsunami to reach the sea off Sanriku in Japan was about 23 hours. Calculate the average speed $c$ of this tsunami.

(b) Let us assume that our one-dimensional model holds; ignore structures of the floor of the Pacific Ocean such as submarine ridges and trenches, take the floor to be horizontal, and approximate the depth $d$ as constant. Calculate the average depth $d$ that gives the propagation speed above. Take $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

(c) Based on the observational data above, take the period of the tsunami to be 1 hour. How large is the wavelength $\lambda$ of this tsunami? Show that, in this case, the first inequality of condition (1) stated at the beginning holds.

(d) As shown in Q4(b), the sea water at the surface describes an elliptic orbit. For the example of this problem, calculate the ratio $\dfrac{b}{a}$ of the semi-axes of the ellipse to 1 significant figure. Explain what this means.

It is known that the height of a tsunami increases as the water depth decreases. Even a small wave height in the open sea becomes a large wave height as the wave approaches the coast, and it causes great damage to harbours (= tsu). From here on, let us examine in more detail the relation between the height $h$ of the tsunami and the water depth $d$.

We examine the mechanical energy of a shallow-water wave in the rest frame. First consider the potential energy. The potential energy per unit volume of sea water at height $z$ is $\rho gz$, where $\rho$ is the density, and integrating from the sea floor ($z=-d$) up to the height of the wave at the water surface ($z=f$) gives the total potential energy per unit area of the floor.

$$U_{\mathrm{t}}=\int_{-d}^{f}\rho gz\,\mathrm{d}z=\frac{1}{2}\rho gf^2-\frac{1}{2}\rho gd^2$$

Of this, it is appropriate to consider as the potential energy of the tsunami (shallow-water wave) only the first term on the right-hand side, which is the change from the case where no shallow-water wave exists ($f=0$). That is,

$$U=\frac{1}{2}\rho gf^2$$

Averaging this over one period gives

$$\langle U\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\rho g\langle f^2\rangle \qquad (6)$$

Here the brackets $\langle\ldots\rangle$ denote the average described above.

On the other hand, the kinetic energy per unit volume of the sea water is expressed as $\dfrac{1}{2}\rho u^2$. Integrating this as before from the sea floor ($z=-d$) up to the height of the wave at the water surface ($z=f$), we obtain the kinetic energy per unit area of the floor

$$K=\int_{-d}^{f}\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2\mathrm{d}z=\frac{1}{2}\rho u^2(d+f)$$

Averaging over one period as before,

$$\langle K\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\rho d\langle u^2\rangle \qquad (7)$$

Using here the relation of equation (5),

$$\langle K\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\rho g\langle f^2\rangle$$

and $\langle K\rangle=\langle U\rangle$. The average value $\langle E\rangle$ of the mechanical energy of the tsunami per unit area of the floor is

$$\langle E\rangle=\langle K\rangle+\langle U\rangle$$

and

$$\langle E\rangle=\rho g\langle f^2\rangle=\rho d\langle u^2\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\rho dV^2 \qquad (8)$$

Here, in the last equality, the concrete functional form of equation (4) and the average value $\langle\sin^2(kx-\omega t)\rangle=\dfrac{1}{2}$ were used. $V$ is the amplitude of the flow velocity $u$ of the sea water, and is the flow velocity at the crest of the wave shown in Fig. 1.

Multiplying the mechanical energy of the tsunami (shallow-water wave) per unit area of the floor, that is, the surface density of the energy, by the speed of the shallow-water wave $c=\sqrt{gd}$, we can evaluate the amount of energy flowing per unit length in the $y$ direction and per unit time in the direction of propagation (positive $x$ direction). This energy flow rate is called the energy flux $\varPhi$. It is given by the following equation.

$$\varPhi=\langle E\rangle c=\frac{1}{2}\rho dV^2\sqrt{gd} \qquad (9)$$

If, during the propagation of the wave, no energy is supplied from outside or lost to the outside, the energy flux $\varPhi$ is constant. If there is a large step in the sea floor, reflection of the wave occurs, and there is also energy lost by friction at the sea floor; but below we examine what happens in the ideal case where the sea floor changes gently, the reflection of the wave can be neglected, friction can also be neglected, and the energy flux can be regarded as constant. Using $\varPhi$, the flow velocity $V$ at the crests and troughs of the tsunami is

$$V=\left(\frac{2\varPhi}{\rho g^{1/2}}\right)^{1/2}d^{-3/4} \qquad (10)$$

Q6. Taking into account that the energy flux $\varPhi$ is constant, find the dependence of the wave height $h$ of the tsunami on the depth $d$ (including the coefficient).

[Hint] Consider the relation of equation (5).

The wave height $h$ of a tsunami (shallow-water wave) increases, as the depth $d$ becomes shallower, with the depth dependence of the answer to Q6, and likewise the flow velocity $V$ increases with the depth dependence $d^{-3/4}$.

At present it is predicted that earthquakes due to crustal movements of the sea floor at the Kuril Trench, the Japan Trench and the Nankai Trough will occur with high probability. Accordingly, the possibility of tsunamis originating from them has been pointed out. Answer the following questions on the basis of the considerations made so far.

Q7. An earthquake tsunami was generated at a place $200\,\mathrm{km}$ from the coast. Assume that the water depth is almost constant, $1000\,\mathrm{m}$, from the place of generation to near the coast.

(a) What is the speed of the tsunami in km per hour?

(b) Calculate the shortest arrival time $\tau$ of the tsunami at the coast.

Q8. In a sea area with water depth $d=4000\,\mathrm{m}$, a wave source with wave height $h=1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ was generated and a tsunami occurred.

(a) Calculate the speed $c$ of the tsunami in this sea area, the speed $V$ of the back-and-forth motion of the sea water, and the energy flux $\varPhi$ of the tsunami. Use $\rho=1.0\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ for the density of sea water.

(b) When the above energy flux is constant, there exists an $\alpha$ that makes $hd^{\alpha}$ constant. Find the value of $\alpha$ and the constant value of $hd^{\alpha}$ (including the unit).

[Hint] Refer to Q6.

(c) When this tsunami reaches sea areas of depth $400\,\mathrm{m}$, $100\,\mathrm{m}$ and $25\,\mathrm{m}$ while keeping the energy flux $\varPhi$ constant, calculate the speed $c$ of the tsunami, the wave height $h$ and the flow velocity $V$ of the sea water in each of these sea areas.

When a tsunami approaches the coast and the depth becomes shallow, the propagation speed $c$ becomes slower, but both the wave height $h$ and the flow velocity $V$ of the sea water increase, causing great damage. The name tsunami (tsu = harbour) comes from this. We point out that the one-dimensional model adopted here cannot describe effects due to topography, such as the shape of bays on the coast or the presence of capes, but that when these are taken into account the above tendency may be enhanced in some cases.

problems.title: Problem 2: Connecting two charged conducting spheres
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (80 points)

Connecting two charged conducting spheres

Around a point charge $q$ an electric field is produced radially, and the strength $E(r)$ of the electric field at a point at distance $r$ from the point charge is expressed as

$$E(r)=k\frac{q}{r^2} \qquad (1)$$

Here $k$ is the proportionality constant of Coulomb's law; if the point charge is in vacuum, it is related to the permittivity of vacuum (electric constant) $\epsilon_0$ by $k=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}$. The electric potential $V(r)$ at a point at distance $r$ from the point charge, taking the reference point of the potential at infinity, is expressed as

$$V(r)=-\int_{\infty}^{r}E(r)\,\mathrm{d}r=k\frac{q}{r} \qquad (2)$$

A space in which there is an electric field stores energy. This energy of the electric field is also called electrostatic energy. If the strength of the electric field in vacuum is $E$, the energy of the electric field per unit volume (the energy density of the electric field) is, according to the theory of electromagnetism, expressed as

$$\frac{1}{8\pi k}E^2=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2 \qquad (3)$$

Next, suppose that in vacuum a charge $q$ is uniformly distributed on the surface of a conducting sphere of radius $r_0$. From symmetry, the electric field around the conducting sphere is expected to be produced radially. In fact, the electric field around the sphere is equal to the electric field that a point charge $q$ placed at the centre of the sphere produces in the region $r\geqq r_0$, and the electric field lines are as in Fig. 1. The potential of the conducting sphere is

$$V=k\frac{q}{r_0}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r_0} \qquad (4)$$

and since the conducting sphere stores the charge $q$, it can be regarded as a capacitor of capacitance

$$C=\frac{q}{V}=\frac{r_0}{k}\quad\text{or}\quad 4\pi\epsilon_0r_0 \qquad (5)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Electric field lines around a charged conducting sphere (for $q>0$)

The other electrode of the capacitor is then at infinity.

Let us calculate the energy of the electric field (electrostatic energy) $\mathcal{E}$ around the conducting sphere. The energy in a thin spherical shell from $r$ to $r+\mathrm{d}r$ ($r>r_0$) from the centre of the conducting sphere is the product of the energy density of the electric field in the shell and the volume of the shell,

$$\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E(r)^2\times4\pi r^2\,\mathrm{d}r=\frac{q^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{r^2} \qquad (6)$$

so, integrating from $r=r_0$ to $\infty$, we obtain

$$\mathcal{E}=\frac{q^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0}\int_{r_0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{r^2}=\frac{q^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0r_0} \qquad (7)$$

Using equations (4) and (5), it is expressed as

$$\mathcal{E}=\frac{q^2}{2C}=\frac{1}{2}CV^2 \qquad (8)$$

This is the electrostatic energy stored by the conducting sphere.

[I] A conducting sphere of radius $a$ (conductor 1) and a conducting sphere of radius $2a$ (conductor 2), sufficiently far apart, were connected by a straight thin wire. As shown in Fig. 2, a switch S and an electrical resistance $R$ are inserted in the wire. Initially the switch is open, and a charge $Q$ is uniformly distributed on the surface of each of the two conducting spheres. The distance between the two conducting spheres is such that they are far enough apart that neither affects the electric field of the other, but such that electrical signals may be regarded as being transmitted instantaneously. Also, the wire is thin, and disturbance of the electric field around each conducting sphere from spherical symmetry can be neglected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-2-fig2.png

[導体1 = conductor 1, 導体2 = conductor 2]

Fig. 2. Two charged conducting spheres connected through a resistor

Let us consider the current flowing in the wire when the switch is closed. The potentials of conductor 1 and conductor 2 are $V_1=k\dfrac{Q}{a}$ and $V_2=k\dfrac{Q}{2a}$, respectively. If $Q>0$, then $V_1-V_2>0$, so when the switch is closed a current flows from conductor 1 to conductor 2. Taking the instant at which the switch is closed as $t=0$, let the current at a later time $t$ be $I(t)$, and the charges on conductor 1 and conductor 2 be $Q_1(t)$ and $Q_2(t)$, respectively.

Q1. Show that the following relation holds between the current $I$ and the charges $Q_1$, $Q_2$. Explain the derivation.

$$IR=k\frac{Q_1}{a}-k\frac{Q_2}{2a} \qquad (9)$$

Q2. Expressing the current $I$ in equation (9) as a time derivative of $Q_1$, and expressing $Q_2$ in terms of $Q_1$ on the basis of the law of conservation of charge, one obtains an equation containing a derivative that describes the time variation of $Q_1$. Write down this equation.

Q3. The equation containing the derivative of $Q_1$ obtained in the previous question has a solution of the following form.

$$Q_1(t)=Q_0+Q'\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau} \qquad (10)$$

Here $Q_0$, $Q'$, $\tau$ are constants. Taking into account that $Q_1=Q$ at $t=0$, find the constants $Q_0$, $Q'$, $\tau$.

Q4. Find $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ after a sufficiently long time has passed.

Fig. 2, consisting of the two conducting spheres and the resistor, is represented by an equivalent circuit as in Fig. 3. $C_1$ and $C_2$ are the capacitances of conductor 1 and conductor 2, respectively. The part enclosed by the broken line is considered to be at infinity.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Equivalent circuit of Fig. 2

Q5. Find the energy dissipated in the resistor from the time the switch is closed until a sufficiently long time has passed.

Q6. When a charge $Q=1.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C}$ is uniformly distributed on the surface of a single isolated conducting sphere of radius $a=0.10\,\mathrm{m}$, calculate the potential $V$ of the conductor and the electrostatic energy $\mathcal{E}$ of the conductor. Here $k\fallingdotseq9.0\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{m/F}$.

[II] Next, as in Fig. 4, consider the case where a switch S and a coil of inductance $L$ are inserted in a straight thin wire connecting a conducting sphere of radius $a$ (conductor 1) and a conducting sphere of radius $2a$ (conductor 2), each carrying charge $Q$. As in the case of Fig. 2, the distance between the two conducting spheres is such that they are far enough apart that neither affects the electric field of the other, but such that electrical signals may be regarded as being transmitted instantaneously. The electrical resistance of the wire can be neglected, and the disturbance of the electric field by the wire can also be neglected. Furthermore, radiation of energy accompanying variations of the electromagnetic field need not be considered.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-2-fig4.png

[導体1 = conductor 1, 導体2 = conductor 2]

Fig. 4. Two charged conducting spheres connected through a coil

Q7. After the switch is closed, let the charges on conductors 1 and 2 be $Q_1(t)$, $Q_2(t)$, and the current flowing in the coil be $I(t)$; show that the following relation holds. Explain the derivation. Here $I>0$ when the current flows in the direction of the arrow in the figure.

$$L\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}=k\frac{Q_1}{a}-k\frac{Q_2}{2a} \qquad (11)$$

Q8. Expressing the current $I$ in equation (11) as a time derivative of $Q_1$, and expressing $Q_2$ in terms of $Q_1$ on the basis of the law of conservation of charge, one obtains an equation containing a second derivative that describes the time variation of $Q_1$. Write down this equation.

Q9. Solve the equation containing the derivative obtained in the previous question to find $Q_1(t)$, and express the angular frequency $\omega$ of the electrical oscillation in terms of $k$, $a$, $L$. Note that $Q_1=Q$, $I=0$ at $t=0$.

[Hint]

When $y$ is a function of $t$, the general solution of the equation containing the second derivative $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}t^2}$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}t^2}=-A\,(y-B)\qquad\text{where }A\,(>0),\ B\text{ are constants}$$

is, putting $\omega=\sqrt{A}$, given by

$$y=B+c_1\sin\omega t+c_2\cos\omega t\qquad c_1,\ c_2\text{ are constants of integration}$$

Q10. Find the maximum and minimum values of $Q_1$ and $Q_2$.

The equivalent circuit of Fig. 4, consisting of the two conducting spheres and the coil, is represented as in Fig. 5, in which the resistor of Fig. 3 is replaced by the coil. $C_1$ and $C_2$ are the capacitances of conductor 1 and conductor 2, respectively, and the part enclosed by the broken line is considered to be at infinity.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-2-fig5.png

Fig. 5. Equivalent circuit of Fig. 4

Q11. Calculate the electrostatic energy of each conducting sphere and the magnetic energy of the coil at an arbitrary time $t$ ($>0$). Also verify that their sum is constant, independent of time.

Q12. In Fig. 4, when the radius of conductor 1 is $a=0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ and the inductance of the coil is $L=1.5\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{H}$, calculate the frequency $f=\dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$ of the electrical oscillation.

[III] As in Fig. 6, consider the case where a charge $Q$ is uniformly distributed on the surface of each of a thin conducting spherical shell of radius $a$ and a concentric thin conducting spherical shell of radius $2a$. A switch S and an electrical resistance $R$ are inserted in a straight thin wire connecting the two spherical shells. Even when a current flows in the wire, the spherically symmetric charge distribution and the radial electric field are maintained.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-2-fig6.png

Fig. 6. Two concentric conducting spherical shells

Q13. After the switch is closed and a sufficiently long time has passed, find the charge $Q_1$ on the inner spherical shell and the charge $Q_2$ on the outer spherical shell.

Q14. Find the energy dissipated in the resistor from the time the switch is closed until a sufficiently long time has passed.

problems.title: Problem 3: Evaporation of water and saturated vapour pressure (rise of sea-water temperature and precipitation)
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (70 points)

Evaporation of water and saturated vapour pressure (rise of sea-water temperature and precipitation)

Saturated vapour pressure and heat of vaporization

In dry air, water molecules escape through the interface between air and water (the water surface), as in Fig. 1. This is the evaporation of water. Water molecules in water attract nearby water molecules mainly through hydrogen bonds, and only water molecules with a large kinetic energy can escape from the water surface into the atmosphere. Therefore extra energy is needed for evaporation; this is the heat of vaporization. Conversely, water molecules in the air are taken from the water surface into the water. When the partial pressure of water vapour equals the saturated vapour pressure, the numbers of escaping molecules and of molecules taken in balance, and an equilibrium state is reached. Let us consider the relation between the temperature dependence of the saturated vapour pressure and the heat of vaporization.

In the following questions, use the physical constants given in Table 1 as needed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-3-fig1.png

[表面 = surface, 熱運動エネルギーの大きい分子 = molecules with large thermal kinetic energy, 水分子 = water molecules, 水 = water, 熱 = heat]

Fig. 1. Evaporation of water

A process in which a system goes through a series of changes of state and returns to its original state is called a cycle, and a system that, by repeating cycles, converts part of the heat energy received into work done on the outside is called a heat engine. The substance that performs the operation of a heat engine is called the working substance. The Carnot cycle, an important process in heat engines, is a cycle that returns to its original state via the following four reversible processes (quasi-static processes).

Table 1. Symbols, values and units of physical quantities

$$\begin{array}{llll} \text{Physical quantity} & \text{Symbol} & \text{Value} & \text{Unit} \\ \hline \text{Gas constant} & R & 8.31 & \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}} \\ \text{Boltzmann constant} & k_{\mathrm{B}} & 1.38\times10^{-23} & \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}} \\ \text{Avogadro constant} & N_{\mathrm{A}} & 6.02\times10^{23} & \mathrm{mol^{-1}} \\ \text{Magnitude of the gravitational acceleration} & g & 9.8 & \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} \\ \text{Average mass of an air molecule} & M_{\mathrm{a}} & 4.78\times10^{-26} & \mathrm{kg} \\ \text{Mass of a water molecule} & M & 2.99\times10^{-26} & \mathrm{kg} \end{array}$$

(a) Isothermal expansion process

(b) Adiabatic expansion process

(c) Isothermal compression process

(d) Adiabatic compression process

In the isothermal expansion process (a), the system is in contact with a high-temperature heat reservoir at absolute temperature (hereafter simply called temperature) $T_1$, and the system receives heat from the high-temperature reservoir. In the isothermal compression process (c), the system is in contact with a low-temperature heat reservoir at temperature $T_2$ ($T_2<T_1$), and the system releases heat to the low-temperature reservoir. If the amount of heat that the system receives from the high-temperature reservoir is $Q_1$ and the amount of heat released to the low-temperature reservoir is $Q_2$, then the work $W$ done by the system on the outside during one cycle is, from the first law of thermodynamics, $W=Q_1-Q_2$.

In general, the ratio of the work done by the system on the outside to the amount of heat that the system receives from the high-temperature reservoir is called the thermal efficiency of the heat engine. Writing the thermal efficiency as $\eta$, in the case of the Carnot cycle above,

$$\eta=\frac{W}{Q_1}=\frac{Q_1-Q_2}{Q_1} \qquad (1)$$

It is known that the thermal efficiency $\eta$ of the Carnot cycle does not depend on the working substance and is

$$\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1} \qquad (2)$$

Below, with $T_1=T$ and $T_2=T-\varDelta T$, we assume a system in which water in a state of gas–liquid two-phase coexistence is enclosed as the working substance in a cylinder fitted with a piston, as in Fig. 2, and consider a Carnot cycle in which the system is operated according to the following processes (a)–(d) while the water vapour is kept in the saturated state.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-3-fig2.png

[膨張・収縮 = expansion / contraction, 水蒸気 = water vapour, 水 = water, 放熱 = heat release, 吸熱 = heat absorption, 蒸気圧 = vapour pressure, 体積 = volume, 等温膨張 = isothermal expansion, 断熱膨張 = adiabatic expansion, 等温圧縮 = isothermal compression, 断熱圧縮 = adiabatic compression]

Fig. 2. Carnot cycle with water in a state of gas–liquid two-phase coexistence as the working substance

(a) The system, in the two-phase coexistence state at temperature $T$ and volume $V_1$, is brought into contact with a high-temperature reservoir at temperature $T$ and expanded isothermally to volume $V_2$. During this, the system absorbs the amount of heat $Q_1$ and part of the liquid water vaporizes, and the pressure $P$ of the system is kept at the saturated vapour pressure at temperature $T$.

(b) The system is detached from the high-temperature reservoir and expanded adiabatically. During this, the temperature of the system changes from $T$ to $T-\varDelta T$ and the pressure from $P$ to $P-\varDelta P$.

(c) The system is brought into contact with a low-temperature reservoir at temperature $T-\varDelta T$ and compressed isothermally. During this, the system releases the amount of heat $Q_2$ and part of the water vapour liquefies, and the pressure $P-\varDelta P$ of the system is kept at the saturated vapour pressure at temperature $T-\varDelta T$.

(d) Finally, the system is detached from the low-temperature reservoir and compressed adiabatically to the original volume $V_1$. During this, the temperature of the system changes from $T-\varDelta T$ to $T$ and the pressure from $P-\varDelta P$ to $P$, and the system returns to its original state.

Note here that in the isothermal expansion process (a), in which part of the water evaporates and the volume increases while the saturated state of the water vapour is maintained, and in the isothermal compression process (c), in which part of the water vapour condenses and the volume decreases, the pressures are constant, equal to the saturated vapour pressures $P$ and $P-\varDelta P$ at the respective temperatures.

Q1. Let the volume per mole of water in the liquid state at the saturated vapour pressure $P$ at temperature $T$ be $V_{\mathrm{liq}}$, the volume per mole of water vapour be $V_{\mathrm{gas}}$, and the heat of vaporization per mole of water be $L$. Express the amount of heat $Q_1$ absorbed by the working substance in process (a) in terms of these quantities.

The work $W$ done by the system on the outside during one cycle is equal to the area of the part enclosed by the quadrilateral in the state diagram of Fig. 2. Now suppose that the pressure change $\varDelta P$ and the temperature change $\varDelta T$ are sufficiently small, so that the work $W$ can be approximated as

$$W\fallingdotseq(V_2-V_1)\varDelta P$$

Q2. Using the fact that the thermal efficiency (1) of the Carnot cycle is equal to equation (2), derive the relation

$$\frac{\varDelta P}{\varDelta T}\fallingdotseq\frac{L}{T\,(V_{\mathrm{gas}}-V_{\mathrm{liq}})} \qquad (3)$$

You may use the approximation $\varDelta T\ll T$.

Taking the limit in which the temperature change $\varDelta T$ in equation (3) is infinitesimal, we obtain the following relation, which expresses the temperature dependence of the saturated vapour pressure.

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T}=\frac{L}{T\,(V_{\mathrm{gas}}-V_{\mathrm{liq}})} \qquad (4)$$

This equation is called the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.

Q3. Show that, if the volume of water $V_{\mathrm{liq}}$ can be neglected compared with the volume of water vapour $V_{\mathrm{gas}}$, and the equation of state of water vapour is approximated by that of an ideal gas, equation (4) becomes

$$\frac{1}{P}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T}=\frac{L}{RT^2} \qquad (5)$$

Here $R$ is the gas constant.

Q4. Let the saturated vapour pressure of water at temperature $T_0$ be $P_0$. Assuming that the heat of vaporization $L$ does not depend on temperature, integrate equation (5) and show that the saturated vapour pressure at temperature $T$ is given by

$$P=P_0\exp\left[\left(\frac{1}{T_0}-\frac{1}{T}\right)\frac{L}{R}\right] \qquad (6)$$

Here $\exp[x]$ denotes the exponential function $\mathrm{e}^x$.

Q5. According to measurements, the saturated vapour pressures of water at $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are $0.611\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{Pa}$ and $3.17\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{Pa}$, respectively. Using equation (6), find the heat of vaporization $L$ of water. Also find the saturated vapour pressure $P_{27}$ at $27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Use the value given in Table 1 for the gas constant $R$.

The measured value of the heat of vaporization of water is $L=4.40\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{J/mol}$ at temperature $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and it is known to decrease slightly with temperature. Below, answer the questions using $L=4.4\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{J/mol}$ as the value of the heat of vaporization of water, independently of temperature.

Q6. The heat of vaporization $L$ of water minus the work $P(V_{\mathrm{gas}}-V_{\mathrm{liq}})$ done on the outside may be regarded as the energy needed for water molecules to escape from the water. Find the energy $U_{\mathrm{v}}$ needed for one water molecule to escape from the water at $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Also, how many times the average value $K_{25}$ of the translational kinetic energy of a water molecule at that temperature is this $U_{\mathrm{v}}$? As in Q3, you may neglect $V_{\mathrm{liq}}$ compared with $V_{\mathrm{gas}}$. Use the numerical values of the physical constants in Table 1 if necessary.

Amount of water in the atmosphere and the possibility of heavy rain due to global warming

When the temperature of the sea water of the South Pacific rises by $2^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, from $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, let us estimate how much the amount of water vapour in the air above increases per unit area, and consider how much the amount of rain may increase due to the rise of the sea-water temperature.

Let the air temperature (absolute temperature) at altitude $x$ be $T(x)$, the atmospheric pressure $P_{\mathrm{a}}(x)$, and the partial pressure of water vapour in the atmosphere $P(x)$. Writing $T(x)=T(0)f(x)$, according to observations the average decrease of air temperature with altitude $x$ is given by

$$f(x)=1-\frac{\alpha}{T(0)}x\,,\qquad(\alpha=6.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{K/m}) \qquad (7)$$

Here $T(0)$ is the air temperature at sea level ($x=0$). If we consider the range of the troposphere, $0\leqq x\leqq10^{4}\,\mathrm{m}$, as the altitude $x$, then even if the sea-surface temperature $T(0)$ is about $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the second term of $f(x)$ is $0\leqq\dfrac{\alpha}{T(0)}x<0.22$, which is considerably smaller than the first term.

Q7. Let $P_{\mathrm{s}}(x)$ be the saturated vapour pressure of equation (6) for the air temperature $T(x)$ at altitude $x$. When $1\gg\dfrac{\alpha}{T(0)}x$, it can be approximated as

$$P_{\mathrm{s}}(x)\fallingdotseq P_{\mathrm{s}}(0)\,\mathrm{e}^{-Ax} \qquad (8)$$

Find $A$. Express it, apart from its dependence on $T(0)$, as a numerical value with units.

Q8. We want to find the dependence of the atmospheric pressure $P_{\mathrm{a}}(x)$ on the altitude $x$.

(a) Letting the density of the atmosphere at altitude $x$ be $\rho(x)$, derive the equation of balance between the force due to pressure and gravity.

(b) By solving it, show that

$$P_{\mathrm{a}}(x)=P_{\mathrm{a}}(0)\exp\left[-\frac{M_{\mathrm{a}}g}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T(0)}\int_0^x\frac{1}{f(x')}\,\mathrm{d}x'\right]$$

Here $P_{\mathrm{a}}(0)$ is the atmospheric pressure at sea level. Take air to be an ideal gas whose average mass per molecule is $M_{\mathrm{a}}$.

(c) With the approximation $f(x)\fallingdotseq1$, it can be expressed as

$$P_{\mathrm{a}}(x)\fallingdotseq P_{\mathrm{a}}(0)\,\mathrm{e}^{-Bx} \qquad (9)$$

Find this $B$. Express it, apart from its dependence on $T(0)$, as a numerical value with units. Use the numerical values of the physical quantities in Table 1 if necessary.

Now, using these expressions, let us find the altitude at which the partial pressure of water vapour in the atmosphere becomes equal to the saturated vapour pressure.

First, as the altitude increases, the atmospheric pressure $P_{\mathrm{a}}(x)$ decreases. We assume that the partial pressure of water vapour in the atmosphere $P(x)$ also decreases in proportion to the atmospheric pressure, that is,

$$\frac{P(x)}{P(0)}=\frac{P_{\mathrm{a}}(x)}{P_{\mathrm{a}}(0)} \qquad (10)$$

Q9. Let the ratio of the partial pressure of water vapour $P(0)$ to the saturated vapour pressure $P_{\mathrm{s}}(0)$ at sea level be $q$ (the humidity), that is,

$$q=\frac{P(0)}{P_{\mathrm{s}}(0)}\,,\qquad(0\leqq q\leqq1)$$

(a) Using the expressions already obtained for the variation with altitude of $P_{\mathrm{s}}(x)$ and $P_{\mathrm{a}}(x)$ (equations (8) and (9), respectively), find the expression for the altitude $x_{\mathrm{s}}$ at which the partial pressure of water vapour becomes equal to the saturated vapour pressure.

(b) When $q=0.6$ and the sea-surface temperature is $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, what is the altitude $x_{\mathrm{s}}$ at which the partial pressure of water vapour becomes equal to the saturated vapour pressure?

The result of Q9 means that when $q<1$, that is, even if the humidity at sea level is not $100\%$, the humidity reaches $100\%$ high up, and clouds form above that altitude. That is, $x_{\mathrm{s}}$ is "the altitude at which clouds form", and is called the "cloud-base altitude". When the humidity at sea level is $100\%$, the cloud base is at sea level.

Finally, assuming $q=1$, that is, that the partial pressure of water vapour at sea level has reached the saturated vapour pressure, let us find the mass $F$ $[\mathrm{kg/m^2}]$ of water vapour per unit area contained in the atmosphere above the sea surface.

Q10. Neglecting the contribution of clouds, the mass density $\rho_{\mathrm{s}}(x)$ of saturated water vapour in the atmosphere at altitude $x$ is given by $\dfrac{N_{\mathrm{A}}MP_{\mathrm{s}}(x)}{RT(x)}$. Here $M$ is the mass of a water molecule.

(a) Under the approximation $\rho_{\mathrm{s}}(x)\fallingdotseq\dfrac{N_{\mathrm{A}}MP_{\mathrm{s}}(x)}{RT(0)}$, find the expression for $F$. Assume that this approximation holds for any $x$.

(b) Find the values $F_{25}$ and $F_{27}$ of $F$ when the sea-water temperature is $25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $27^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Use the values of the saturated vapour pressure given in Q5 and the one found there.

The amount of water vapour $F$ contained in the atmosphere is called the precipitable water. The above result suggests that the amount of rain increases with the rise of the sea-water temperature. However, how precipitation in each region changes due to global warming is not simple, since complicated processes not considered here, such as the formation of clouds and the flow of the atmosphere, are also involved.

problems.title: Problem 4: Luminosity and surface temperature of main-sequence stars
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (70 points)

Luminosity and surface temperature of main-sequence stars

Let us consider the physics of stars, the fundamental building blocks of the universe.

Fig. 1 is called the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram (HR diagram), and shows the surface temperature and the luminosity (the amount of energy radiated per unit time) of individual stars. By historical convention, the temperature on the horizontal axis of the HR diagram is displayed decreasing from left to right. Since a sequence from upper left to lower right is prominently seen, this sequence is called the main sequence, and the stars distributed on it are called main-sequence stars. Let us consider the physical meaning of this main sequence, making appropriate use of the table of physical constants in Table 1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-4-fig1.jpg

[表面温度 [K] = surface temperature [K], ガイア絶対等級 = Gaia absolute magnitude, 光度 (太陽光度 = 1) = luminosity (solar luminosity = 1), 巨星分枝 = giant branch, 主系列 = main sequence, 白色矮星 = white dwarfs, 色指数 (BP−RP) = colour index (BP−RP), ←より青く = ← bluer, より赤く→ = redder →]

Fig. 1. The European Space Agency's observation satellite Gaia aims to make a precise three-dimensional map of the Galaxy, and is measuring the positions and motions of as many as 100 billion stars as well as various physical quantities. This figure is a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram (HR diagram) of stars measured by Gaia, with the luminosity $L$ of the stars, taking the solar luminosity as 1, on the right vertical axis, and the surface temperature $T_{\mathrm{e}}$ of the stars (in K) on the upper horizontal axis*1 (source: European Space Agency https://sci.esa.int/web/gaia/-/60198-gaia-hertzsprung-russell-diagram).

*1 The scale of the left vertical axis is the "Gaia absolute magnitude", in which only the effect of the distance measured by Gaia has been corrected for in the apparent brightness. The luminosity shown on the right vertical axis has been tentatively converted from it with the addition of other calibrations.

Table 1. Table of physical constants

$$\begin{array}{llll} \text{Name} & \text{Symbol} & \text{Value} & \text{Unit} \\ \hline \text{Speed of light in vacuum} & c & 3.00\times10^{8} & \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \\ \text{Gravitational constant} & G & 6.67\times10^{-11} & \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,kg^{-2}} \\ \text{Mass of the proton} & m_{\mathrm{p}} & 1.67\times10^{-27} & \mathrm{kg} \\ \text{Boltzmann constant} & k & 1.38\times10^{-23} & \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}} \\ \text{Avogadro constant} & N_{\mathrm{A}} & 6.02\times10^{23} & \mathrm{mol^{-1}} \\ \text{Radiation density constant} & a & 7.56\times10^{-16} & \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}\,s\,K^{-4}} \end{array}$$

In the following questions, a star consists of a ball of gas, and its mass is distributed spherically symmetrically about the centre. The symbols and values of the constants given in the table of physical constants may be used freely.

Q1. As in the schematic diagram of Fig. 2, take inside the star a sphere of radius $r$ and mass $m$ about the centre, and consider the spherical shell of thickness $\Delta r$ and mass $\Delta m$ just outside it. $\Delta r$ and $\Delta m$ are infinitesimal quantities, and the density in the shell is regarded as a constant value $\rho$. If terms of second and higher order, containing products of infinitesimal quantities, are dropped, the volume of the shell is $4\pi r^2\Delta r$, so

$$\Delta m=4\pi r^2\Delta r\rho$$

can be written.

By taking the limit $\varDelta m\to0$, express the derivative $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}m}$ in terms of $r$ and $\rho$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2022-4-fig2.png

[球殻 = spherical shell: 厚さ $\varDelta r$ = thickness $\varDelta r$, 質量 $\varDelta m$ = mass $\varDelta m$, 密度 $\rho$ = density $\rho$; 星の質量 $M$ = mass of the star $M$, 星の半径 $R$ = radius of the star $R$; 同心球 = concentric sphere: 質量 $m$ = mass $m$, 半径 $r$ = radius $r$]

Fig. 2. Schematic diagram of a cross-section of the star

Below, taking the mass $m$ as the independent variable, let us regard physical quantities such as the radius $r$ and the density $\rho$ as functions of $m$.

Q2. A star is in a state of mechanical equilibrium, in which the force by which gravity tends to contract it and the force due to the pressure of the gas acting to expand it balance each other. Since the gravitational force acting on the spherical shell is only that exerted by the inner gas sphere, taking outward as positive it is

$$-\frac{Gm\varDelta m}{r^2}$$

On the other hand, writing the gas pressure acting per unit area as $p$, the force due to the gas pressure acting on the shell, taking outward as positive, is the area of the shell $4\pi r^2$ multiplied by the difference $\varDelta p\equiv p(m+\varDelta m)-p(m)$ between the pressure $p(m)$ at the inner surface of the shell and the pressure $p(m+\varDelta m)$ at the outer surface,

$$-4\pi r^2\varDelta p$$

By taking the limit $\varDelta m\to0$, express the derivative $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}m}$ in terms of $m$ and $r$, and the physical constant $G$.

Q3. At the centre of the star, the mass is $m=0$ and the radius is $r(0)=0$. Let the density at the centre of the star be $\rho(0)=\rho_{\mathrm{c}}$ and the pressure $p(0)=p_{\mathrm{c}}$. On the other hand, at the surface of the star, the mass $m$ is equal to the total mass $M$ of the star, and, if the radius of the star is $R$, $r(M)=R$. Since the density $\rho(M)$ and the pressure $p(M)$ at the surface are sufficiently smaller than $\rho_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{c}}$, respectively, we set both $\rho(M)=0$ and $p(M)=0$.

(a) The derivative obtained in Q1 is expressed in the form

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}m}=f(r,\rho)$$

Taking the left-hand side $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}m}$ as the average rate of change of $r(m)$ between the centre and the surface of the star, and using for $r$ and $\rho$ on the right-hand side the averages of the values at the centre and at the surface of the star, express $\rho_{\mathrm{c}}$ in terms of $M$ and $R$.

(b) The derivative obtained in Q2 is expressed in the form

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}m}=g(m,r)$$

Taking the left-hand side $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}m}$ as the average rate of change of $p(m)$ between the centre and the surface of the star, and using for $m$ and $r$ on the right-hand side the averages of the values at the centre and at the surface of the star, express $p_{\mathrm{c}}$ in terms of $M$ and $R$, and the physical constant $G$.

(c) Taking the mass and the radius of the star to be about the present values for the Sun, $M=2\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $R=7\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}$, find rough values of $\rho_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{c}}$, each to 1 significant figure.

Q4. Let us assume that the star consists of hydrogen. In the central part of the star the temperature is high, so the hydrogen atoms are considered to be ionized into ions $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ and electrons $\mathrm{e}^{-}$. The gas can also be regarded as an ideal gas.

(a) Estimate the sum of the number densities (numbers of particles per unit volume) of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-}$ at the centre, and express the temperature $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ of the gas in terms of $M$ and $R$, and the physical constants $G$, $k$, $m_{\mathrm{p}}$.

(b) With $M=2\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $R=7\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}$, find a rough value of $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ to 1 significant figure.

The centre has a high temperature and the surface a low temperature, so energy necessarily flows from the inside to the outside. As a result, how brightly does a star shine? To consider this, let us first derive the derivative $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}m}$ of the temperature $T(m)$.

Q5. Here we treat all energy as being carried by the radiation of light (electromagnetic waves). The interior of a star is extremely opaque to light, and because of absorption and emission by ions and electrons, the path of light (photons) becomes extremely irregular (a random walk), and the distance it can advance outward in 1 second is only of the order of centimetres in the central part of the star. Let us consider the force that the spherical shell of gas of mass $\varDelta m$, radius $r(m)$ and thickness $\varDelta r$ receives from the radiation in this process.

The amount of radiation energy absorbed by the shell per unit time is proportional to the amount of energy incident on the shell per unit time (the radiative luminosity) $\ell(m)$ and to the thickness $\varDelta r$ of the shell, and also depends on the degree of opacity of the shell. So, if the opacity per unit density is $\kappa$ (with dimensions $[\text{length}]^{-1}[\text{density}]^{-1}$), the energy absorbed by the shell per unit time is expressed as

$$\kappa\rho\,\ell\varDelta r$$

Therefore, with the speed of light $c$, the shell receives from the radiation a force

$$F=\frac{\kappa\rho\,\ell}{c}\varDelta r$$

acting outward.

On the other hand, it is known that the radiation pressure $p_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is proportional to the fourth power of the temperature $T$. Its proportionality coefficient is $1/3$ of $a$, called the radiation density constant, and it is expressed as

$$p_{\mathrm{rad}}=\frac{a}{3}T^4$$

Therefore, since the outward force $F$ due to the radiation acting on the shell is the area of the shell $4\pi r^2$ multiplied by the difference $\varDelta p_{\mathrm{rad}}\equiv p_{\mathrm{rad}}(m+\varDelta m)-p_{\mathrm{rad}}(m)$ between the radiation pressure $p_{\mathrm{rad}}(m)$ at the inner surface of the shell and the radiation pressure $p_{\mathrm{rad}}(m+\varDelta m)$ at the outer surface, it can also be expressed, using the difference $\varDelta T\equiv T(m+\varDelta m)-T(m)$ between the temperature $T(m)$ at the inner surface and the temperature $T(m+\varDelta m)$ at the outer surface, as

$$F=-4\pi r^2\frac{4a}{3}T^3\varDelta T$$

Based on the above considerations, express the derivative $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}m}$ of the temperature $T(m)$ in terms of $\ell$, $r$, $T$, $\kappa$, and the physical constants $a$, $c$.

Q6. At the centre of the star, $\ell(0)=0$. Also, the radiative luminosity $\ell(M)$ at the surface of the star is nothing other than the luminosity $L$ of the star.

(a) The derivative obtained in Q5 is expressed in the form

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}m}=h(\ell,r,T,\kappa)$$

By replacing the derivative $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}m}$ on the left-hand side by the average rate of change of $T(m)$ between the centre and the surface of the star, using for $\ell$, $r$, $T$ on the right-hand side the averages of the values at the centre and at the surface of the star, and replacing $\kappa$ by its average value $\langle\kappa\rangle$ over the whole star, express the luminosity $L$ of the star in terms of $M$ and $\langle\kappa\rangle$, and the physical constants $a$, $c$, $G$, $k$, $m_{\mathrm{p}}$. Here, since the temperature at the surface of the star is sufficiently low compared with the temperature $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ at the centre, it may be regarded as 0.

(b) Taking the mass and the radius of the star to be about the present values for the Sun, $M=2\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $R=7\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}$, and $\langle\kappa\rangle=10^{2}\,\mathrm{m^2\,kg^{-1}}$, find a rough value of the luminosity $L$ of the star (in W) to 1 significant figure.

Q7. If the surface temperature of the star is $T_{\mathrm{e}}$, the radiation energy emitted by the star per unit time (the luminosity of the star) $L$ is proportional to the product of the fourth power of $T_{\mathrm{e}}$ and the surface area. Assuming that the radius $R$ of the star is proportional to the mass $M$ of the star, use the result of Q6(a) to find the dependence of $\langle\kappa\rangle^{-2}L$ on $T_{\mathrm{e}}$ (to what power of $T_{\mathrm{e}}$ it is proportional).

Based on the age of the oldest meteorites found on the Earth, the present age of the Sun is estimated to be 4.7 billion years. As a reasonable explanation of such a long lifetime, the energy source of main-sequence stars is considered to be the nuclear fusion reaction from hydrogen to helium in the central part.

Even if a star consisted only of hydrogen when it was born, when the nuclear fusion reaction of hydrogen proceeds until the hydrogen in the central part of the star is exhausted, eventually helium nuclei come to undergo nuclear fusion reactions and produce carbon nuclei. Similarly, when the helium is exhausted, carbon will come to undergo nuclear fusion. However, the HR diagram shows that stars in the main-sequence stage, in which the hydrogen nuclear fusion reaction is taking place, are overwhelmingly numerous. Why is this? Among several contributing factors, let us consider here that the time during which nuclear fusion reactions are the energy source of the star differs according to the kind of nucleus.

Q8. Suppose that, both when the energy source of the star is the nuclear fusion of helium nuclei in the central part and when it is the nuclear fusion of carbon nuclei, the luminosity of the star is of the same order as when it is a main-sequence star. In the nuclear fusion reaction of hydrogen, one helium nucleus is produced from four hydrogen nuclei, and in the nuclear fusion reaction of helium, one carbon nucleus is produced from three helium nuclei. Noting this, and that the atomic weights of hydrogen ($^{1}\mathrm{H}$), helium ($^{4}\mathrm{He}$) and carbon ($^{12}\mathrm{C}$) are 1.008, 4.002 and 12.000, respectively, find the ratio of the length of the time during which the nuclear fusion reaction of hydrogen nuclei is the energy source to the time during which the nuclear fusion reaction of helium nuclei is the energy source.

problems.title: Problem 1: Mechanics and the renormalization group
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (75 points)

Mechanics and the renormalization group

It was K. G. Wilson who greatly developed the theory of the renormalization group, which had emerged in research on quantum field theory, by merging it with scaling theory and the idea of coarse-graining that had advanced in research on phase transitions; he received the 1982 Nobel Prize in Physics. Here, using a problem of Newtonian mechanics, we introduce the way of thinking of the renormalization group.

[I] Artificial satellite

Let us consider the following. Suppose that a particle of mass $m$ is thrown horizontally from the top of a cliff. Since the Earth is not flat but round, when the speed becomes large, the particle will keep going around the Earth without falling to the ground. As shown in Fig. 1, take the centre of the Earth as the origin, and launch the particle horizontally with speed $U_0$ from a point at distance $R$ from the origin. Here, horizontal means the direction perpendicular to the line joining the origin and the particle. Since the universal gravitational force, an inverse-square force directed towards the origin, acts, the Newton equation describing the motion is given by

$$m\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\overrightarrow{r}(t)=-mK\frac{\overrightarrow{r}(t)}{|\overrightarrow{r}(t)|^3} \qquad (1)$$

$\overrightarrow{r}(t)$ is the three-dimensional position vector at time $t$, and $K$ is a constant of proportionality which, using the gravitational constant $G$ and the mass $M$ of the Earth, can be written $K=GM$. Let us write $R_{\max}(U_0)$ for the distance from the origin when the particle is farthest from the origin. Once the initial speed $U_0$ is fixed, this maximum distance is uniquely determined.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Q1. Let $U_{\max}$ be the speed of the particle at the point farthest from the origin. Write down the law of constant areal velocity (conservation of angular momentum) and the law of conservation of energy that hold among $U_0, R, U_{\max}, R_{\max}(U_0)$. Note that when the particle is farthest from the origin, the velocity has no vertical component.

Q2. Find the initial speed $U_{01}$ at which the body begins to go around the Earth (the first cosmic velocity) and the initial speed $U_{02}$ at which it begins to escape from the Earth (the second cosmic velocity). Taking the gravitational constant $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}}$, the mass of the Earth $M=5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and the radius of the Earth $R=6.38\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$, calculate $U_{01}$ and $U_{02}$.

Q3. For a given $U_0$, find the equation that determines $R_{\max}(U_0)$. It suffices to eliminate $U_{\max}$ from the equations of the two conservation laws. Also, show in a graph the approximate behaviour of $R_{\max}(U_0)$ in the range $U_{01}\sim U_{02}$. Also, substitute $U_0=U_{01}$ into the obtained expression for $R_{\max}(U_0)$ to calculate $R_{\max}(U_{01})$, and confirm that it takes the value it should.

Q4. When $U_0$ approaches $U_{02}$ $(U_0<U_{02})$, $R_{\max}(U_0)$ diverges as

$$R_{\max}(U_0)\fallingdotseq\frac{C}{(U_{02}-U_0)^{\theta}}$$

Find the coefficient $C$ and the exponent $\theta$.

Below, we aim to find $\theta$ with the way of thinking of the renormalization group.

[II] Scale transformation

For the position vector $\overrightarrow{r}$ and the time $t$, with $\alpha$ and $s$ constants, consider the new variables $\overrightarrow{r}'$ and $t'$, each a constant multiple of the original,

$$\overrightarrow{r}'=\alpha\overrightarrow{r},\quad t'=\alpha^{s}t$$

Since this transformation corresponds to transforming the original variables $(\overrightarrow{r},t)$ into variables $(\overrightarrow{r}',t')$ measured with a different measure (scale), it is called a scale transformation.

Q5. Show that the condition for the equation of motion (1), when expressed in the scale-transformed variables $(\overrightarrow{r}',t')$, to be independent of $\alpha$ and exactly the same as the original equation is $s=\dfrac{3}{2}$. That the form of an equation does not change when it is expressed in scale-transformed variables is called scale invariance. Below, we proceed with the discussion using the value $s=\dfrac{3}{2}$ found here.

Here, as in [I], consider launching the particle from a point at distance $R$ from the origin. Suppose that the initial velocity has not only a horizontal component $U>0$ but also a vertical component (in the direction away from the origin) $V>0$. Setting $(U,V)=(U_0,0)$ gives the same initial condition as in [I]. When the scale transformation with $0<\alpha<1$ is applied to this initial condition, the above initial condition is mapped, as shown in Fig. 2, to the new initial condition of launching the particle from a point at distance $R'=\alpha R$ from the origin with the initial velocity

$$(U',V')=(\alpha^{-1/2}U,\alpha^{-1/2}V)$$

This is because, since $\overrightarrow{r}'=\alpha\overrightarrow{r}$, $t'=\alpha^{s}t$, the speed is transformed as $U'=\alpha^{1-s}U=\alpha^{-1/2}U$. By scale invariance, this particle also moves according to the same equation (1) as the particle before the scale transformation. Let the velocity when the trajectory of the scale-transformed particle reaches the distance $R$ from the origin be

$$(\widetilde{U},\widetilde{V})$$

This depends on the initial condition $(U,V)$ before the scale transformation and on the parameter $\alpha$ of the scale transformation.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Q6. Write down the equation expressing the law of constant areal velocity for the time evolution of the scale-transformed system from $(R',(U',V'))$ to $(R,(\widetilde{U},\widetilde{V}))$. Also, setting $\alpha=e^{-\tau}$ and expressing the parameter $\alpha$ of the scale transformation by $\tau>0$, show from the law of constant areal velocity that $\widetilde{U}(\tau)$ satisfies the following relation containing a derivative (differential equation).

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}\widetilde{U}(\tau)=-\frac{\widetilde{U}(\tau)}{2} \qquad (2)$$

Q7. Similarly, write down the equation expressing the law of conservation of energy, and show that the following differential equation for $\widetilde{V}(\tau)$ is obtained.

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}\widetilde{V}(\tau)=\frac{\widetilde{V}(\tau)}{2}-\frac{K}{R\widetilde{V}(\tau)}+\frac{\widetilde{U}(\tau)^2}{\widetilde{V}(\tau)} \qquad (3)$$

The velocity $(\widetilde{U}(\tau),\widetilde{V}(\tau))$ of the scale-transformed particle at distance $R$ can be regarded as the velocity obtained as the result of "renormalizing" (folding in), by the scale transformation, the trajectory of the particle before the scale transformation from distance $R$ until it reaches $e^{\tau}R$ into a trajectory up to distance $R$. Equations (2) and (3) express how the velocity of the scale-transformed particle at distance $R$ changes when, as the particle reaches farther and farther, we successively apply scale transformations and keep renormalizing the trajectory so that the distance from the origin is always $R$; they are called the renormalization group equations.

Even if you cannot solve Q6 and Q7, you can proceed with the following questions starting from equations (2) and (3). To simplify the equations, we make $\widetilde{U}(\tau),\widetilde{V}(\tau)$ dimensionless quantities with $\sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{R}}$, which has the dimension of speed, as the unit, and denote them $u(\tau),v(\tau)$. That is,

$$u(\tau)=\frac{\widetilde{U}(\tau)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{R}}},\quad v(\tau)=\frac{\widetilde{V}(\tau)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{R}}} \qquad (4)$$

Q8. Show that, using the dimensionless variables, equations (2) and (3) can be rewritten as follows.

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}u(\tau)=-\frac{u}{2} \qquad (5)$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}v(\tau)=\frac{v}{2}+\frac{1}{v}\Big(u^2-\frac{1}{2}\Big) \qquad (6)$$

Working with the dimensionless equations makes the equations simple and gives a better overview, but note that when analysing the results it is necessary to consider the meaning of the original variables with the dimensions restored.

We interpret the set of renormalization group equations (5), (6) by regarding $\tau$ as a time-like variable, so that $u(\tau),v(\tau)$ change as time advances.

Q9. In this case, a point that does not change even as the "time" $\tau$ advances is called a fixed point and is written $(u^*,v^*)$. $u^*=0$ is found immediately. Find $v^*(>0)$.

To analyse the motion according to the renormalization group equations very close to the fixed point, we take $u(\tau)-u^*$, $v(\tau)-v^*$, measured from the fixed point, as new variables. However, for $u(\tau)$, since the fixed point is $u^*=0$, we use $u$ as it is. That is, we describe the motion with the two variables

$$u(\tau),\quad w(\tau)\equiv v(\tau)-v^*$$

We find the differential equations obeyed by these two variables $u(\tau),w(\tau)$ near the fixed point. In this case, $u(\tau),w(\tau)$ are small quantities, $u(\tau)\ll1$, $w(\tau)\ll1$, and their second-order quantities may be neglected compared with first-order quantities. The differential equations written with only these first-order quantities are called the linearized renormalization group equations.

Q10. Find the linearized renormalization group equation for $w(\tau)$ when $w$ is small. Note that the differential equation for the deviation of $u(\tau)$ from the fixed point $u^*=0$ is linear, as given in equation (5).

Let us examine the time evolution on the $u-v$ plane of the renormalization group equations (5), (6). As $\tau$ increases, $u(\tau)$ decreases, by equation (5), as $u(\tau)\propto e^{-\tau/2}$. If we trace back the flow that is drawn into the fixed point, it hits the $u$ axis; call this point $(u_{\mathrm{c}},0)$. A flow starting from a point on the $u$ axis to the right of $(u_{\mathrm{c}},0)$ deviates to above the flow drawn into the fixed point and goes up along the $v$ axis from the upper right of the fixed point. On the other hand, a flow starting from a point to the left of $(u_{\mathrm{c}},0)$ goes down along the $v$ axis from the lower right of the fixed point and hits the $u$ axis again. In correspondence with the problem setting of [I], this corresponds to the problem of throwing the body with initial velocity $(u_0,0)$ ($u_0=u(0)$ is $U_0$ made dimensionless), and the value $u_{\mathrm{c}}$ of $u_0$ that qualitatively changes the renormalization group flow is nothing other than the second cosmic velocity $u_{02}$.

Below, consider the case where $u(0)\,(<u_{\mathrm{c}})$ is brought closer to $u_{\mathrm{c}}$. If the "instant" at which the solution curve bends downwards and $v$ becomes $0$ (crosses the $u$ axis) is $\tau_{\max}$, then from the properties of the scale transformation, the distance of the highest point is given by $R_{\max}=e^{\tau_{\max}}R$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-1-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

Therefore, to see the behaviour in which $R_{\max}$ becomes infinite as $u(0)$ approaches $u_{\mathrm{c}}$, it suffices to examine the behaviour in which $\tau_{\max}$ becomes infinite. Let us analyse the solution curve by dividing it into three regions. These are the three regions: from the starting point ($\tau=0$) to the instant ($\tau_1$) at which it enters the neighbourhood of the fixed point; while it is moving in the neighbourhood of the fixed point (from $\tau_1$ to $\tau_2$); and from the instant ($\tau_2$) at which it leaves the neighbourhood of the fixed point to $\tau_{\max}$ at which it crosses the $u$ axis. The neighbourhood of the fixed point is the region $0<u<\delta$ and $0<|w|<\delta$ shown in grey in Fig. 3. If $\delta$ is a sufficiently small quantity ($\delta\ll1$), then in this neighbourhood of the fixed point the linearized renormalization group equations for $u,w$ can be used.

When the starting point $u(0)$ is brought closer to $u_{\mathrm{c}}$, the solution curve hardly changes its location. $\tau_1$ approaches a certain finite value, and $\tau_{\max}-\tau_2$ also approaches a certain finite value and never diverges. What becomes infinite is the time $\tau_2-\tau_1$ during which it is moving in the neighbourhood of the fixed point, so it suffices to examine the behaviour in which $\tau_2$ becomes infinite. The instant $\tau_1$ of entering the neighbourhood of the fixed point is determined by $u(\tau_1)=u_0e^{-\tau_1/2}=\delta$. The magnitude of $w(\tau_1)$ at this time is of course a small quantity, determined as a function of $u(0)$. The instant $\tau_2$ of leaving the neighbourhood of the fixed point is determined by

$$w(\tau_2)=-\delta \qquad (7)$$

Q11. By solving the linearized renormalization group equation for $w$ found in Q10 and comparing with equation (7), show that

$$e^{\tau_2}=-\frac{e^{\tau_1}\delta}{w(\tau_1)}$$

$w(\tau_1)$ is a function of $u(0)$ and should be $0$ when $u(0)=u_{\mathrm{c}}$; therefore, expanding it in a Taylor series, it can be written

$$w(\tau_1)=C(u(0)-u_{\mathrm{c}})+O((u(0)-u_{\mathrm{c}})^2)$$

$C$ is a constant. Also, $O(x^2)$ means that, as $x$ approaches $0$, the quantity is of magnitude $x^2$ or smaller.

Q12. Substitute the expression of the Taylor series expansion of $w(\tau_1)$ into the expression for $e^{\tau_2}$, show that the diverging behaviour of $R_{\max}$ is expressed as

$$R_{\max}\propto(u_{\mathrm{c}}-u(0))^{-\theta}$$

and find $\theta$. Here "$\propto$" denotes proportionality.

Q13. Looking at the discussion so far, we see that the exponent of the divergence was determined from the coefficient of the linear term in the linearized renormalization group equation for $w$. If the coefficient of the linearized renormalization group equation for $w$ were $k$, that is, if

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}w=kw$$

what would the exponent be?

Note that in the argument for finding the exponent, we did not use the fact that $u_{02}$ is the value found in Q2. In fact, the differential equations (5), (6) can be solved exactly, and one can show that $u_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the $u_{02}$ found in Q2 as a problem of mechanics. The linear coefficient of the renormalization group equations near the fixed point (so to speak, a microscopic property) directly determines the exponent of the very large-scale behaviour of the system (so to speak, a macroscopic property). This shows the uniqueness and power of the renormalization group method, which other methods do not have.

In general, the procedure of the renormalization group consists of:

1. Define the renormalization group transformation.
2. Find the fixed point.
3. Find the linearized renormalization group transformation by approximation in the neighbourhood of the fixed point.
4. From its linear coefficient, find the exponent of the divergence of the physical quantity.

As mentioned above, it has achieved success in research on critical phenomena of phase transitions and elsewhere, for example in the calculation of critical exponents.

problems.title: Problem 2: Propagation of electromagnetic waves and pressure
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (75 points)

Propagation of electromagnetic waves and pressure

A Faraday's law (of electromagnetic induction) and Ampère's law

A.1 Faraday's law (of electromagnetic induction)

If the magnetic flux through a closed circuit is $\mathit{\Phi}\,[\mathrm{Wb}]$, the electromagnetically induced electromotive force $V\,[\mathrm{V}]$ produced in the closed circuit is expressed by the time derivative of the magnetic flux $\mathit{\Phi}$ as

$$V=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathit{\Phi} \qquad (1)$$

Here, the direction of the magnetic flux and the direction of the closed circuit are related by the right-hand screw rule. The minus sign means that the electromotive force is in the direction that drives a current which opposes the change of the magnetic flux.

On the other hand, the electromotive force $V$ is given, as the line integral (see [Note]) of the component of the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}\,[\mathrm{V/m}]$ along the direction of the circuit, by

$$V=\oint\overrightarrow{E}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{s}$$

Therefore, Faraday's law (of electromagnetic induction) is expressed in the following form.

$$\oint\overrightarrow{E}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{s}=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathit{\Phi} \qquad (2)$$

[Note] Divide the curve $\ell$ going from point P1 to point P2 into $\{\overrightarrow{s}_i\}_{i=1,\ldots N}$ and take the sum $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{E}_i\cdot\overrightarrow{s}_i$ of the scalar products of the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}_i$ at each point and $\overrightarrow{s}_i$. $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{s}_i$ is the vector going from P1 to P2. The limit of this sum of scalar products when the division is made infinitely fine is written as the right-hand side below,

$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{E}_i\cdot\overrightarrow{s}_i=\int_{\mathrm{P1}}^{\mathrm{P2}}\overrightarrow{E}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{s}$$

and is called "the line integral from P1 to P2 of the component of the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ tangential to the curve $\ell$". The symbol $\oint$ indicates going once around a closed curve.

To drive a current by an electromotive force, a physical circuit is needed, but independently of the existence of a physical body, an electric field satisfying equation (2) is produced on a circuit considered in space. Below, "circuit" has this meaning.

A.2 Ampère's law

The magnetic field lines of the magnetic field $\overrightarrow{H}\,[\mathrm{A/m}]$ produced by a steady straight current of magnitude $I\,[\mathrm{A}]$ are concentric circles centred on the current in a plane perpendicular to the current, and their direction is related to the direction of the current by the right-hand screw rule. The magnitude of the magnetic field at a point at distance $r\,[\mathrm{m}]$ from the current is

$$H=\frac{I}{2\pi r} \qquad (3)$$

Taking the line integral, once around, of the circumferential component of the magnetic field along a circle of radius $r$ centred on the current in a plane perpendicular to the current, we obtain

$$\oint\overrightarrow{H}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{s}=\frac{I}{2\pi r}\times2\pi r=I \qquad (4)$$

Here, the direction of the circle is taken to be related to the direction of the current by the right-hand screw rule. The meaning of the symbol $\oint$ is the same as in the case of Faraday's law.

Equation (4) was obtained for a circle centred on the current, with direction related to the direction of the current by the right-hand screw rule. In fact, equation (4) holds as it is even if the circle is replaced by an arbitrary closed circuit that goes once around the current and whose direction is related to the direction of the current by the right-hand screw rule. Let us show this.

Q1. Consider a closed circuit as in Fig. 1 on a plane perpendicular to the current. Focusing on a small part $\overrightarrow{s}_i$ of the closed circuit, show that, if the magnetic field there is $\overrightarrow{H}_i$ and, seen from the intersection of the current and the plane, $\overrightarrow{s}_i$ subtends an angle $\mathit{\Delta}\theta_i$ in the right-hand screw sense with respect to the direction of the current, then $\overrightarrow{H}_i\cdot\overrightarrow{s}_i=\dfrac{I}{2\pi}\mathit{\Delta}\theta_i$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1. A closed circuit on a plane perpendicular to the current

From Q1 we see that the integral once around is $I$.

$$\oint_{\text{closed circuit in the right-hand screw relation}}\overrightarrow{H}\cdot\mathrm{d}\overrightarrow{s}=I \qquad (5)$$

It can also be shown that the closed circuit need not lie in a single plane. Furthermore, when there are many currents passing through the closed circuit, the right-hand side becomes their sum. Equation (5) is called Ampère's law.

Below, $x, y, z$ are rectangular Cartesian coordinates (right-handed system).

Q2. As in Fig. 2, a uniform current in the $x$ direction flows in the $xy$ plane (the plane $z=0$) (the current is concentrated in the plane $z=0$). In the $y$ direction the current extends infinitely, and the magnitude of the current is $I_0\,[\mathrm{A/m}]$ per unit length in the $y$ direction. Show that the $x, y, z$ components of the magnetic field $\overrightarrow{H}$ in $z>0$ and $z<0$ are $\overrightarrow{H}(z>0)=\Big(0,\ -\dfrac{1}{2}I_0,\ 0\Big)$, $\overrightarrow{H}(z<0)=\Big(0,\ \dfrac{1}{2}I_0,\ 0\Big)$.

Hint: Try considering the current divided into small straight-line currents.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2. A uniform current flowing in the $x$ direction in the plane $z=0$

B Electromagnetic waves in vacuum and the displacement current

Suppose that in vacuum there exists an electromagnetic wave as in the following equations (6), (7), in which the electric field $\overrightarrow{E}$ has only an $x$ component $E_x$ and the magnetic field $\overrightarrow{H}$ has only a $y$ component $H_y$, propagating in the $z$ direction ($t$ is time). Within an $xy$ plane the electromagnetic field is uniform.

$$E_x=E_0\sin(kz-\omega t) \qquad (6)$$

$$H_y=H_0\sin(kz-\omega t) \qquad (7)$$

Here $\omega,\ k>0$, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, and the wavelength is $2\pi/k$ ($k$ is called the wave number).

Q3. Let the magnetic constant (permeability of vacuum) be $\mu_0$; then the magnetic flux density $\overrightarrow{B}$ is $\overrightarrow{B}=\mu_0\overrightarrow{H}$.
