Considering in the $xz$ plane a long thin rectangular closed circuit as in Fig. 3, with its long sides parallel to the $\pm x$ direction, and using Faraday's law (2), show that the ratio of $H_0$ to $E_0$ is $f_0=\dfrac{H_0}{E_0}=\dfrac{k}{\mu_0\omega}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3. A long thin rectangular closed circuit in the $xz$ plane

Now, suppose that the magnetic field of equation (7) were produced by a current; what kind of current would it be?

Q4. Consider in the $yz$ plane a long thin rectangular closed circuit as in Fig. 4, with its long sides parallel to the $\pm y$ direction. Show that, according to Ampère's law (5), it suffices that there exist, as the current density in the $x$ direction (the quantity of electric charge passing through the $yz$ plane in the $x$ direction per unit time and per unit area),

$$-\frac{k^2}{\mu_0\omega}E_0\cos(kz-\omega t) \qquad (8)$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4. A long thin rectangular closed circuit in the $yz$ plane

When the electromagnetic wave of equations (6), (7) propagates in vacuum, no current actually flows, so Ampère's law (5), which is a relation between a steady current and a magnetic field, needs to be corrected when there is time variation. Maxwell discovered that the time variation of the electric flux density also acts as a current, and showed that, if this is included on the right-hand side, equation (5) holds also when there is time variation (the Ampère–Maxwell law). The time derivative of the electric flux density $\varepsilon_0\overrightarrow{E}$ at each point is called the electric flux current density. Here, $\varepsilon_0$ is the electric constant (permittivity of vacuum).

In a wave motion such as equations (6), (7), the phase is equal on the plane $z=\dfrac{\omega}{k}t+(\text{constant})$, and the surface of equal phase (equiphase surface) advances in the $z$ direction with speed $\dfrac{\omega}{k}$. In general, the speed $\dfrac{\omega}{k}$ at which the equiphase surface advances is called the phase velocity.

The phase velocity of electromagnetic waves in vacuum is the speed of light $c$. Therefore, there is the relation $\omega=ck$. Using this and $c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}}$, we see that equation (8) is the electric flux current density in the $x$ direction

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varepsilon_0E_0\sin(kz-\omega t)=-\omega\varepsilon_0E_0\cos(kz-\omega t) \qquad (9)$$

Equations (6), (7) are an electromagnetic wave with an electric field in the $x$ direction and a magnetic field in the $y$ direction, propagating in the $z$ direction; the following electromagnetic wave ($\phi_0$ is a constant), with an electric field in the $y$ direction and a magnetic field in the $x$ direction,

$$E'_y=E'_0\sin(kz-\omega t+\phi_0), \qquad (10)$$

$$H'_x=-f_0E'_0\sin(kz-\omega t+\phi_0) \qquad (11)$$

also propagates in the $z$ direction with the same phase velocity.

Q5. When $E_0=E'_0\ (\neq0)$, we want to superpose the electromagnetic wave (6), (7) and the electromagnetic wave (10), (11) to make an electromagnetic wave in which the vector representing the electric field describes a circle in a plane perpendicular to the $z$ axis (a circularly polarized electromagnetic wave). Find the value of $\phi_0$ $(0\leqq\phi_0<2\pi)$.

C Electromagnetic waves in matter

In space there is an electrically neutral, uniform gas consisting of positively and negatively charged particles. The positive charges are positive ions and the negative charges are electrons; the number density of electrons (number of particles per unit volume) is $n$, and the charge of one electron is $-e$ and its mass is $m$. In this case, what kind of influence does the electromagnetic wave considered in B receive? Assume that the thermal motion and recombination of the positively and negatively charged particles can be neglected, and that, since the mass of the positive ions is sufficiently large compared with that of the electrons, their motion can also be neglected. Also, the amplitude of the electromagnetic wave is assumed to be sufficiently small.

If we consider how the electromagnetic wave expressed by equations (6), (7) in vacuum changes, in the present case the current density produced by the motion of the electrons due to the electric field (6) is added to the electric flux current density (9). Therefore, the relation between $\omega$ and $k$ becomes different from $\omega=ck$ (however, it is still true that the time derivative of the electric flux density at each point is the electric flux current density).

Q6. (a) When there is the electric field of equation (6), find the current density $j_x(z,t)$ in the $x$ direction due to the electrons. Assume that the time average of $j_x(z,t)$ is $0$.

(b) In the present case, the sum of the electric flux current density $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varepsilon_0E_x=-\omega\varepsilon_0E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)$ and $j_x(z,t)$ contributes to the right-hand side of equation (5). Noting that there is no change in Faraday's law, show that the relation between $\omega$ and $k$ becomes as follows.

$$\omega^2=c^2k^2+\frac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m} \qquad (12)$$

According to equation (12), in order to propagate as an electromagnetic wave, the angular frequency must satisfy $\omega\geqq\sqrt{\dfrac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}}$. For example, when an electromagnetic wave of angular frequency $\omega<\sqrt{\dfrac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}}$ is incident from vacuum on a region containing charged particles, it is reflected at the boundary (surface) of that region and does not propagate into the region.

Q7. In the following cases, find, to one significant figure, the value of the angular frequency $\sqrt{\dfrac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}}$ and the wavelength in vacuum of an electromagnetic wave having that angular frequency.

(a) The case of copper, with free electrons of number density $n=9\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$

(b) The case of the ionosphere, with electrons of number density $n=1\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$

You may use the following numerical values as approximations: speed of light in vacuum $c=3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, magnitude of the electron charge $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, electron mass $m=9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, electric constant (permittivity of vacuum) $\varepsilon_0=8.9\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$.

Q8. The region $z>0$ is filled with many thin conducting wires in the $x$ direction; on average, electrons of number density $n$ are present, but the motion of the electrons is restricted to the $x$ direction only. When $\omega<\sqrt{\dfrac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0m}}$ and a circularly polarized electromagnetic wave as in Q5 comes from the vacuum region $z<0$, what kind of electromagnetic wave results in the region $z>0$?

D Reflection of electromagnetic waves and the force exerted by electromagnetic waves

You probably know from everyday experience that visible light is reflected at the surface of a metal. Now suppose that the region $z>0$ is a metal and that the electromagnetic wave (light) given by equations (6), (7) travels from the region $z<0$ (vacuum) in the positive direction of the $z$ axis and is reflected at the metal surface $z=0$.

Since a metal is a conductor, the components of the electric field along the metal surface ($x$, $y$ components) should be $0$. The electromagnetic wave must satisfy this condition. To satisfy this condition, we note that in vacuum the following electromagnetic wave propagates in the $-z$ direction.

$$\begin{aligned}(x\text{ component of the electric field})&=E'_0\sin(-kz-\omega t)\\(y\text{ component of the magnetic field})&=-f_0E'_0\sin(-kz-\omega t)\end{aligned}$$

If, in the vacuum region $z<0$, in addition to the electromagnetic wave of equations (6), (7), there exists the following reflected wave with $E'_0=-E_0$, the condition at $z=0$ can be satisfied.

$$\begin{aligned}(x\text{ component of the electric field of the reflected wave})&=-E_0\sin(-kz-\omega t)\\(y\text{ component of the magnetic field of the reflected wave})&=f_0E_0\sin(-kz-\omega t)\end{aligned}$$

Q9. In the present case, since the electromagnetic field is zero inside the metal, the magnetic field in the $y$ direction is discontinuous at the metal surface as follows.

$$H_y(z<0)=2f_0E_0\sin(-\omega t) \qquad (13)$$

$$H_y(z>0)=0 \qquad (14)$$

Therefore, a current flows in the $x$ direction on the metal surface ($z=0$). Using Ampère's law of equation (5), find the current $I_S\,[\mathrm{A/m}]$ flowing per unit length in the $y$ direction.

Since the current $I_S$ on the metal surface receives a force from the magnetic field of the electromagnetic wave, a force from the electromagnetic wave acts on the metal surface. However, since, as in Q2, $I_S$ itself also produces a magnetic field, when finding the force that $I_S$ receives, the magnetic field acting on $I_S$ must be taken as the magnetic field of equations (13), (14) minus the magnetic field produced by $I_S$ itself.

Q10. Find the direction of the force acting per unit area of the metal surface, and the time average of its magnitude.

It can be considered that a force such as that found in Q10 acts on the metal surface because the electromagnetic wave has momentum. This has been confirmed by various experiments and observations.

problems.title: Problem 3: Another Einstein relation — Estimating the Avogadro constant from Brownian motion
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (75 points)

Another Einstein relation — Estimating the Avogadro constant from Brownian motion —

Hearing "the Einstein relation", many people probably think of "the mass–energy equivalence $E=mc^2$". However, in the field of statistical physics there is another, different relation that is called "the Einstein relation". It is the formula giving the relation between the diffusion coefficient $D$ and the mobility $\mu$ of a colloidal particle undergoing Brownian motion,

$$D=\frac{R}{N_{\mathrm{A}}}\,T\,\mu \qquad (1)$$

Here, $R$ is the gas constant, $N_{\mathrm{A}}$ is the Avogadro constant, and $T$ is the absolute temperature.

The diffusion coefficient $D$ is a quantity that expresses how small particles spread out by Brownian motion, and it can be measured by observing the trajectories of the particles. The mobility $\mu$ is a coefficient that gives the speed with which a particle in a liquid moves when a weak force is applied to it, and it can be calculated using fluid mechanics.

The relation (1) connecting this diffusion coefficient and the mobility is also called the fluctuation–dissipation theorem, and it is one of the most fundamental relations in statistical physics. Einstein derived this relation on the basis of the idea that the Brownian motion of colloidal particles is caused by collisions with the surrounding water molecules. Using it, the Avogadro constant can be estimated by observing colloidal particles undergoing Brownian motion. Because this agreed almost with the value known at the time, Brownian motion came to be considered as visible evidence that molecules and atoms actually exist.

Let us derive this other Einstein relation below.

Random walk in one dimension: The simplest mathematical model of Brownian motion is called the random walk. Suppose that a colloidal particle moves on a straight line, with step width $\mathit{\Delta}x$, every time $\mathit{\Delta}t$, to the left or right with equal probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (Fig. 1). If it starts from $x=0$ at time $t=0$, its position $x(t)$ at time $t=s\mathit{\Delta}t$ $(s=0,1,2,\cdots)$ is given by

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Random walk in one dimension

$$x(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\mathit{\Delta}x_i$$

Here, $\mathit{\Delta}x_i$ is the step of the colloidal particle between time $t=(i-1)\mathit{\Delta}t$ and $t=i\mathit{\Delta}t$, a variable (random variable) that takes either the value $+\mathit{\Delta}x$ or $-\mathit{\Delta}x$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$. $\mathit{\Delta}x_i$ and $\mathit{\Delta}x_j$ $(i\neq j)$ at different times are assumed to be uncorrelated, that is, statistically independent.

Let us denote the statistical average (expectation value) of a quantity $A$ by $\langle A\rangle$. Then, for the statistical averages of the steps of the colloidal particle,

$$\langle\mathit{\Delta}x_i\rangle=0,\qquad\langle\mathit{\Delta}x_i\mathit{\Delta}x_j\rangle=(\mathit{\Delta}x)^2\,\delta_{i,j} \qquad (2)$$

holds. Here, $\delta_{i,j}$ is called the Kronecker delta symbol and denotes the function, for two integers $i$ and $j$, whose value is given by

$$\delta_{i,j}=\begin{cases}1 & (i=j)\\0 & (i\neq j)\end{cases}$$

From equation (2), the statistical average $\langle x(t)\rangle$ of the position $x(t)$ of the colloidal particle at time $t=s\mathit{\Delta}t$ is calculated as

$$\langle x(t)\rangle=\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{s}\mathit{\Delta}x_i\right\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\langle\mathit{\Delta}x_i\rangle=0$$

and is zero. Similarly, the statistical average $\left\langle x(t)^2\right\rangle$ of $x(t)^2$ becomes

$$\left\langle x(t)^2\right\rangle=\frac{(\mathit{\Delta}x)^2}{\mathit{\Delta}t}\,t \qquad (3)$$

and we see that it is proportional to the time $t$.

Q1. Using equation (2), show equation (3).

Diffusion phenomena: A diffusion phenomenon is a phenomenon in which many particles spread throughout the whole system while undergoing random motion. A typical example is the phenomenon in which small colloidal particles of about $1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ dispersed in water diffuse by Brownian motion. Let us consider how the number density of particles, that is, the concentration, changes on average when each particle performs a random walk on discrete points in one dimension.

Suppose that at some time $t$ there are $N_i(t)\ (\gg1)$ particles at position $x=i\mathit{\Delta}x$ $(i=0,\pm1,\pm2,\cdots)$. Suppose that afterwards, between time $t$ and $t+\mathit{\Delta}t$, $\dfrac{N_i(t)}{2}$ particles move to the right neighbour $x=(i+1)\mathit{\Delta}x$ and the remaining $\dfrac{N_i(t)}{2}$ particles move to the left neighbour $x=(i-1)\mathit{\Delta}x$. If such moves occur for the particles at all positions every time $\mathit{\Delta}t$, how does the number $N_i(t)$ of particles at each position change in time?

If $J_i(t)$ is the net number of particles that moved from $x=i\mathit{\Delta}x$ to $x=(i+1)\mathit{\Delta}x$ between time $t$ and $t+\mathit{\Delta}t$, it is expressed as

$$J_i(t)=\frac{1}{2}N_i(t)-\frac{1}{2}N_{i+1}(t) \qquad (4)$$

Also, the change in the number of particles at $x=i\mathit{\Delta}x$ between time $t$ and $t+\mathit{\Delta}t$ is expressed, using $J_i(t)$, as

$$N_i(t+\mathit{\Delta}t)-N_i(t)=J_{i-1}(t)-J_i(t) \qquad (5)$$

Let us consider the limit in which $\mathit{\Delta}x$ and $\mathit{\Delta}t$ are small in these equations, and express them using the concentration $n(x,t)$ and the flux $j(x,t)$ of the particles in one dimension. The concentration $n(x,t)$ is the number of particles per unit length at position $x$ and time $t$. The flux $j(x,t)$ is the net number of particles passing position $x$ in the positive direction per unit time, with the $+x$ direction taken as positive, that is, the number of particles passing in the $+x$ direction minus the number of particles passing in the $-x$ direction. When $\mathit{\Delta}x$ and $\mathit{\Delta}t$ are sufficiently small, they are expressed as

$$n(x,t)=\frac{N_i(t)}{\mathit{\Delta}x}\,,\quad j(x,t)=\frac{J_i(t)}{\mathit{\Delta}t} \qquad (6)$$

where $x=i\mathit{\Delta}x$. From equations (4) and (5) above we obtain [Note]

$$j(x,t)=-D\,\frac{\partial n(x,t)}{\partial x} \qquad (7)$$

$$\frac{\partial n(x,t)}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial j(x,t)}{\partial x} \qquad (8)$$

The coefficient $D$ appearing in the first equation is a quantity called the diffusion coefficient, and in the present random-walk model it is given by

$$D=\frac{(\mathit{\Delta}x)^2}{2\mathit{\Delta}t} \qquad (9)$$

[Note] For a function that has several variables as arguments, such as $n(x,t)$ or $j(x,t)$, the derivative obtained by regarding the other variables as constants and differentiating with respect to one variable is called a partial derivative, and the symbol $\partial$ is used instead of $\mathrm{d}$. For example, the concentration $n(x,t)$ is a function of the two variables $x$ and $t$, and we write

• the partial derivative with respect to the variable $x$, regarding the variable $t$ as a constant, as $\dfrac{\partial n(x,t)}{\partial x}$

• the partial derivative with respect to the variable $t$, regarding the variable $x$ as a constant, as $\dfrac{\partial n(x,t)}{\partial t}$

The symbol $\partial$ is a symbolized cursive d, and is also called rounded d.

Q2. When $\mathit{\Delta}t$ and $\mathit{\Delta}x$ are sufficiently small, derive equations (7) and (8) above from equations (4) and (5).

Equation (7) shows that the flux due to diffusion is proportional to the concentration gradient. Equation (8) is called the equation of continuity, and it is a relation that holds in general for the concentration and flux of any conserved physical quantity, such as the number of particles.

Substituting equation (7) into equation (8), we obtain the equation satisfied by the partial derivatives of $n(x,t)$, that is, the partial differential equation

$$\frac{\partial n(x,t)}{\partial t}=D\,\frac{\partial^2n(x,t)}{\partial x^2} \qquad (10)$$

This is called the diffusion equation.

The resistive force that a moving body receives from a liquid: Like a colloidal particle undergoing Brownian motion, a body moving in a liquid receives a resistive force from the liquid. Let us consider how this resistive force is expressed.

The properties of the liquid as a fluid are characterized by its density $\rho\,[\mathrm{kg/m^3}]$ and its viscosity coefficient $\eta\,[\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}]$. On the other hand, if the body is a sphere, its shape is characterized only by its radius $a\,[\mathrm{m}]$. Therefore, the force received by a body moving in the liquid with constant velocity should be expressible as a function only of $\rho$, $\eta$, $a$ and the speed $v$ of the body.

Now, the resistive force that a moving body receives from the surrounding liquid has two contributions: the inertial resistance, which is the reaction of the force with which the body moves the surrounding liquid, and the viscous resistance, which originates in the viscous dissipation of the liquid. The former depends mainly on the density $\rho$ of the liquid, and the latter depends mainly on the viscosity coefficient $\eta$.

Keeping these points in mind, let us find the speed dependence of the resistive force that a moving spherical body receives from the liquid by the following simple considerations.

Q3. When the speed $v$ of the body is slow, the inertial resistance can be neglected, and the resistive force received by the body is given by the viscous resistance, which does not depend on the density $\rho$ of the liquid. From this, using dimensional analysis, show that the resistive force $F$ that the body receives from the liquid is proportional to $\eta av$.

Q4. Conversely, when the speed of the body is large, the resistive force $F$ is mainly the inertial resistance, and the viscous resistance, which depends on $\eta$, can be neglected. Using dimensional analysis, find the values of the exponents $x$, $y$, $z$ when, in that case, the resistive force $F$ that the body receives from the liquid is taken to be proportional to $\rho^xa^yv^z$.

The speed of a colloidal particle undergoing Brownian motion is slow, and the resistive force it receives from the fluid is given by the viscous resistance. The viscous resistance in the case of a spherical particle of radius $a$ is, by a fluid-dynamical calculation,

$$F=6\pi\eta a\,v \qquad (11)$$

Solving this for $v$,

$$v=\mu\,F\,;\qquad\mu=\frac{1}{6\pi\eta a}. \qquad (12)$$

the coefficient $\mu$ is the mobility. Equation (11) or (12) is called Stokes' law.

Derivation of the Einstein relation: Now, the diffusion coefficient $D$ is proportional to the mobility $\mu$, and the Einstein relation (1) holds. This can be shown by considering the following situation (Fig. 2).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Now, take the $x$ axis pointing to the right, and suppose that a force $F$ in the positive direction of the $x$ axis (to the right) is applied to each Brownian particle. If there is a wall at the right end and the particles cannot go further to the right, the particles move to the right according to equation (12), so the particle concentration on the right side of the system becomes high and that on the left side becomes low. On the other hand, since the particles are undergoing Brownian motion, when such a concentration gradient forms, a flow arises, conversely, from the higher concentration to the lower concentration because of diffusion by Brownian motion. Eventually the two balance and a steady state is reached.

Considering the case in which the particle concentration $n$ per unit volume varies only in the $x$ direction, the flux due to Brownian motion is given by equation (7). In this case, the flux $j$ denotes the number of particles passing through a plane perpendicular to the $x$ axis in the $+x$ direction per unit cross-sectional area and per unit time.

Q5. Find the flux $j_{\mathrm{F}}$ of the flow of particles due to the force $F$.

Q6. Assuming that in the steady state the flux $j_{\mathrm{F}}$ due to the force $F$ and the flux $j$ due to Brownian motion balance, derive the relation satisfied by $n$ and $\dfrac{\partial n}{\partial x}$.

Now, let us analyse from another point of view the balance just considered between the flow of particles due to the external force $F$ and the diffusion due to Brownian motion.

We interpret the Brownian motion of the colloidal particles as a manifestation of the thermal motion of the surrounding water molecules, and regard the collection of colloidal particles as an ideal gas. The temperature $T$ of this ideal gas is the same as the temperature of the water, and the osmotic pressure of the colloidal particles is given by the equation of state of an ideal gas. Then the balance between the flow due to the external force and the flow due to diffusion can be seen as a balance between the externally applied force $F$ and the osmotic pressure.

Q7. Consider a cylindrical region whose central axis is parallel to the $x$ axis, and let its cross-sectional area be $S$ (Fig. 3). Assuming that the external force received by the particles in the small region between the coordinates $x$ and $x+\mathit{\Delta}x$ balances the osmotic pressure of the particles received from the two ends of that region, derive the relation satisfied by $n$ and $\dfrac{\partial n}{\partial x}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

Q8. The two balance conditions found in Q6 and Q7 are given for the same physical situation. From the fact that they should be the same, derive the Einstein relation (1).

Estimating the Avogadro constant: Expressing the right-hand side of equation (3) with the diffusion coefficient $D$ of equation (7), we have

$$\left\langle x(t)^2\right\rangle=2Dt \qquad (13)$$

By measuring, from the trajectories of the motion of many colloidal particles, how much the $x$ coordinate of each particle was displaced in a fixed time, and finding the average of the squares, the diffusion coefficient $D$ can be estimated from this equation. If the mobility $\mu$ is given by equation (12), the Avogadro constant can be found from the Einstein relation (1).

Q9. Einstein, conversely, estimated the mean square displacement of colloidal particles using the value $N_{\mathrm{A}}=6\times10^{23}\,/\mathrm{mol}$ known at the time as the Avogadro constant. If the relation (1) is correct, estimate what the square root of the mean square $\sqrt{\langle x^2\rangle}$ of the displacement of the $x$ coordinate of a colloidal particle of diameter $1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ at $t=1\,\mathrm{s}$ should be. Take the temperature of the water to be $17\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the viscosity coefficient of water $\eta=0.1\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$, and the gas constant $R=8.3\ \mathrm{J/(K\cdot mol)}$.

problems.title: Problem 4: The Fabry–Pérot interferometer
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (75 points)

The Fabry–Pérot interferometer

In this problem, as a preparation, we first consider the interference of light incident on a parallel thin film. Next, we consider the principle of the Fabry–Pérot interferometer (Fabry-Pérot interferometer, abbreviated below as FPI), which has a high resolving power (the ability to separate and distinguish two lights of close wavelengths) and is used when observing lights of close wavelengths by distinguishing them (spectroscopy).

The optical path length (or optical distance) is given by the product of the actual path length and the refractive index of the medium. The light used in this problem has a long coherence length (interference is observed even when the lights are superposed with a long optical path difference (difference of optical path lengths)), and parallel rays are assumed to interfere sufficiently far away (or when focused on the focal plane by a convex lens). Also, all the apparatus is assumed to be placed in air, and the refractive index of air is taken to be 1.

1. Interference in a thin film

A transparent parallel thin film of refractive index $n\ (>1)$ and thickness $d$ is placed in air, and, as in Fig. 1, a plane wave of wavelength $\lambda$ (in air) is incident on it. Let the angle of incidence at point B be $\theta$ (the angle of reflection is also $\theta$), the angle of refraction be $\phi$, the foot of the perpendicular drawn from point D to the straight line BF be E, and the foot of the perpendicular drawn from point B to CD be H.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1. [Labels in the figure: 空気 = air; 平行薄膜 = parallel thin film.]

Q1. Show that the optical path length between B and E is equal to the optical path length between H and D.

Q2. With reference to Fig. 1, show that the optical path difference (difference of optical path lengths) between the rays ABE and ABCD is given by

$$l=2d\sqrt{n^2-\sin^2\theta} \qquad (1)$$

and find the condition for the parallel rays BF and DG to interfere with each other sufficiently far away and reinforce each other (be in phase), using $d$, $n$, $\theta$, $\lambda$ and the integer $m=0,\,1,\,2,\,\cdots$ representing the order of interference. Here, note the difference in the phase change of the reflected rays at point B and at point C. The phase of the transmitted rays does not change at points B and D.

2. The Fabry–Pérot interferometer

When plane-wave light is incident on an apparatus E in which two thin plane mirrors M1, M2 having a small transmittance are placed parallel, facing each other, in close contact with both sides of a plate-shaped transparent material of refractive index 1, only light of particular wavelengths is transmitted because of multiple reflections. Also, as in Fig. 2, by placing a convex lens L1 in front of E and using an extended light source, the angle of incidence of the parallel rays incident on E can be given a certain spread. The parallel rays that have passed through E produce, by the convex lens L2, concentric bright fringes as in Fig. 3 on a screen S placed in the focal plane of L2 (the plane containing the focus and perpendicular to the optical axis). Such an apparatus is called a Fabry–Pérot interferometer (FPI). Here, the thickness of the transparent material in E is $d$, the focal length of lens L2 is $f$, and the screen is placed in the focal plane of lens L2. Also, the points $\mathrm{O_1}$, $\mathrm{O_2}$ are the centres of the lenses L1, L2, respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Schematic diagram of the Fabry–Pérot interferometer (FPI). [Labels in the figure: 光源 = light source; 装置 E = apparatus E; 透明物質 = transparent material; 入射角 $\theta$ = angle of incidence $\theta$; 出射角 $\theta$ = angle of emergence $\theta$.]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Concentric bright fringes produced on the screen S

Q3. Light of wavelength $\lambda$ in air is emitted from the light source; among the parallel rays emerging from apparatus E at angle $\theta$ $(|\theta|\ll1)$, the light passing through the centre $\mathrm{O_2}$ of the convex lens L2 goes straight on, and the point at which the light going straight reaches the screen S is the point where the parallel rays of emergence angle $\theta$ reinforce each other. Also, let the centre O of the concentric circles shown in Fig. 3 be the point where the parallel rays of angle $\theta=0$ reinforce each other. Express the minimum radius $R$ of the concentric bright fringes produced on the screen in terms of the emergence angle $\theta$ for the bright fringe of minimum radius and the focal length $f$ of lens L2. Here, use the approximation $\tan\theta\fallingdotseq\theta$.

Q4. Write down the condition for the rays incident on apparatus E at angle $\theta$ to reinforce each other on the screen, using a positive integer (order of interference) $m$. Also, for the concentric circles produced on the screen, answer whether the order of interference $m$ is larger or smaller for the outer circle. Assume that, after passing through apparatus E, no new phase difference arises between the parallel rays. Here, the phase change on reflection at the plane mirrors M1, M2 is $\pi$, and the phase change on transmission is $0$.

Q5. Taking the minimum radius of the concentric circles produced on the screen to be $R$, express the wavelength $\lambda$ of the light emitted from the light source using $d$, $f$, $R$. Also, when $d=5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$, $f=30\ \mathrm{cm}$, $R=0.95\ \mathrm{mm}$, find the wavelength $\lambda$ as a numerical value to two significant figures. Here, use, for $|\theta|\ll1$, the approximation

$$\cos\theta\fallingdotseq1-\frac{\theta^2}{2}$$

Complex representation of wave expressions

It is often convenient to represent the expression giving the displacement of a wave (the wave equation) with complex numbers. In that case, the actual displacement of the wave (a real number) is represented by the real part of the complex number. In doing so, Euler's formula

$$e^{i\alpha}=\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha\quad(\alpha\text{: real}) \qquad (2)$$

is used. Here, $i=\sqrt{-1}$.

The expression of a one-dimensional sinusoidal wave propagating in the $x$-axis direction with amplitude $A$, wave number $k$ $\Big(=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda},\ \lambda:\text{wavelength}\Big)$ and angular frequency $\omega$ ($A$, $k$, $\omega$ are taken to be real),

$$y=A\cos(kx-\omega t+\varphi)\quad(\text{the phase }\varphi\text{ is taken to be real})$$

is expressed using complex numbers as

$$z=A\,e^{i(kx-\omega t+\varphi)}=A\,e^{i\varphi}\,e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$$

and its real part is regarded as the actual wave expression. In this way, by considering, in place of the originally real amplitude $A$, the complex amplitude $A'=Ae^{i\varphi}$ (this is called the complex amplitude), the phase $\varphi$ can be incorporated, which is convenient.

Amplitude transmittance

As in Fig. 4, let the ray incident on apparatus E be $\mathrm{a_0}$, and the transmitted rays of ray $\mathrm{a_0}$ be $\mathrm{a_1},\,\mathrm{a_2},\,\mathrm{a_3},\,\cdots$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-4-fig4.png

Fig. 4. [Labels in the figure: 装置 E = apparatus E; 空気 = air; 透明物質 = transparent material; 反射光線 = reflected rays; 透過光線 = transmitted rays; 入射光線 $\mathrm{a_0}$ = incident ray $\mathrm{a_0}$.]

In this case, the phase difference $\delta$ between the transmitted rays $\mathrm{a_1}$ and $\mathrm{a_2}$ is expressed, using the optical path difference $l$ found in Q2, as

$$\delta=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,l \qquad (3)$$

Let us find the resultant transmittance using complex amplitudes.

Now, for light incident from air on the plane mirror M1 or M2 of apparatus E, let

$$\text{amplitude reflectance}=\frac{\text{complex amplitude of reflected light}}{\text{complex amplitude of incident light}}\ \text{be } r,\quad\text{amplitude transmittance}=\frac{\text{complex amplitude of transmitted light}}{\text{complex amplitude of incident light}}\ \text{be } t,$$

and for light incident from the transparent material on the plane mirror M1 or M2, let the amplitude reflectance be $r'$ and the amplitude transmittance be $t'$. In general, $r$, $r'$, $t$, $t'$ depend on the angle of incidence $\theta$ and the wavelength $\lambda$ of the incident light, but since in this problem we consider only the case $|\theta|\ll1$, $\left|\dfrac{\mathit{\Delta}\lambda}{\lambda}\right|\ll1$ ($\mathit{\Delta}\lambda$: difference of wavelengths), the dependence of $r$, $r'$, $t$, $t'$ on $\theta$ and $\lambda$ is neglected and they are taken to be constant values. Also, $r$, $r'$, $t$, $t'$ are taken to be real numbers.

Q6. Let $A_0$ be the complex amplitude of the ray $\mathrm{a_0}$ incident on apparatus E, $A_1,\,A_2,\,\cdots$ the complex amplitudes of the transmitted rays $\mathrm{a_1},\,\mathrm{a_2},\,\cdots$ respectively, and $A_{\mathrm{t}}=A_1+A_2+\cdots$ the resultant complex amplitude of the transmitted rays at a point sufficiently far from apparatus E (see Fig. 4).

(a) The complex amplitude of the transmitted ray $\mathrm{a_1}$ can be written $A_1=tt'e^{i\delta/2}A_0$. Here, $e^{i\delta/2}$ represents the contribution to the complex amplitude of the phase change of the ray $\mathrm{a_0}$ incident on plane mirror M1 until it reaches plane mirror M2. Write down the complex amplitude $A_2$ of the ray $\mathrm{a_2}$ transmitted through the plane mirror and the complex amplitude $A_3$ of the transmitted ray $\mathrm{a_3}$, using those of $A_0$, $\delta$, $t$, $t'$, $r$, $r'$ that are needed.

(b) Derive that the amplitude transmittance $T_{\mathrm{A}}=\dfrac{A_{\mathrm{t}}}{A_0}$ of the resultant transmitted ray with respect to the incident ray $\mathrm{a_0}$ is expressed as

$$T_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{tt'}{1-r'^2\,e^{i\delta}}\,e^{i\delta/2} \qquad (4)$$

Energy transmittance of the interferometer (FPI)

Let us consider how the energy transmittance $T=|T_{\mathrm{A}}|^2$ of the resultant transmitted ray is expressed in terms of the energy reflectance for a ray incident from air on the plane mirror M1 or M2 and the phase difference $\delta$ due to the path difference in the transparent material. There is assumed to be no absorption of light.

As in Fig. 5, consider the phenomenon in which a ray of complex amplitude $A$ is incident from air on the plane mirror M1 or M2 at point O, the complex amplitude of the reflected ray into air is $rA$, and the complex amplitude of the transmitted ray into the transparent material is $tA$. For this phenomenon, we assume time-reversal symmetry, that is, the reversibility of rays. Then, at point O, the complex amplitude of the reflected ray into air when a ray of complex amplitude $rA$ is incident from air can be written $r(rA)$, and the complex amplitude of the transmitted ray into air when a ray of complex amplitude $tA$ is incident from the transparent material can be written $t'(tA)$; these rays overlap in phase, and a ray of complex amplitude $A$ goes out into the air. At this time, no ray travels into the transparent material.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-4-fig5.png

Fig. 5. [Labels in the figure: 空気 = air; M1 あるいは M2 = M1 or M2; 透明物質 = transparent material.]

Q7. From the above explanation, derive the relation between $r$, $r'$ and the relation between $r$, $t$, $t'$, and then, taking the energy reflectance of light incident from air on the plane mirror M1 or M2 to be $r_0=r^2$, derive that the energy transmittance $1-r_0$ is expressed as

$$1-r_0=tt' \qquad (5)$$

Q8. Using equation (5) of the preceding Q7, show that the resultant energy transmittance $T=|T_{\mathrm{A}}|^2$ for the incident ray $\mathrm{a_0}$ of apparatus E in Fig. 4 is expressed as

$$T=\frac{1}{1+4F^2\sin^2\dfrac{\delta}{2}}\ ,\quad F=\frac{\sqrt{r_0}}{1-r_0} \qquad (6)$$

Here, note that, if the complex conjugate of the complex number $z=a+ib$ ($a$, $b$: real) is $\overline{z}=a-ib$, one can write

$$|z|^2=z\overline{z}=a^2+b^2$$

Resolving power of the interferometer (FPI)

The energy transmittance $T$ of apparatus E varies with the phase difference $\delta$ and is given by equation (6). Its values for $r_0=0.2,\ 0.9$ are as in Fig. 6. As this figure shows, as the value of $r_0$ becomes larger and approaches 1, the peak at $\delta=2m\pi$ becomes progressively sharper. This sharp peak can be used in the FPI to distinguish (spectroscopically separate) light of wavelengths $\lambda$ and $\lambda+\mathit{\Delta}\lambda$ $\Big(\left|\dfrac{\mathit{\Delta}\lambda}{\lambda}\right|\ll1\Big)$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2023-4-fig6.png

Fig. 6.

First, with $m$ a positive integer, consider the case in which the energy transmittance $T$ of light of wavelength $\lambda$ gives a peak. In this case,

$$\delta=2m\pi \qquad (7)$$

holds.

We regard the case in which the value of the transmittance $T$ of light of wavelength $\lambda+\mathit{\Delta}\lambda$ becomes $\dfrac{1}{2}$ as the limit for distinguishing the two lights of wavelengths $\lambda$ and $\lambda+\mathit{\Delta}\lambda$ (the condition for the limit of resolution). The resolving power is defined by the ratio $\dfrac{\lambda}{\mathit{\Delta}\lambda}$ of $\lambda$ and $\mathit{\Delta}\lambda$ at the limit of resolution. Let the phase difference be $\delta$ when the wavelength is $\lambda$, and $\delta-\mathit{\Delta}\delta$ when the wavelength is $\lambda+\mathit{\Delta}\lambda$.

Q9. Using equation (7) and $\mathit{\Delta}\delta\ll1$, show from equation (6) that the resolving power $\dfrac{\lambda}{\mathit{\Delta}\lambda}$ of the interferometer FPI can be written

$$\frac{\lambda}{\mathit{\Delta}\lambda}\fallingdotseq\frac{\sqrt{r_0}}{1-r_0}\,\delta \qquad (8)$$

Q10. Find, to one significant figure, the resolving power when light of wavelength $\lambda=5\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ is shone on an FPI with $d=5\ \mathrm{cm}$. Take $r_0=0.9$, and, since $|\theta|\ll1$, take $\cos\theta\fallingdotseq1$.

problems.title: Problem 1: Coupled pendulums and neutrino oscillations
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (75 points)

Coupled pendulums and neutrino oscillations

Oscillation phenomena appear in many fields: not only mechanical oscillations such as those of springs and pendulums, but also oscillations of electric circuits, oscillations appearing in biological phenomena, and so on. Basic concepts in physics such as oscillation have a common mathematical structure. Here we consider connecting two pendulums by a medium (such as a spring) that transmits their oscillations to each other. This is called coupled pendulums. When two or more oscillations are linked in this way, the idea of normal modes (eigen-oscillations) becomes important.

You may have heard of neutrino oscillation, the oscillation of the neutrino, one of the elementary particles, since Takaaki Kajita received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2015. In the second half of this problem, we try to obtain an intuitive understanding of neutrino oscillation, based on the fact that it obeys the same physical laws as coupled pendulums. Even if you cannot solve all of the questions in [I], you can work on [II] independently.

[I] Coupled pendulums

As in Fig. 1, the bobs a and b of two pendulums of lengths $L_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{b}}$ are connected by a spring. The masses of both bobs are $m$; the mass of the spring is negligible, the natural length of the spring is equal to the distance between the bobs of the two pendulums at their equilibrium positions, and the spring constant is $k$. The motion of the bobs of the pendulums is restricted to one vertical plane, and assuming that the swing angles of the pendulums are small, the motion of the bobs and the spring may be considered to take place approximately on a horizontal straight line (the $x$ axis). Let the displacements of the bobs a and b from their respective equilibrium points be $x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}$. The extension of the spring from its natural length is then $x_{\mathrm{b}}-x_{\mathrm{a}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Coupled pendulums

Q1 The equations of motion of the bobs a and b can be written in the following form.

$$\left.\begin{aligned} m\frac{\mathrm{d}^2x_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{d}t^2}&=-m(Ax_{\mathrm{a}}+Cx_{\mathrm{b}})\\ m\frac{\mathrm{d}^2x_{\mathrm{b}}}{\mathrm{d}t^2}&=-m(Cx_{\mathrm{a}}+Bx_{\mathrm{b}}) \end{aligned}\right\}\qquad(1)$$

Express the coefficients $A, B, C$ in terms of $m, k, L_{\mathrm{a}}, L_{\mathrm{b}}$ and the magnitude $g$ of the gravitational acceleration.

Next, we will show that by the change of variables

$$\left.\begin{aligned} x_{\mathrm{a}}&=\cos\theta\ x_1+\sin\theta\ x_2\\ x_{\mathrm{b}}&=-\sin\theta\ x_1+\cos\theta\ x_2 \end{aligned}\right\}\qquad(2)$$

and an appropriate choice of $\theta$, the equations can be expressed as

$$\left.\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2x_1}{\mathrm{d}t^2}&=-\lambda_1x_1\\ \frac{\mathrm{d}^2x_2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}&=-\lambda_2x_2 \end{aligned}\right\}\qquad(3)$$

The inverse transformation of equation (2) is

$$\begin{aligned} x_1&=\cos\theta\ x_{\mathrm{a}}-\sin\theta\ x_{\mathrm{b}}\\ x_2&=\sin\theta\ x_{\mathrm{a}}+\cos\theta\ x_{\mathrm{b}} \end{aligned}$$

Q2 Show that the condition on $\theta$ for equation (3) to be satisfied is

$$(A-B)\tan\theta+C(1-\tan^2\theta)=0\qquad(4)$$

Then express $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ in terms of $A, B, C$ and $\theta$.

Q3 Now consider the case $L_{\mathrm{a}}=L_{\mathrm{b}}\ (=L)$. Express $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ satisfying $\lambda_1>\lambda_2$ in terms of $A, B, C$, and show that $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Q4 (a) In the case $L_{\mathrm{a}}=L_{\mathrm{b}}\ (=L)$, find $x_{\mathrm{a}}(t), x_{\mathrm{b}}(t)$, where $x_{\mathrm{a}}(0)=x_0$, $x_{\mathrm{b}}(0)=0$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x_{\mathrm{a}}(0)}{\mathrm{d}t}=0$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x_{\mathrm{b}}(0)}{\mathrm{d}t}=0$. Here you may use $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ as they are.

(b) Taking $\dfrac{k/m}{g/L}=\dfrac{kL}{mg}=\dfrac{9}{32}$, draw the graph of $x_{\mathrm{a}}(t)$. Take the range of $t$ to be $t=\left[\,0,\ 8\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}\,\right]$. If a sum of trigonometric functions appears, use the sum-to-product formula and draw auxiliary lines that make the behaviour of the oscillation easy to understand.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-1-fig2.png

[Editorial note: blank graph printed on the answer sheet for Q4 (b).]

The amplitude was found to vary periodically as a result of the superposition of two waves; this phenomenon is called beats.

Q5 (a) In the general case $L_{\mathrm{a}}\neq L_{\mathrm{b}}$, solve the quadratic equation (4) for $\tan\theta$ and show that

$$\begin{aligned} \cos^2\theta&=\frac{1}{2}\left(1\mp\frac{(A-B)}{\sqrt{(A-B)^2+4C^2}}\right)\\ \sin^2\theta&=\frac{1}{2}\left(1\pm\frac{(A-B)}{\sqrt{(A-B)^2+4C^2}}\right)\\ \sin\theta\cos\theta&=\pm\frac{C}{\sqrt{(A-B)^2+4C^2}} \end{aligned}$$

(b) Find $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ and express them in terms of $m, g, L_{\mathrm{a}}, L_{\mathrm{b}}, k$.

In this problem, when the transformation of equation (2) is written in matrix form, as shown in 1. of the "Common mathematical expressions", it is expressed as

$$\begin{pmatrix} x_{\mathrm{a}}\\ x_{\mathrm{b}} \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta\\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{pmatrix}$$

The equations of motion (1) for $x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}$ found in Q1 can also be expressed in matrix form. Equation (3) can be expressed as

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\begin{pmatrix} x_1(t)\\ x_2(t) \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2x_1}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\\ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2x_2}{\mathrm{d}t^2} \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} -\lambda_1 & 0\\ 0 & -\lambda_2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{pmatrix}\qquad(3')$$

and transforming into such a diagonal form in $x_1, x_2$ is called diagonalization of the matrix. The fact that $x_{\mathrm{a}}(t), x_{\mathrm{b}}(t)$ are described by sums of $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$, which perform harmonic oscillations, is expressed by saying that they are superpositions of normal modes with two normal-mode frequencies. There is a general method of diagonalizing a matrix to find the normal-mode frequencies, but here we argued directly from the condition that the off-diagonal terms become 0.

Q6 (a) From the result of Q5, express the kinetic energy of the system

$$T=\frac{m}{2}\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x_{\mathrm{b}}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2\right]$$

and the potential energy

$$V=\frac{m}{2}\left(\frac{g}{L_{\mathrm{a}}}{x_{\mathrm{a}}}^2+\frac{g}{L_{\mathrm{b}}}{x_{\mathrm{b}}}^2+\frac{k}{m}(x_{\mathrm{b}}-x_{\mathrm{a}})^2\right)$$

in terms of $x_1, x_2$. Show that each of the kinetic energy and the potential energy can be written as the sum of a term containing only $x_1$ and a term containing only $x_2$.

(b) Show that the total energy of the terms containing only $x_1$, $E_1=T_1+V_1$, and the total energy of the terms containing only $x_2$, $E_2=T_2+V_2$, are each constants independent of time.

[II] Neutrino oscillations

The neutrino is an elementary particle whose existence was predicted by Pauli in 1930, and it has no electric charge. Because it hardly reacts with matter, experimental verification of its existence was very difficult, and it was discovered only in 1956 by observing neutrinos from a nuclear reactor. Subsequent research has shown that, corresponding to the three charged leptons (electron, muon, tau), there are three kinds (generations) of neutrinos, namely the electron neutrino $\nu_e$, the muon neutrino $\nu_\mu$ and the tau neutrino $\nu_\tau$ (and their antiparticles). The phenomenon in which one neutrino changes into another neutrino is neutrino oscillation, and the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Takaaki Kajita and Arthur B. McDonald with the citation "for the discovery of neutrino oscillations, which shows that neutrinos have mass".
In the Standard Model of elementary particles, completed in the 1970s, neutrinos are formulated as massless, but neutrino oscillation provided ground-breaking evidence that neutrinos have a mass, albeit a small one.

The motion of neutrinos obeys the Schrödinger equation of quantum mechanics. The solution of the Schrödinger equation is generally called the wave function; it determines the quantum states that a quantum system can take and also describes the time evolution of the quantum state of the system. The wave function takes complex values and is not a directly observable quantity; the square of the absolute value of the wave function gives the probability of existence.

The equation of motion describing neutrino oscillation (the Schrödinger equation) has a form very similar to the equations of the coupled pendulums of a classical system. There are three kinds of neutrinos, but let us now consider two kinds of neutrinos. If the wave functions of the $\alpha$-type neutrino (e.g. $\nu_\mu$) and the $\beta$-type neutrino (e.g. $\nu_\tau$) are $\Psi_\alpha, \Psi_\beta$, they satisfy the following Schrödinger equations

$$\left.\begin{aligned} i\hbar\frac{\mathrm{d}\Psi_\alpha}{\mathrm{d}t}&=E_\alpha\Psi_\alpha+a\Psi_\beta\\ i\hbar\frac{\mathrm{d}\Psi_\beta}{\mathrm{d}t}&=a\Psi_\alpha+E_\beta\Psi_\beta \end{aligned}\right\}\qquad(5)$$

Here $\hbar$ is the Planck constant $h$ divided by $2\pi$, $\hbar=1.05\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$. When expressed in matrix form, these equations have the same form as the equations of motion (1) of the two coupled pendulums, and $a$ represents the degree of mixing of the two wave functions. Now consider applying to $\Psi_\alpha, \Psi_\beta$ the same transformation as equation (2),

$$\begin{aligned} \Psi_\alpha&=\cos\theta\ \Psi_1+\sin\theta\ \Psi_2\\ \Psi_\beta&=-\sin\theta\ \Psi_1+\cos\theta\ \Psi_2 \end{aligned}$$

to transform the equations into the form

$$\left.\begin{aligned} i\hbar\frac{\mathrm{d}\Psi_1}{\mathrm{d}t}&=\hbar\omega_1\Psi_1\\ i\hbar\frac{\mathrm{d}\Psi_2}{\mathrm{d}t}&=\hbar\omega_2\Psi_2 \end{aligned}\right\}\qquad(6)$$

similar to equation (3). Using matrix notation,

$$i\hbar\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\begin{pmatrix} \Psi_1\\ \Psi_2 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} i\hbar\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Psi_1}{\mathrm{d}t}\\ i\hbar\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Psi_2}{\mathrm{d}t} \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} \hbar\omega_1 & 0\\ 0 & \hbar\omega_2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \Psi_1\\ \Psi_2 \end{pmatrix}\qquad(6')$$

What should be noted here is that, as mentioned above, the wave functions of quantum mechanics take complex values. It is known that when dealing with classical oscillations, using Euler's formula

$$e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$$

makes things clearer, but it is the real part, or the imaginary part, of the complex solution obtained that represents the actual motion. In quantum mechanics, on the other hand, the wave function essentially takes complex values.
Newton's equation of motion for classical oscillations is an equation containing second derivatives, whereas the Schrödinger equation is a first-order differential equation containing complex numbers. However, since the form of the transformation is common, the problem can be solved by using the results obtained so far as they are. Since equation (5) corresponds to equation (1) and equation (6) to equation (3), the equation corresponding to equation (4) is obtained immediately.

The solutions of equation (6) are

$$\begin{aligned} \Psi_1(t)&=D_1e^{-i\omega_1t}\\ \Psi_2(t)&=D_2e^{-i\omega_2t} \end{aligned}$$

Q7 In the case $E_\alpha=E_\beta=E$, find $\omega_1, \omega_2$. Also, when $\Psi_\alpha(0)=1, \Psi_\beta(0)=0$ at $t=0$, find $\Psi_\alpha(t), \Psi_\beta(t)$. Note that this question corresponds to Q3 and Q4.

Q8 In quantum mechanics, the square of the absolute value of the wave function represents the probability of existence at time $t$. Under the conditions of the previous question, write down $|\Psi_\alpha(t)|^2, |\Psi_\beta(t)|^2$. Also represent $|\Psi_\alpha(t)|^2, |\Psi_\beta(t)|^2$ by graphs.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-1-fig3.png

[Editorial note: blank graph printed on the answer sheet for Q8.]

Q9 In the general case $E_\alpha\neq E_\beta$, calculate $|\Psi_\alpha(t)|^2, |\Psi_\beta(t)|^2$. Derive that the expression $\sin^2(2\theta)\sin^2\dfrac{(\omega_1-\omega_2)\,t}{2}$ appears in $|\Psi_\alpha(t)|^2, |\Psi_\beta(t)|^2$. $\theta$ is the angle satisfying equation (4). Here $\Psi_\alpha(0)=1, \Psi_\beta(0)=0$. This question corresponds to Q5.

The $\theta$ appearing here means a rotation angle in the two-dimensional space formed by $\Psi_\alpha, \Psi_\beta$, and it is sometimes called the Cabibbo angle. The Cabibbo angle was originally a term used not for neutrinos but for the transformation of quarks (the elementary particles that make up nucleons). Furthermore, it was shown that there are three generations of quarks, and the extension to three dimensions is called the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix. The 2008 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Makoto Kobayashi and Toshihide Maskawa with the citation "for the discovery of the origin of the broken symmetry which predicts the existence of at least three families of quarks in nature". It was shared with Yoichiro Nambu, who received it "for the discovery of the mechanism of spontaneous broken symmetry in subatomic physics".

The $\alpha$-type neutrino (e.g. $\nu_\mu$) and the $\beta$-type neutrino (e.g. $\nu_\tau$) are called flavour eigenstates, whereas the diagonalized states are called mass eigenstates. The normal-mode frequencies $\omega_1, \omega_2$ of the mass eigenstates appear in the transition probability $P_{\alpha\to\beta}$ from $\alpha$ to $\beta$.

Q10 (a) Super-Kamiokande is an experiment that directly observed neutrino oscillation experimentally. $\hbar\omega_1, \hbar\omega_2$ on the right-hand side of equation (6) correspond to $\hbar$ times the two normal-mode frequencies in the case of coupled pendulums, but in the case of neutrino oscillation they represent the respective energies of the two different mass eigenstates of the neutrino. For a neutrino of very small mass flying at almost the speed of light, its energy $E$ is expressed by the relativistic formula as a function of the mass $m$ and the momentum $p$, and furthermore, imposing the condition that the mass $m$ is sufficiently small,
it can be approximated as follows using the first-order approximation of 3. of the "Common mathematical expressions".

$$\begin{aligned} \hbar\omega_1=E_1&=\sqrt{{p_1}^2c^2+{m_1}^2c^4}\fallingdotseq p_1c\left(1+\frac{{m_1}^2c^2}{2{p_1}^2}\right)\\ \hbar\omega_2=E_2&=\sqrt{{p_2}^2c^2+{m_2}^2c^4}\fallingdotseq p_2c\left(1+\frac{{m_2}^2c^2}{2{p_2}^2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

In what follows, for simplicity, the momenta of the neutrinos of the respective masses are taken to be equal ($p_1=p_2=p$), and we define $E_0\equiv pc\fallingdotseq E_1\fallingdotseq E_2$. Show that, using the difference of the squares of the two masses $\varDelta{m_{12}}^2\equiv({m_1}^2-{m_2}^2)$, the period $T$ of neutrino oscillation is given by

$$T=\frac{4\pi\hbar E_0}{\varDelta{m_{12}}^2c^4}$$

Note that the beats are represented by the term $\sin^2\dfrac{(\omega_1-\omega_2)\,t}{2}$.

(b) According to the observational data on atmospheric neutrinos by Super-Kamiokande, the distance ($L$) travelled by a muon neutrino with an energy of about $1.6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}$ during one period of its oscillation (the time it takes to change from the muon type once into the tau type and back again into the muon type) was about $1000\ \mathrm{km}$. Assuming that the neutrino travels at almost the speed of light (that is, $L=cT$), find the value of $\varDelta m^2$ in units of $\mathrm{kg}^2$ to one significant figure. $c=3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

What was discussed here is the difference of the squares of the masses of the mass eigenstates. Comparing with the electron mass of $9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, you can see that it is small in order of magnitude. Experiments are currently continuing with the aim of measuring $\sin^2(2\theta)$ and $\varDelta m^2$ for $\nu_e\leftrightarrow\nu_\mu$, $\nu_\mu\leftrightarrow\nu_\tau$, $\nu_e\leftrightarrow\nu_\tau$ with high precision.

We have discussed neutrinos mixing and oscillating, but there are strange aspects if elementary particles are thought of as "particles". This phenomenon can be understood if elementary particles are regarded as oscillations (excitations) of quantum fields.

References:

Evidence for Oscillation of Atmospheric Neutrinos, Y. Fukuda, et al. (Super-Kamiokande Collaboration), Phys. Rev. Lett. 81, 1562 (1998).

[Editorial note: "Common mathematical expressions" printed at the front of the paper for use in several problems:

1. Product of a matrix and a column vector. The product of the 2-by-2 matrix $\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ and the column vector $\begin{pmatrix} x\\ y \end{pmatrix}$ is a column vector, defined as follows.

$$\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x\\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} ax+by\\ cx+dy \end{pmatrix}$$

2. Euler's formula. Extending the exponential function to complex numbers, the exponential function and the trigonometric functions can be related. For real $\theta$, the relation

$$e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$$

is called Euler's formula.

3. First-order approximation. For $|h|\ll1$, the approximation

$$(1+h)^\alpha\fallingdotseq1+\alpha h$$

holds, where $\alpha$ is any real number. This follows from the fact that a general differentiable function $f(x)$ can be approximated for $|h|\ll1$ as

$$f(a+h)\fallingdotseq f(a)+f'(a)\,h$$
]

problems.title: Problem 2: Accelerating elementary particles
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (75 points)

Accelerating elementary particles

"What is this world of ours made of?" is a fundamental question of natural science. In 1911, Rutherford made natural radiation ($\alpha$ rays) collide with a thin gold foil and showed that an atom consists of a very small nucleus at its centre and many electrons around it. To investigate the internal structure of the nucleus, machines that artificially accelerate protons, accelerators, were developed, and experiments in which accelerated protons were made to collide with nuclei revealed that nuclei are made of protons and neutrons. Aiming at still higher energies to investigate the internal structure of protons and neutrons, ever larger accelerators were built one after another, and in the 1970s it became clear that protons and neutrons also have an internal structure and are made of elementary particles called quarks.

In this problem, we consider the basic elements of accelerators, the machines that accelerate particles. The effects of the theory of relativity need not be taken into account.

[I] Acceleration and control

To accelerate particles and control their orbits, electric and magnetic fields are used. Let the mass of the particle to be accelerated be $m$ and its charge $e\,(>0)$. As in Fig. 1, a potential difference $V$ is applied between two plates and the particle is accelerated by the electric field between the plates.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Q1 Let the initial velocity of the particle to be accelerated be 0. Find the magnitude $v$ of the velocity of the particle after acceleration.

Q2 Taking the potential difference in Fig. 1 to be that of one dry cell, $1.50\ \mathrm{V}$ (volts), what is the falling distance needed to obtain, by free fall of a proton in the gravitational field at the Earth's surface, the velocity obtained when a proton is accelerated? Give the answer to 2 significant figures. The mass of the proton is $1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$, its charge is $1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface is $9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ and is constant independent of height, and air resistance is neglected.

From this result, the effect of gravity on the motion of the particles is neglected in what follows.

Q3 The motion of accelerated particles is controlled by magnetic fields. Prove that when a particle moves in a space where there is only a time-independent magnetic field, the magnitude of its velocity does not change.

To produce a high-energy beam, a high voltage is necessary, but voltages exceeding 1 million V are difficult to handle. Therefore, as in Fig. 2, a method was devised in which particles accelerated in the accelerating section A$\to$B are made to circulate by a magnetic field and returned to the starting point, and are accelerated by passing through the accelerating section many times (multiple acceleration).

Q4 In the accelerator of Fig. 2, show that multiple acceleration is impossible if the voltage between the plates A and B of the accelerating section is constant, independent of time.

From this result, an alternating voltage is essential in the accelerating section. The particles travel inside a fixed thin tube (the beam pipe) and circulate by means of magnetic fields that control their orbit. As the particles are accelerated their velocity increases, and to make them go round the same orbit, the frequency of the alternating voltage of the accelerating section is raised and the strength of the magnetic field is increased in synchronism. Modern large accelerators are all of this synchronous type, the synchrotron.

In a synchrotron, the particles go round tens of thousands of times. The particles go round in clumps (called bunches), but the distributions of velocity and position of the particles swell and spread out, deviate from the designed orbit, and finally collide with the beam pipe and are lost. Unless this phenomenon of the bunch spreading out is prevented, multiple acceleration by a synchrotron cannot be realized. There are two kinds of directions in which the bunch spreads: the direction of travel of the particles (called the beam-axis direction) and the directions perpendicular to the beam axis (2 dimensions).

[II] Principle of strong focusing

Consider suppressing the spread in the directions perpendicular to the beam axis. For light, rays can be focused using a convex lens. For beam particles, a quadrupole magnet as in Fig. 3 (denoted Q) is used. An iron core with a cross-shaped gap is made, and four magnetic poles (two pairs of N and S poles) are formed. Taking as the origin the central orbit, along which the beam particles travel perpendicular to the page from top to bottom, the deviation of the particle position from the central orbit is expressed by the $x, y$ coordinates of Fig. 3.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

[In the figure: 鉄コア = iron core.]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

[In the figure: ビーム軸方向 = beam-axis direction.]

The $x, y$ components of the magnetic flux density at position $x, y$ in the gap are adjusted to be

$$B_x=-by\ ,\quad B_y=-bx\qquad(1)$$

with a constant $b\,(>0)$, and the component in the beam-axis direction is 0. This magnetic flux density does not depend on the position in the beam-axis direction. Let the thickness of Q in the beam-axis direction (the length of the part where the magnetic field exists) be $D$.

Let the position of the particle when it enters Q be $x, y$, and the $x, y$ components of its velocity vector be $v_x, v_y$. Here $v_x, v_y$ are very small compared with the magnitude $v$ of the velocity of the particle; the component of the velocity in the beam-axis direction is treated as always having the constant value $v$, and the time required for the particle to pass through Q is taken to be the constant value $\dfrac{D}{v}$ independent of $v_x, v_y$. Also, the thickness $D$ of Q is sufficiently thin, and the position coordinates $x, y$ do not change inside Q.

Q5 Write the equations of motion of the particle inside Q using the velocities $v_x(t), v_y(t)$.

The $x$ and $y$ components of the equations of motion obtained are independent of each other and can be treated separately. First, consider the $x$ component. As in Fig. 4, let the coordinate of the particle immediately after passing through Q be $x'$ and the $x$ component of its velocity be $v'_x$. From the explanation above, the coordinate $x$ and the velocity $v$ in the beam-axis direction can be taken to be constant and unchanged while the particle passes through Q. Then, following 1. of the "Common mathematical expressions", the following relation is obtained using a matrix and column vectors.

$$\begin{pmatrix} x'\\ v'_x \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0\\ -q & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x\\ v_x \end{pmatrix}\ ,\qquad \text{where } q \text{ is a positive constant}\qquad(2)$$

Q6 By calculating $v'_x-v_x$ from the equation of motion, find the positive constant $q$ of equation (2).

In the following questions, answer using this constant $q$.

Q7 As in Fig. 5, using the transformation (2), show that all particles entering Q parallel to the beam axis reach the central orbit ($x=0$) at point F, that is, that Q acts as a convex lens, and find the distance $f$ (focal length) from Q to point F. Neglect the thickness of Q.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig5.png

Fig. 5.

[In the figure: ビーム軸方向 = beam-axis direction.]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig6.png

Fig. 6.

[In the figure: ビーム軸方向 = beam-axis direction.]

Repeating the calculations so far for the $y$ component and finding the matrix giving the transformation of $y$ and $v_y$, it turns out that it can be written as follows using the same constant $q\,(>0)$.

$$\begin{pmatrix} y'\\ v'_y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0\\ +q & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} y\\ v_y \end{pmatrix}\qquad(3)$$

Q8 Using the transformation (3), analyse the motion of particles entering Q parallel to the beam axis, show that for the $y$ component Q has the same action as a concave lens, and find its focal length.

It was found that the quadrupole magnet of Fig. 3 acts as a convex lens in the $x$ direction and as a concave lens in the $y$ direction. If, instead of equation (1), a magnetic flux density with the sign of $B_x$ reversed could be prepared, the $y$ component would also become a convex lens, but it can be proved from Ampère's law that this is impossible.

In the history of accelerators, the epoch-making "principle of strong focusing" was discovered in 1952 by Livingston, Courant and others. It is a method in which two quadrupole magnets $\mathrm{Q_1}$, $\mathrm{Q_2}$ are installed a distance $d$ apart. However, the second one, $\mathrm{Q_2}$, is installed rotated by 90 degrees about the beam axis. Then, for the $x$ component, $\mathrm{Q_1}$ is a convex lens and $\mathrm{Q_2}$ a concave lens, and for the $y$ component, $\mathrm{Q_1}$ is a concave lens and $\mathrm{Q_2}$ a convex lens.

Let us find the coordinates and velocity at the exit of $\mathrm{Q_2}$ of a particle that enters $\mathrm{Q_1}$ parallel to the beam axis at coordinates $x, y$. First consider the $x$ component (Fig. 6). In $\mathrm{Q_1}$, by the transformation (2), the coordinate does not change and the velocity $v'_x$ is determined.

Next, up to the entrance of $\mathrm{Q_2}$ the particle moves freely for a time $\dfrac{d}{v}$, so the velocity remains $v'_x$ without change, but the coordinate changes to $x+\dfrac{d}{v}v'_x$. This can be expressed by the following transformation.

$$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & d/v\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x\\ v'_x \end{pmatrix}\qquad(4)$$

In $\mathrm{Q_2}$ the transformation (3) is added. Combining these 3 steps, the coordinate $x''$ and the velocity $v''_x$ at the exit of $\mathrm{Q_2}$ can be expressed as

$$\begin{pmatrix} x''\\ v''_x \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0\\ +q & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & d/v\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0\\ -q & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x\\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\qquad(5)$$

The 3 matrices act on the vector at the right end in order from the right. The $y$ component can be considered in the same way, but since only the roles (convex and concave) of $\mathrm{Q_1}$ and $\mathrm{Q_2}$ are interchanged, the coordinate and velocity of the $y$ component at the exit of $\mathrm{Q_2}$ can be obtained from the above result for the $x$ component simply by $q\to-q$.

Q9 Show that particles after passing through $\mathrm{Q_2}$, independently of their coordinates on entering $\mathrm{Q_1}$, converge onto the central axis at a point at distance $f_x$ from $\mathrm{Q_2}$ for the $x$ component, and at a point at distance $f_y$ from $\mathrm{Q_2}$ for the $y$ component, and find $f_x, f_y$. Assume $d<f$.

From the above result, it can be seen that the combined system of $\mathrm{Q_1}, \mathrm{Q_2}$ acts as a convex lens for both the $x$ and $y$ components. This principle of strong focusing was implemented immediately after its discovery, and the synchrotron was realized.

[III] Principle of phase stability

Next, consider the spread in the beam-axis direction. An alternating voltage as in Fig. 7 is applied as the potential of A relative to B in the accelerating section of Fig. 2; by design, a particle passes through the accelerating section at time $a$ and, after one revolution, is accelerated again at $a'$. If a particle arriving late at the back of the bunch passes through the accelerating section at time $b$, the accelerating voltage is higher than at time $a$, the increase in velocity is larger than the design value, the time taken for one revolution becomes shorter, and it returns to the accelerating section before $b'$, recovering from its delay. This principle of phase stability was discovered independently by Veksler and McMillan in 1944. Let us consider this principle quantitatively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig7.png

Fig. 7.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig8.png

Fig. 8.

Here we consider the situation in which the beam particles are made to circulate at a constant speed without acceleration; by design, they pass through the accelerating section at time 0 of Fig. 7 and come back after exactly one period. The neighbourhood of the origin of Fig. 7 is enlarged and linearly approximated as in Fig. 8, and the horizontal axis is expressed not by time but by the phase $\phi$ (one period of the alternating voltage is $2\pi$). That is, the potential of A relative to B in the accelerating section is a linear function of the phase $\phi$ at the time of passage, with a constant $K\,(>0)$:

$$V(\phi)=K\phi\qquad(6)$$

In Fig. 8, a particle that enters the accelerating section late, at phase $\phi_1$ behind the design phase 0 (but with the particle velocity at its design value), is accelerated in the accelerating section and its velocity becomes faster than the design value. Therefore it goes round in a time shorter than the period of the alternating accelerating voltage, returns to the accelerating section at a phase $\phi_2$ earlier than the phase $\phi_1$, and approaches the design phase 0.

Consider the change, revolution by revolution, of the phase $\phi$ and of the velocity $v$ in the beam-axis direction. The velocity is expressed by its fractional deviation from the design velocity $\bar{v}$, $u\equiv\dfrac{v-\bar{v}}{\bar{v}}$, and this deviation is assumed to be sufficiently small ($|u|\ll1$). In Fig. 2, let the phase on entering the accelerating section at A be $\phi_0$ and the velocity $u_0$, and let the phase on leaving the accelerating section at B be $\phi'$ and the velocity $u'$. The accelerating section is short, and the phase, which represents the position in the beam-axis direction within the bunch, does not change before and after the accelerating section. By acceleration or deceleration the kinetic energy of the particle changes by $eV(\phi_0)$, but the fractional change is assumed to be sufficiently small.

Within the linear approximation, that is, the approximation in which $u^2$ is neglected compared with $u$ since $|u|\ll1$, the changes of phase and velocity due to passing through the accelerating section can be written as follows, with a constant $k$.

$$\phi'=\phi_0\ ,\quad u'=u_0+k\phi_0\qquad(7)$$

Q10 Find the constant $k$ in equation (7).

In the following questions, answer using this constant $k$.

If the length of the circulating orbit is $L$, the design revolution time is $T=\dfrac{L}{\bar{v}}$. If there is a velocity deviation $u$, a deviation $\varDelta T$ of the revolution time arises, whose fractional value is $\dfrac{\varDelta T}{T}=\dfrac{1}{1+u}-1\fallingdotseq-u$ ("Common mathematical expressions" 3.), and the change of phase is $-2\pi u$. The velocity in the beam-axis direction does not change during the revolution. Therefore, expressing the velocity $u_1$ and the phase $\phi_1$ when the particle has gone round once and arrives again at the entrance A of the accelerating section in terms of $\phi'$ and $u'$,

$$\phi_1=\phi'-2\pi u'\ ,\quad u_1=u'\qquad(8)$$

Q11 Combining equations (7) and (8), recurrence relations for the phase and velocity $\phi_n, u_n$ at the entrance A of the accelerating section for each number of revolutions ($n$) are obtained. Find the recurrence relations expressing each of $\phi_{n+1}, u_{n+1}$ in terms of $\phi_n, u_n$.

Q12 From the above simultaneous recurrence relations, derive a three-term recurrence relation in $\phi_n$ only, of the following form, and find the constants $b, c$.

$$\phi_{n+2}+b\phi_{n+1}+c\phi_n=0\qquad(9)$$

To solve the three-term recurrence relation (9), first look for a solution that is a simple geometric sequence: $\phi_n=\lambda^n$ with a constant $\lambda$. Substituting this into equation (9), the quadratic equation in $\lambda$: $\lambda^2+b\lambda+c=0$ is obtained. If the constant $k$ is sufficiently small, its two solutions are mutually complex-conjugate numbers of absolute value 1, and can be written, using a real number $\theta$, as $\lambda_1=e^{i\theta}, \lambda_2=e^{-i\theta}$. Since the three-term recurrence relation (9) is a sum of linear expressions in its terms, the sum of the two geometric-sequence solutions found, $\lambda_1^n, \lambda_2^n$, each multiplied by a constant coefficient ($C_1, C_2$),

$$\phi_n=C_1\lambda_1^n+C_2\lambda_2^n=C_1e^{in\theta}+C_2e^{-in\theta}\qquad(10)$$

is also a solution. Since the two constant coefficients $C_1, C_2$ can be determined for arbitrary first and second terms $\phi_0, \phi_1$, any solution can be expressed by equation (10). Equation (10) is called the general solution.

Q13 Using the general solution (10), find the solution $\phi_n$ in the case where the initial values of $\phi_n, u_n$ are $\phi_0=0, u_0=\varepsilon$. You may use the real number $\theta$ as it is.

From this solution, it can be seen that the deviations of the phase and velocity from the design values vary in an oscillatory manner and are stable without diverging. This is the principle of phase stability, an essential element for realizing the synchrotron.

[IV] Necessity of colliding-beam accelerators

Let us consider what fraction of the energy given by acceleration is used effectively when an accelerated particle is made to hit a target particle. Let the mass of the particle to be accelerated be $M$, the mass of the target particle at rest be $m$, and the potential energy due to the Coulomb force (repulsive force) between the two particles be $V(r)=\dfrac{C}{r}$ ($C$ is a positive constant). In the initial state, the two particles are sufficiently far apart, so the potential energy due to the Coulomb force can be neglected.

For simplicity, as in Fig. 9, the beam particle and the target particle undergo a head-on collision and move on the same straight line after the collision as well. How close they can approach against the Coulomb force (repulsive force) is an important index, because the closer they approach, the more data are obtained for investigating finer internal structure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig9.png

Fig. 9.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-2-fig10.png

Fig. 10.

Q14 Express the ratio $\dfrac{V_{\max}}{\frac{1}{2}Mv^2}$ of the potential energy $V_{\max}$ due to the Coulomb force when the two particles are closest to each other to the energy $\frac{1}{2}Mv^2$ given to the beam particle by acceleration, in terms of $M$ and $m$.

The ratio found above approaches 0 when $\dfrac{M}{m}$ is made large, and only a very small part of the energy given by acceleration is used effectively. In fact, since part of the relativistic effects of high-speed particles can also be understood in the form of an increase of mass, the fraction of energy used effectively decreases sharply the higher the energy to which the particles are accelerated, and it becomes impossible to probe the internal structure of particles.

What was newly devised, therefore, is the method of making accelerated beam particles collide head-on with each other (the colliding-beam type). As in Fig. 10, particles of mass $M$ accelerated to velocity $v$ from both sides are made to collide with each other.

Q15 What is the ratio $\dfrac{V_{\max}}{Mv^2}$ of the potential energy $V_{\max}$ due to the Coulomb force when the two beam particles are closest to each other to the energy $Mv^2$ given to the two particles by acceleration?

In colliding-beam experiments, the energy that the accelerator gave to the beam particles can be used effectively to explore microstructure. The energy-frontier accelerators that investigate the micro-world are of this colliding-beam type, and the largest of them is the LHC (Large Hadron Collider) with a circumference of 27 km, installed at CERN, the international joint research institute spanning Switzerland and France. It was in 2012, 100 years after Rutherford's experiment, that the LHC discovered the Higgs particle, which had been predicted theoretically.

[Editorial note: "Common mathematical expressions" printed at the front of the paper and referred to in this problem:

1. Product of a matrix and a column vector. The product of the 2-by-2 matrix $\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ and the column vector $\begin{pmatrix} x\\ y \end{pmatrix}$ is a column vector, defined as follows.

$$\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x\\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} ax+by\\ cx+dy \end{pmatrix}$$

2. Euler's formula. Extending the exponential function to complex numbers, the exponential function and the trigonometric functions can be related. For real $\theta$, the relation

$$e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$$

is called Euler's formula.

3. First-order approximation. For $|h|\ll1$, the approximation

$$(1+h)^\alpha\fallingdotseq1+\alpha h$$

holds, where $\alpha$ is any real number. This follows from the fact that a general differentiable function $f(x)$ can be approximated for $|h|\ll1$ as

$$f(a+h)\fallingdotseq f(a)+f'(a)\,h$$
]

problems.title: Problem 3: Polarization and interference of photons
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (75 points)

Polarization and interference of photons

Is light a particle or a wave? There was a long historical debate. In the 19th century, the question seemed to have been settled by Maxwell's electromagnetic theory in the form that light is an electromagnetic wave, that is, a wave. However, in the 20th century, phenomena that cannot be understood by regarding light simply as a wave were discovered one after another, such as the spectrum of cavity radiation, the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering. Today, light is described by quantum mechanics as photons that have both wave and particle properties.

Here, focusing in particular on the polarization and interference of light, let us clarify the puzzling points of the behaviour of photons when they are viewed as ordinary particles.

I. Light as an electromagnetic wave

According to electromagnetism, light is a wave consisting of an oscillating electric field and magnetic field. In the case of a simple plane wave, the electric field, the magnetic field and the direction of propagation are mutually perpendicular and form a right-handed system in this order (Fig. 1). For example, the electric field and magnetic field of light propagating in the $z$ direction oscillate in mutually perpendicular directions in the $x-y$ plane. Since the electric field and magnetic field are related to each other, in what follows we describe the propagation of light by the oscillating electric field.
