https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Propagation of the electromagnetic field

[In the figure: 伝播方向 = direction of propagation.]

In general, the direction of the oscillating electric field of light is not fixed in the $x-y$ plane but rotates or changes in a complicated way; here we consider light whose electric field (and magnetic field) oscillates in a fixed direction. Such light is called linearly polarized light, or simply polarized light, and the direction of its oscillating electric field is called the polarization direction.

For example, the oscillating electric field $\overrightarrow{E}(z,t)$ of linearly polarized light propagating in the $z$ direction is expressed, with its amplitude $E_0$ and the unit vector $\overrightarrow{t}$ representing the direction of the oscillating electric field in the $x-y$ plane, as

$$\overrightarrow{E}(z,t)=E_0\,\overrightarrow{t}\cos\big(kz-\omega t+\delta\big)\qquad(1)$$

The argument of cos, $(kz-\omega t+\delta)$, is called the phase, and the coefficients $k$ and $\omega$ of the coordinate $z$ and the time $t$ are parameters called the wave number and the angular frequency, respectively. Note here that the oscillating electric field of light represented by the vector $\overrightarrow{t}$ and the oscillating electric field of $-\overrightarrow{t}$ are not distinguished as polarization directions of light.

Q1 Express equation (1) using the wavelength $\lambda$ and the period $\tau$ instead of the wave number $k$ and the angular frequency $\omega$.

Representation of waves using complex numbers

To represent waves mathematically, it is often convenient to express them by functions of complex numbers using Euler's formula (see 2. of the "Common mathematical expressions").

Introducing the complex amplitude $\widetilde{E}_0$, an extension of the amplitude to complex numbers, and defining the vector multiplied by a complex coefficient

$$\overrightarrow{\widetilde{E}}(z,t)=\widetilde{E}_0\,\overrightarrow{t}\,e^{i(kz-\omega t)}$$

the electric field vector is given by its real part:

$$\overrightarrow{E}(z,t)=\mathrm{Re}\left[\overrightarrow{\widetilde{E}}(z,t)\right].\qquad(2)$$

Here $\overrightarrow{t}$ is a unit vector in the $x-y$ plane and represents the polarization direction of the light.

Q2 How should the complex amplitude $\widetilde{E}_0$ be taken so that equation (1) is given by equation (2)? Express it in terms of $E_0$ and $\delta$. Also, what does $\widetilde{E}_0$ become when $\delta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and when $\delta=\pi$, respectively?

In what follows, to simplify the notation, the complex amplitude $\widetilde{E}_0$ and the complex oscillating electric field $\overrightarrow{\widetilde{E}}(z,t)$ are written simply as $E_0$ and $\overrightarrow{E}(z,t)$, respectively. The actual amplitude is given by the absolute value of $E_0$, and the electric field by the real part of $\overrightarrow{E}(z,t)$.

Light carries energy. The intensity of light is defined as the energy carried per unit time and per unit area, and is proportional to the square of the amplitude of the oscillating electric field. With $E_0$ the complex amplitude, the intensity $I$ of the light is expressed as

$$I=a|E_0|^2=a{E_0}^*E_0;\qquad a:\ \text{proportionality coefficient}.\qquad(3)$$

Here ${E_0}^*$ denotes the complex conjugate of $E_0$.

Action of a polarizer

The oscillating electric field of linearly polarized light polarized in a general direction $\overrightarrow{t}$ is expressed as the sum of a component oscillating in the $x$ direction and a component oscillating in the $y$ direction:

$$\begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{E}(z,t)&=E_0\,\overrightarrow{t}\,e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\\ &=E_0\cos\phi\,\overrightarrow{x}\,e^{i(kz-\omega t)}+E_0\sin\phi\,\overrightarrow{y}\,e^{i(kz-\omega t)} \end{aligned}\qquad(4)$$

Here $\phi$ is the angle between the polarization-direction vector $\overrightarrow{t}$ and the $x$ axis, and $\overrightarrow{x}$ and $\overrightarrow{y}$ are the unit vectors in the $x$-axis and $y$-axis directions, respectively (Fig. 2).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Vector $\overrightarrow{t}$ representing the polarization direction

When light is passed through an element called a polarizer (Fig. 3), only light having the component of the oscillating electric field parallel to its transmission axis is transmitted, and the component perpendicular to the transmission axis is reflected or absorbed and not transmitted. As a result, the light transmitted through the polarizer becomes linearly polarized light polarized in the direction of the transmission axis. Real polarizers do not work so ideally, but in what follows we consider an ideal polarizer through which only the polarization component parallel to the transmission axis is completely transmitted.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Polarizer

[In the figure: 透過軸 = transmission axis.]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4. Polarizer $\mathrm{P}_x$

[In the figure: 透過軸 = transmission axis.]

Q3 Consider polarized light whose oscillating electric field is expressed by equation (4).

(a) When this light is passed through the polarizer $\mathrm{P}_x$ whose transmission axis is parallel to the $x$ axis (Fig. 4), what is the complex amplitude $E_1$ of the electric field of the transmitted light?

(b) Further, when this transmitted light is passed through a polarizer $\mathrm{P}_\theta$ whose transmission axis is inclined at an angle $\theta$ from the $x$ axis, what is the complex amplitude $E_2$ of the electric field of the transmitted light?

(c) Express the intensities $I_1$ and $I_2$ of the respective transmitted lights found above in terms of the intensity $I_0$ of the incident light.

Ordinary light (natural light) is a superposition of light from many emitters, and the light emitted from each individual emitter has an electric field with a different direction of oscillation. Now let the incident light be a superposition of light propagating in the $z$ direction from $N$ ($N\gg1$) emitters, and let the light of the $j$-th emitter be linearly polarized in the direction $\phi_j$. The polarization directions $\phi_1, \phi_2, \cdots, \phi_N$ of the light from the emitters are assumed to be randomly and uniformly distributed over all directions. For simplicity, let the wave numbers and complex amplitudes of the oscillating electric fields from all emitters have the same values $k$ and $E_0$.

Q4 Suppose that this incident light passes in turn through two polarizers as in Q3. Express the intensity $I_1$ of the light after passing through the polarizer $\mathrm{P}_x$, and the intensity $I_2$ of the light after passing through the polarizers $\mathrm{P}_x$ and $\mathrm{P}_\theta$, in terms of the intensity $I_0$ of the incident light.

[Hint] Since the polarizations of the emitters are random, the intensity of the light is expressed as the sum of the intensities of the light from the individual sources, and a sum of a function of the polarization directions $\phi_j$ of the sources is obtained as

$$\sum_{j=1}^{N}f(\phi_j)=\frac{N}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(\phi)d\phi$$

You may use this.

II. Photons: light as particles

In the 20th century it became clear that light also shows properties as particles. The energy of light takes discrete values, and the energy of one particle making up light, that is, of one photon, is proportional to its frequency $f$.
However, since the energy of one photon is very small, even light of the intensity we see in everyday life is made up of an enormous number of photons and looks like a spatially extended continuous wave. But when the intensity of the light is weakened until the photons come flying one at a time, it is observed that the grains of light arriving at a photographic plate expose the photosensitive molecules one by one, and the properties as particles become apparent. It was shown that the behaviour of photons as particles is very strange. Let us look at this below.

Behaviour of photons at a polarizer

The behaviour of light as an electromagnetic wave transmitted through a polarizer, examined in I., corresponds to the behaviour of a collection of many photons. Based on this, let us consider the behaviour of photons as particles.

The light represented by equation (1) is a stream of an enormous number of photons, proportional to its intensity $I_0=a|E_0|^2$. When this light is passed through the polarizer $\mathrm{P}_x$ whose transmission axis is parallel to the $x$ axis, a number of photons proportional to the intensity $I_1$ of the transmitted light is transmitted, and the transmitted photons become linearly polarized in the $x$-axis direction ($x$ polarization).

Then how does each individual photon making up the incident light behave? First, let us represent the polarization state of one photon by the symbol $\overrightarrow{\psi}$. Since the vector $\overrightarrow{t}$ of equation (1) completely specifies the polarization of the light, the polarization state $\overrightarrow{\psi}$ of each individual photon making it up is also specified by the same unit vector $\overrightarrow{t}$:

$$\overrightarrow{\psi}=\overrightarrow{t}=\cos\phi\,\overrightarrow{x}+\sin\phi\,\overrightarrow{y}=\begin{pmatrix} \cos\phi\\ \sin\phi \end{pmatrix}.\qquad(5)$$

What happens when one photon in this state passes through the polarizer $\mathrm{P}_x$? Judging from the behaviour of the collection of photons discussed above, each individual photon passes through the polarizer $\mathrm{P}_x$ with probability $|\cos\phi|^2$, and is blocked at the polarizer, being absorbed or reflected, with probability $1-|\cos\phi|^2=|\sin\phi|^2$. The polarization state $\overrightarrow{\psi}_1$ of a photon that has passed through changes to

$$\overrightarrow{\psi}_1=\overrightarrow{x}=\begin{pmatrix} 1\\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\qquad(6)$$

Each photon is a particle with a definite energy proportional to its frequency, and it does not happen that one photon splits at the polarizer, part of it being blocked and the rest transmitted. Moreover, since the polarizations of all the photons are described by the same equation (5) and are indistinguishable, which photons pass through the polarizer and which are blocked is probabilistic and cannot be predicted.

If photons in the same polarization state (5) are passed through a polarizer $\mathrm{P}_y$ parallel to the $y$ axis, this time they pass through with probability $|\sin\phi|^2$ and are blocked with probability $|\cos\phi|^2$. The polarization state $\overrightarrow{\psi}_1$ of a photon that has passed through becomes

$$\overrightarrow{\psi}_1=\overrightarrow{y}=\begin{pmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\qquad(7)$$

This behaviour of photons is strange. That is, even photons in the same state may pass through the polarizer or be blocked, and which will happen cannot be predicted.

"The result of a measurement on a photon in a definite state can be predicted only probabilistically" is hard to accept as a physical law. The question arises: "In reality, are the polarizations of the photons represented by $\overrightarrow{t}$ of equation (5) perhaps not all in the same state, but is it rather that photons in several different polarization states are statistically mixed?" That is, the idea is that perhaps

• $x$ polarization and $y$ polarization are definite polarization states, and the results of polarization measurements on those photons can be predicted with certainty, but

• the photons represented by $\overrightarrow{t}$ are a statistical mixture of $x$-polarized and $y$-polarized photons in the ratio $|\cos\phi|^2:|\sin\phi|^2$, and as a result the result of a polarization measurement can be predicted only probabilistically.

Indeed, $x$-polarized photons are certainly transmitted through the polarizer $\mathrm{P}_x$, and $y$-polarized photons are certainly blocked. And if photons of the polarization represented by $\overrightarrow{t}$ were a mixture in the above ratio, the probability that they are transmitted through the polarizer $\mathrm{P}_x$ would indeed be $|\cos\phi|^2$.

However, with this interpretation, a contradiction with actual results clearly arises for a different polarization measurement.

Q5 Let $\mathrm{P}_t$ be a polarizer whose transmission axis is parallel to the vector $\overrightarrow{t}$ of equation (5). Find the transmission probability when each of the following photons passes through the polarizer $\mathrm{P}_t$.

(a) An $x$-polarized photon.

(b) A $y$-polarized photon.

(c) A photon that is a statistical mixture of $x$-polarized photons and $y$-polarized photons in the ratio $|\cos\phi|^2:|\sin\phi|^2$.

In the present standard interpretation of quantum mechanics, the state $\overrightarrow{\psi}$ given by equation (5) is, just like $\overrightarrow{x}$ and $\overrightarrow{y}$, a quantum-mechanically definite state. That is, even if the polarization state of a photon is definite, depending on the direction of the polarization measured, there are cases in which whether it is transmitted or blocked can be predicted with certainty, and cases in which which will happen can be predicted only probabilistically.

Beam splitter

An optical element that splits incident light from one direction into outgoing light in two directions is called a beam splitter (BS, half mirror). A BS in general has two possible incident directions and two outgoing directions; as in the figure, the two incident directions are called port 1 and port 2, and the corresponding outgoing directions port $1'$ and port $2'$ (Fig. 5).

To simplify the discussion, we consider as incident light only linearly polarized light having an oscillating electric field component parallel to the reflecting surface (perpendicular to the page) (called S polarization). Then the reflected and transmitted waves are also S-polarized, and polarization need not be considered in the following discussion.

When light of complex amplitude $E_1$ is incident from port 1, the complex amplitudes $E'_1$ and $E'_2$ of the transmitted wave going out at port $1'$ and the reflected wave going out at port $2'$ are obtained from electromagnetism and, using complex numbers $t$ and $r$, are

$$E'_1=tE_1,\qquad E'_2=rE_1$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-3-fig5.png

Fig. 5. Beam splitter (BS)

[In the figure: 入射ポート1 = incident port 1; 入射ポート2 = incident port 2; 出射ポート2′ = outgoing port 2′; 出射ポート1′ = outgoing port 1′; 半透明反射面 = semi-transparent reflecting surface.]

Similarly, when light of complex amplitude $E_2$ is incident from port 2, the complex amplitudes $E'_2$ and $E'_1$ of the transmitted wave at port $2'$ and the reflected wave at port $1'$ are assumed to be given by

$$E'_2=t'E_2,\qquad E'_1=r'E_2$$

When there are incident waves from both port 1 and port 2, the amplitudes of the outgoing waves are the sums of the outgoing waves from the two incident ports, and the relation between the incident waves and the outgoing waves is expressed using a 2-by-2 matrix $U$ as

$$\begin{pmatrix} E'_1\\ E'_2 \end{pmatrix}=U\begin{pmatrix} E_1\\ E_2 \end{pmatrix}\qquad(8)$$

(For the product of a matrix and a vector, see 1. of the "Common mathematical expressions".)

Q6 When incident light comes only from port 1, what are the transmittance $T$ and the reflectance $R$ of the BS? Express them in terms of $t$ and $r$. The transmittance and the reflectance are the ratios of the intensities of the transmitted wave and of the reflected wave, respectively, to the intensity of the incident wave.

Q7 Write down explicitly the 2-by-2 matrix $U$ of equation (8) using $t, t', r, r'$.

Q8 Consider a BS without loss, for which the total intensity of the incident waves and the total intensity of the outgoing waves are equal.

(a) Derive the conditions that the complex coefficients $t, t', r, r'$ must satisfy.

(b) When $t=t'=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, $r=r'$, find the possible values of $r$.

Mach-Zehnder interferometer

An interferometer as in Fig. 6, in which light from one light source is split into two by BS1, the light that has passed along the two paths A and B is made to interfere at BS2, and the light is detected by detectors C and D, is called a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Path B has a longer optical path than path A, and light taking path B acquires an extra phase $\phi$.

The matrix $U$ representing the change of the complex amplitudes of the light at BS1 and BS2 is given by

$$U=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & i\\ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

and, with M1 and M2 perfectly reflecting mirrors, answer the following questions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-3-fig6.png

Fig. 6. Mach-Zehnder interferometer

[In the figure: 光源 = light source; 鏡 M1, 鏡 M2 = mirror M1, mirror M2; 経路 A, 経路 B = path A, path B; 検出器 C, 検出器 D = detector C, detector D.]

Q9 When the complex amplitude of the light from the light source is $E_0$, find the complex amplitudes $E_{\mathrm{AC}}$ and $E_{\mathrm{AD}}$ of the light that passes along path A and goes out to C and D. Neglect the phase changes due to reflection at M1 and M2.

Q10 Similarly, find the complex amplitudes $E_{\mathrm{BC}}$ and $E_{\mathrm{BD}}$ of the light that passes along path B and goes out to C and D.

Q11 Express the intensities $I_{\mathrm{C}}$ and $I_{\mathrm{D}}$ of the light detected at detectors C and D in terms of the intensity $I_0$ of the light source. Draw a graph of the general shape of $I_{\mathrm{C}}$ as a function of the phase difference $\phi$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-3-fig7.png

[Editorial note: blank graph printed on the answer sheet for Q11.]

If light is a collection of photons, the ratio of the statistical probabilities that each individual photon reaches C or D is equal to the ratio of the intensities $I_{\mathrm{C}}$ and $I_{\mathrm{D}}$ of the light observed at detectors C and D. Even if the states of the photons leaving the light source are exactly the same and completely definite, which of C and D a photon reaches cannot be predicted and is probabilistic. This shows that specifying one initial condition does not determine the result uniquely, that is, photons behave non-deterministically.

Also, even if the intensity of the light source is weakened so that two or more photons never exist in this interferometer at the same time, when observed over a long time, the way the ratio of the photon detection probabilities at detectors C and D depends on the phase difference $\phi$ of the two paths does not change. That is, the behaviour of each photon depends on the optical path difference of two spatially separated paths. This shows that each individual photon does not come along one or the other of the paths, but that a single photon is a non-local entity that depends on the conditions of both paths.

Whether this non-determinism and non-locality are the true face of nature was for a long time the subject of debate. Einstein suspected that things only appear so because the description by quantum mechanics is incomplete, and did not accept them. Today, however, non-determinism and non-locality are believed to be not defects of the description by quantum mechanics but the true nature of nature, and research on quantum technologies using them, such as quantum computers and quantum cryptography, is being actively carried out.

The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to three physicists who clarified, by experiments using so-called quantum entangled states, such behaviour of photons that shows non-determinism and non-locality.

[Editorial note: "Common mathematical expressions" printed at the front of the paper and referred to in this problem:

1. Product of a matrix and a column vector. The product of the 2-by-2 matrix $\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ and the column vector $\begin{pmatrix} x\\ y \end{pmatrix}$ is a column vector, defined as follows.

$$\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x\\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} ax+by\\ cx+dy \end{pmatrix}$$

2. Euler's formula. Extending the exponential function to complex numbers, the exponential function and the trigonometric functions can be related. For real $\theta$, the relation

$$e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$$

is called Euler's formula.

3. First-order approximation. For $|h|\ll1$, the approximation

$$(1+h)^\alpha\fallingdotseq1+\alpha h$$

holds, where $\alpha$ is any real number. This follows from the fact that a general differentiable function $f(x)$ can be approximated for $|h|\ll1$ as

$$f(a+h)\fallingdotseq f(a)+f'(a)\,h$$
]

problems.title: Problem 4: Protoplanetary systems
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (75 points)

Protoplanetary systems

The universe was born about 14 billion years ago, and in it there are many galaxies, which are groups of stars. It has become known that in the galaxy in which we live (the Milky Way Galaxy) there are several hundred billion stars (celestial bodies that shine like the Sun), and that many of them are accompanied by planetary systems. Planets outside the solar system are called exoplanets. Exoplanets were first discovered in 1992, and many exoplanets have been discovered since then. Many of the exoplanets discovered bear no resemblance at all to the solar system, but it is thought that planetary systems very similar to the solar system should also exist.

Stars in the Galaxy and the planetary systems around them are thought to be formed from interstellar molecular clouds, which are the high-density parts of the interstellar medium.

When part of a molecular cloud whose main component is the hydrogen molecule $\mathrm{H_2}$ exceeds a certain critical density, it contracts under its own gravity and a protostar (the central star) is born. At that time, the gas formed from the molecular cloud with a large angular momentum (gas containing solid fine particles, that is, dust) does not revolve around the central star surrounding it spherically, but forms a disk and circulates. This disk is called a protoplanetary disk (Fig. 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Protoplanetary disk

[In the figure: 気体，ダスト = gas, dust; 中心星 = central star.]

The material making up a protoplanetary disk consists largely of light elements such as H and He, but contains a small amount of heavy elements. These elements are all gaseous in a high-temperature state such as inside a star, but in the disk the temperature is generally low, and part of the heavy elements has condensed into dust. The disk is thought to consist of gas (regarded as an ideal gas) and about 1 % of dust. The size of the dust is then about $0.1$–$1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$.

In this problem, we proceed with the discussion following the standard model of the theory of solar system formation, which is almost synonymous with the present theory of planetary system formation, in particular the model developed by Chushiro Hayashi, Kiyoshi Nakazawa and others (called the Kyoto model or the Hayashi model), while adding more modern ideas.

In §1, we clarify the shape and thickness of the disk made of the gas of a protoplanetary system (the gas disk). In §2 we clarify the difference between the motion of the gas and the motion of the dust, and in §3 we consider how large planets are formed from the dust in the disk. Finally, we consider the possibility that the dust contracts under its own gravity to produce planetesimals.

Approximation formula: use as necessary

$$\text{for } |x|\ll1,\ \text{with } \alpha \text{ a real number},\ (1+x)^\alpha\fallingdotseq1+\alpha x\qquad(1)$$

In this problem, radiation pressure from the central star is neglected.

§1 Protoplanetary disk

To consider the protoplanetary disk, first, in Q1 to Q3, we consider the density distribution of the gas disk using the mechanical equilibrium condition of the gas making up the disk (in the direction perpendicular to the equatorial plane of the disk), and clarify the shape of the disk. In Q4, we show that, since the gas is in thermal equilibrium with the dust, the temperature of the gas is determined by the luminosity of the central star and the distance from the central star. In Q5, we find the thickness of the disk using the temperature distribution of the gas. The size of the disk considered is assumed to be about that of the solar system.

Q1 As in Fig. 2, let the pressure of the atmosphere at height $z$ above the Earth be $P(z)$ and the mass density of the atmosphere be $\rho(z)$; a uniform gravity acts in the negative $z$-axis direction, and the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is $g$. Take a right circular cylinder of cross-sectional area $S$ whose central axis is parallel to the $z$ axis, consider the balance of forces acting on the atmosphere between $z-\dfrac{\varDelta z}{2}$ and $z+\dfrac{\varDelta z}{2}$ (this is called hydrostatic equilibrium), and then, taking the limit $\varDelta z\to0$, derive the equation

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}P(z)}{\mathrm{d}z}=-\rho(z)\,g$$

The Earth's surface is taken to be a plane, neglecting its curvature.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

The force per unit mass acting on the Earth's atmosphere at height $z$ in the positive $z$-axis direction due to the pressure gradient (this is called the pressure-gradient force) is expressed as

$$-\frac{1}{\rho}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}z}\qquad(2)$$

Thinking in the same way as for the Earth's atmosphere of Q1, consider the hydrostatic equilibrium of the gas in the $z$ direction perpendicular to the equatorial plane of a protoplanetary disk as in Fig. 3. The forces acting on the gas are symmetric with respect to the equatorial plane $z=0$. Here, the gas making up the disk is not in a turbulent state but moves in circles in planes parallel to the equatorial plane of the disk, and seen in the coordinate system moving in the circle, a centrifugal force acts on the gas parallel to the equatorial plane. The component of the pressure-gradient force parallel to the equatorial plane also acts on the gas, but it is neglected here (Fig. 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Hydrostatic equilibrium of the gas of a protoplanetary disk

[In the figure: 中心星 = central star; 重力 = gravity; 圧力勾配力の z 成分 = z component of the pressure-gradient force; 遠心力 = centrifugal force; 動径方向 = radial direction; 円盤の赤道面 = equatorial plane of the disk.]

In the following Q2 and Q3, the dust is neglected and the (ideal) gas is considered.

On partial derivatives

Consider a function $f(x,y)$ of two independent variables $x$ and $y$. The derivative with respect to $x$ with the variable $y$ held constant is written

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,y)$$

and the derivative with respect to $y$ with the variable $x$ held constant is written

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial y}f(x,y)$$

and they are called the partial derivatives of the function $f(x,y)$ with respect to the variables $x$ and $y$, respectively. Here the differentiation symbol is written $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}$ instead of the ordinary derivative $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}$, and $\partial$ is read "round dee". An equation containing partial derivatives is called a partial differential equation.

Q2 As in Fig. 3, in the direction perpendicular to the equatorial plane of the disk ($z$ direction), the $z$ component of the pressure-gradient force and the $z$ component of the gravity from the central star balance. With the central star at the origin, write down the equation expressing hydrostatic equilibrium at the point at radial distance $R$ along the disk and coordinate $z$ perpendicular to the disk, that is, the equation containing the partial derivative with respect to $z$ of the gas pressure $P(R,z)$, using the gas density $\rho(R,z)$ at that point, the mass $M_{\mathrm{c}}$ of the central star, $R$ and the gravitational constant $G$. Find the equation approximated up to the first-order term in $z$, assuming $R\gg z$.

In the following questions, you may use the fact that, with the pressure of the gas $P$, the (absolute) temperature $T$ and the mass density $\rho$, the speed of sound $c_{\mathrm{s}}$ can be written, with the ratio of specific heats of the gas $\gamma$, the mass of a gas molecule $m$ and the Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm{B}}$, as

$$c_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\gamma\frac{P}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\gamma\frac{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{m}}\qquad(3)$$

Q3 Let the angular velocity of a body that moves in a circle of radius $R$ in the equatorial plane of the disk around a central star of mass $M_{\mathrm{c}}$, which stays at rest without moving, subject only to the gravity of the central star, be $\omega_{\mathrm{K}}(R)$ (this is called the Keplerian angular velocity), and assume that the temperature $T(R)$ of the gas in the disk does not depend on the $z$ coordinate.

(a) Express the Keplerian angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm{K}}(R)$ in terms of $G, M_{\mathrm{c}}, R$.

(b) From the partial differential equation with respect to $z$ for the gas pressure $P(R,z)$ found in Q2, the partial differential equation for the gas density $\rho(R,z)$

$$\frac{1}{\rho}\,\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial z}=-az\qquad(4)$$

can be derived. Express the coefficient $a$, which does not depend on $z$, in terms of $c_{\mathrm{s}}, \gamma, \omega_{\mathrm{K}}$.

Defining the quantity $h(R)$ called the scale height by

$$h(R)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\,\frac{c_{\mathrm{s}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{K}}(R)}\qquad(5)$$

and the mass surface density of the disk $\varSigma(R)$ by

$$\varSigma(R)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\rho(R,z)\,\mathrm{d}z$$

the gas density $\rho(R,z)$ can be obtained, by integrating both sides of equation (4) with respect to $z$, as

$$\rho(R,z)=\rho(R,0)\exp\left[-\frac{z^2}{2h(R)^2}\right]\qquad(6)$$

Here the exponential function $e^x$ has been written as $\exp(x)$.

(c) Taking as the horizontal axis the dimensionless coordinate $\widehat{z}=\dfrac{z}{h(R)}$ and as the vertical axis the dimensionless gas density $\widehat{\rho}(\widehat{z})=\dfrac{\rho(R,\widehat{z})}{\rho(R,0)}$, sketch the general shape of the graph of equation (6), and state briefly the meaning of the scale height $h(R)$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-4-fig4.png

[Editorial note: blank axes printed on the answer sheet for Q3 (c).]

Temperature of the dust

Consider the case in which only one dust grain exists around the central star. If the heat given to the dust per unit time is $\varGamma$ and the heat emitted by the dust per unit time is $\varLambda$, then when the dust is in a state of thermal equilibrium at constant temperature,

$$\varGamma=\varLambda\qquad(7)$$

holds.

The dust is assumed to be a black body that is heated by absorbing, over all wavelengths, only the radiant energy of electromagnetic waves from the central star. The energy $I$ of electromagnetic waves radiated per unit area and per unit time from a black body at temperature $T$ is expressed as

$$I=\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}\,T^4\qquad(8)$$

Here $\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, given by

$$\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}\fallingdotseq5.67\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{Wm^{-2}K^{-4}}$$

Let the luminosity of the central star (the total energy of light emitted per unit time) be $L$, the distance from the central star to the dust be $R$, and let the dust be a sphere of radius $r\,(\ll R)$. The total energy radiated from the central star spreads into the space outside the sphere through a spherical surface of radius $R$. The dust absorbs the energy passing through the area of its great circle, $\pi r^2$.

Q4 Derive that the temperature $T$ of dust in thermal equilibrium is expressed, with the mean distance between the Sun and the Earth taken as $1\,\mathrm{au}$, the luminosity of the Sun (the energy radiated per unit time) as $L_\odot$, and $T_0$ a constant, as

$$T=T_0\left(\frac{R}{1\,\mathrm{au}}\right)^\alpha\left(\frac{L}{L_\odot}\right)^\beta\qquad(9)$$

and find the exponents $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as simple fractions.

$L_\odot=3.84\times10^{26}\,\mathrm{W}$, $1\,\mathrm{au}=1.50\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, and using these values it turns out that $T_0\fallingdotseq2.8\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{K}$. This temperature $T_0$ gives the temperature of dust near the Earth in the solar system.

Thickness of the protoplanetary disk

Q5 The temperature of the gas making up the disk (regarded as an ideal gas) is thought to become equal to the temperature of the dust in thermal equilibrium.

(a) Derive that the speed of sound at a position at distance $R$ from a central star of luminosity $L$ is expressed, with $c_0$ a constant, as

$$c_{\mathrm{s}}=c_0\left(\frac{R}{1\,\mathrm{au}}\right)^b\left(\frac{L}{L_\odot}\right)^c$$

and find the exponents $b, c$ each as simple fractions.

(b) Letting the scale height of the disk at a position at distance $R$ from the central star be $h(R)$, derive that the dimensionless quantity $\dfrac{h(R)}{R}$ is expressed, with $K$ a constant, as

$$\frac{h(R)}{R}=K\left(\frac{R}{1\,\mathrm{au}}\right)^d\left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{c}}}{M_\odot}\right)^e\left(\frac{L}{L_\odot}\right)^f\qquad(10)$$

and find the exponents $d, e, f$ each as simple fractions. Here $M_\odot=1.99\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$ is the mass of the Sun.

Taking the gas to be neutral molecular hydrogen gas and using Q4 and the numerical values given here, if the central star is the Sun ($M_{\mathrm{c}}=M_\odot$, $L=L_\odot$), at the position of the Earth ($R=1\,\mathrm{au}$)

$$\frac{h}{R}\fallingdotseq3.6\times10^{-2}$$

From this it can be seen that this gas disk is thin.

§2 Motion of the gas and the dust

We consider the mechanical equilibrium of the gas and the dust in the direction parallel to the equatorial plane, which was not considered in §1.

The gas and dust making up the protoplanetary disk are subject to gravity from the central star and move in circles around the central star. In general the dust then has a larger angular velocity of rotation than the gas, and the dust receives a resistive force from the gas, gradually decreases its angular velocity (angular momentum), and comes to fall towards the central star. Here, assuming that the resistive force between the dust and the gas can be neglected, we consider how large a difference arises between their angular velocities.

Q6 Consider gas moving in a circle of radius $R$ with angular velocity $\omega$ around the central star in the equatorial plane of the disk. Seen in the coordinate system moving in the circle, only the gravity from the central star and the centrifugal force act on the dust, but on the gas, in addition to the gravity from the central star and the centrifugal force, a force due to the pressure gradient in the direction parallel to the equatorial plane (the radial direction) acts.

(a) When the pressure of the gas at the point at distance $R$ from the central star is $P(R)$ and its mass density is $\rho(R)$, write down the radial equation of motion per unit mass of the gas moving in a circle with angular velocity $\omega$ at that point (the equation of balance of the forces, centrifugal force, gravity and pressure-gradient force, in the rotating coordinate system), using $R$, $\omega$, $\rho(R)$, the Keplerian angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm{K}}$ and the radial pressure gradient $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}R}$.

(b) Using a small positive dimensionless quantity $\eta$, the angular velocity $\omega$ of the gas at the position at distance $R$ from the central star can be written as

$$\omega\fallingdotseq\omega_{\mathrm{K}}\,(1-\eta)\qquad(11)$$

Express $\eta$ in terms of $c_{\mathrm{s}}, v_{\mathrm{K}}, P, R$, the pressure gradient $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}R}$ and the ratio of specific heats $\gamma$. Here $c_{\mathrm{s}}, v_{\mathrm{K}}, P$ are, respectively, the speed of sound, the Keplerian velocity (the speed of a body rotating around the central star with the Keplerian angular velocity) and the gas pressure at the position at distance $R$ from the central star; use the approximation formula (1) ($\alpha=\dfrac{1}{2}$).

Assuming the pressure gradient to be $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}R}=-\dfrac{P}{R}$, and with $M_{\mathrm{c}}=M_\odot$, $L=L_\odot$, it can be seen from the result of Q6 (b) that the value of $\eta$ at $R=1\,\mathrm{au}$ is of the order of $1\times10^{-3}\ (\ll1)$.

§3 Formation of planetesimals in the protoplanetary disk

In planetary systems such as the solar system there are rocky planets, the Earth, Mars, Venus and Mercury, giant gas planets such as Jupiter and Saturn, and further ice planets, Uranus and Neptune. However, how such large planets are formed from tiny dust in a protoplanetary disk is not sufficiently understood so far.

For dust revolving around the central star in the disk, while the dust size is very small, the resistive force (per unit mass) from the gas is very large, and the dust circulates around the central star at almost the same speed as the gas. When the dust grows by collision and coalescence to centimetre size, the resistive force (per unit mass) acting from the gas becomes small, and it comes to move independently of the gas. Then, due to the $z$ component of the gravity from the central star, the dust gradually settles onto the equatorial plane of the disk. As a result, the density of dust increases on the equatorial plane (Fig. 4a). When the density of dust increases, collisions between dust grains occur frequently and they coalesce and grow further, and the dust grows to metre size. Since the orbital angular velocity of metre-size dust is smaller than $\omega_{\mathrm{K}}$, the gravity acting from the central star is larger than the centrifugal force, and the dust falls towards the central star. For this reason, it has been thought that dust cannot grow into kilometre-size planetesimals.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-4-fig5.png

Fig. 4a. High-density dust layer formed on the equatorial plane of the protoplanetary disk

[In the figure: 高密度ダスト層 = high-density dust layer; 赤道面 = equatorial plane; 中心星 = central star.]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-4-fig6.png

Fig. 4b. Planetesimals formed on the equatorial plane of the protoplanetary disk

[In the figure: 微惑星 = planetesimals; 赤道面 = equatorial plane; 中心星 = central star.]

In such circumstances, the idea was proposed that in the centimetre-size dust that has settled onto the equatorial plane, condensation occurs because of instability due to self-gravity (the gravity of the dust itself), so that it can jump over the dangerous metre-size region at once and grow into kilometre-size planetesimals*1. Once kilometre-size planetesimals are formed (Fig. 4b), the resistive force (per unit mass) from the gas becomes very small, and planetesimals of this size circulate around the central star at almost the Keplerian angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm{K}}$. As a result, the planetesimals absorb gas, collide with one another and so on, forming still larger protoplanets of about the size of the Moon, and it is thought that the various planets of the present solar system can also be formed.

*1 However, whether kilometre-size planetesimals can actually be formed is the subject of various discussions and is unresolved.

Below, we consider the possibility that dust contracts under its own gravity and produces planetesimals.

Q7 As in Fig. 5, a spherical planetesimal of mass $m$ and radius $r$ revolves on a circular orbit at distance $R$ from the centre C of a spherical central star of mass $M_{\mathrm{c}}$. Here $m\ll M_{\mathrm{c}}$, and the central star does not move. The rotation of the planetesimal is synchronized with its revolution, and the rotation period and the revolution period are equal. Then the point A in the planetesimal that is farthest from point C at a certain instant always remains farthest from point C afterwards. The deformation of the central star and of the planetesimal can be neglected. The masses of the central star and of the planetesimal are both distributed spherically symmetrically about the centres of the respective bodies, and the universal gravitation exerted by the central star and the planetesimal on bodies on their surfaces and outside, and the universal gravitation exerted by external bodies on the central star and the planetesimal, can be obtained as if the masses of the central star and the planetesimal were concentrated at the single point of their centres.

In the following (a), (b), consider the coordinate system rotating about the centre C of the central star with angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm{K}}$ together with the point A on the planetesimal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2024-4-fig7.png

Fig. 5. Central star and planetesimal

[In the figure: 中心星 = central star; 微惑星 = planetesimal.]

(a) At the point A on the planetesimal farthest from point C, find the resultant force $F$, in the direction away from the centre S of the planetesimal, of the universal gravitation from the central star and the centrifugal force acting per unit mass, in the approximation up to the first-order term in $r$, assuming $\dfrac{r}{R}\ll1$.

(b) As long as the magnitude $F$ of the resultant force per unit mass found in the previous part (a) does not exceed the magnitude of the universal gravitation acting from the planetesimal S, S is not destroyed. Find the lower limit $\rho_{\mathrm{R}}$ of the mean density $\rho$ of the planetesimal S for it not to be destroyed (this is called the Roche density), using $R$ and $M_{\mathrm{c}}$.

It is known from general considerations that the condition for planetesimals to be formed by condensation can be written as

$$Q=\frac{c_{\mathrm{s}}\omega_{\mathrm{K}}}{\pi G\varSigma}<1$$

and $Q$ is called the Toomre Q value. $\varSigma$ is
the mass surface density of the disk. Here, ignoring the numerical coefficient $\sqrt{\gamma}$, the condition is expressed as*2

$$Q=\frac{{\omega_{\mathrm{K}}}^2h}{\pi G\varSigma}<1\qquad(12)$$

Earlier we stated that the thickness of the gas disk found in Q5 is "thin", but the thickness of a disk satisfying condition (12) is very thin, and the thickness of the gas disk does not satisfy condition (12)*3. On the other hand, when the size of the dust in the disk grows to about a centimetre, the dust settles quietly onto the equatorial plane of the disk ($z=0$) due to the $z$ component of the gravity received from the central star, and the dust is distributed in a disk shape. The disk made of the dust distributed in a disk shape (the dust disk) becomes very thin and satisfies condition (12).

To estimate the mass surface density $\varSigma$ of the gas disk or the dust disk, let us imagine making a disk by smearing out the masses of the planets of the solar system. Such a model is called the model of the restored solar system. Following this model, the mass surface density $\varSigma$ of the disk at distance $R=1\,\mathrm{au}$ from the central star is simply taken, using the mass of the Earth $M_\oplus\fallingdotseq5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}$, to be

$$\varSigma=\frac{M_\oplus}{\pi R^2}\qquad(13)$$

Q8 In this Q8, use equation (13) giving the mass surface density of the disk. Also, if necessary, use $M_\odot=1.99\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $M_\oplus=5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

(a) Express the upper limit at $R=1\,\mathrm{au}$ of the value $\dfrac{h}{R}$ of a disk satisfying the planetesimal formation condition (12) in terms of the Earth mass $M_\oplus$ and the mass of the central star $M_\odot$ (taken equal to the solar mass). From this it can be seen that the thickness of the gas disk $\dfrac{h}{R}\fallingdotseq0.036$ does not satisfy condition (12).

(b) When the scale height $h$ of the dust disk satisfies condition (12), condensation occurs. It is known that the mass $m=\varSigma(2\pi h)^2$ within the area $(2\pi h)^2$ of the disk surface then aggregates to form a planetesimal. When condensation occurs with the value $\dfrac{h}{R}$ of the dust disk at its upper limit, how many times the Earth mass $M_\oplus$ is the mass $m_{\mathrm{c}}$ of the planetesimal formed? Give the numerical value to 1 significant figure.

From the result of Q8 (b), it can be seen that the radius of a planetesimal of mass $m_{\mathrm{c}}$ formed is of kilometre size. As stated before, once kilometre-size planetesimals are formed, it is thought that still larger protoplanets of about the size of the Moon are formed, and that the various planets of the present solar system can also be formed.

*2 Using the fact that the density $\rho$ of the disk can be written approximately as

$$\rho=\frac{\varSigma}{h}=\frac{\varSigma}{c_{\mathrm{s}}}\omega_{\mathrm{K}}$$

a result that differs from the generally obtained planetesimal formation condition (12) only slightly in the dimensionless numerical coefficient can be obtained from the expression for the Roche density found in Q7.

*3 When the central star is the Sun, the Roche density at a distance of 1 au from the central star is $\rho_{\mathrm{R}}\fallingdotseq4\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and further, the density on the equatorial plane of the gas disk obtained using the model of the restored solar system is $\rho_{\mathrm{a}}\fallingdotseq2\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Incidentally, the density of air at 1 atmosphere and room temperature is $\rho_{\mathrm{E}}\fallingdotseq1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

problems.title: Problem 1: Kinetic theory of real gases
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (75 points)

Kinetic theory of real gases

In the air at the Earth's surface, more than $10^{19}$ gas molecules per $1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ fly around with speeds of several $100\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The pressure that a gas confined in a container exerts on the walls of the container is due to the forces exerted when such a large number of gas molecules collide with the walls of the container. If the motion of each individual gas molecule obeys classical mechanics, then by solving the equations of motion of the gas molecules one can obtain the trajectories of the individual gas molecules, and from them one can study macroscopic quantities such as pressure, and changes of state of the gas. Below, we examine how the mechanics of microscopic particles such as gas molecules gives rise to macroscopic physical quantities such as pressure.

[I] Kinetic theory of a gas of free particles

Consider a gas consisting of $N$ molecules confined in a spherical container of radius $R$. Below, the gas molecules can be regarded as point masses of mass $m$, and we call them particles. First, consider the case in which the particles exert no forces on each other and move freely. The particles are numbered by $i$, and particle $i$ moves with speed $v_i$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Q1. When particle $i$ collides with the wall of the spherical container at angle of incidence $\theta_i$, find the magnitude of the change in the momentum of the particle in one collision. You may assume that the collisions between the particles and the wall of the container are elastic.

Q2. Find the number of times that particle $i$ of Q1 collides with the wall of the container during a time $\Delta t$. From this, find the force $F_i$, where $F_i\Delta t$ is the total magnitude of the impulse, in the direction perpendicular to the wall surface, that particle $i$ gives to the wall during the time $\Delta t$.

Q3. Show that the force per unit area (pressure) $P$ that the wall of the container receives from the collisions of the particles satisfies the relation

$$PV=\frac{2}{3}K \qquad (1)$$

where $V$ is the volume of the container and $K$ is the sum of the kinetic energies of the particles,

$$K=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{2}m{v_i}^2 .$$

The equation of state of an ideal gas is given, using the Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ and the absolute temperature $T$, by

$$PV=Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T .$$

From this and the result of Q3, the average kinetic energy per particle is given by

$$\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2}=\frac{3}{2}k_{\mathrm{B}}T \qquad (2)$$

and we see that it is related to the temperature, a macroscopic physical quantity. Here

$$\overline{v^2}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{v_i}^2$$

is called the mean square of the particle velocities.

Q4. The atomic weight of the noble-gas element Ar (argon) is 39.9. From this, for Ar atoms in Ar gas at $T=300\ \mathrm{K}$, calculate the square root of the mean square velocity, $\sqrt{\overline{v^2}}$, as a measure of the particle speed. The Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is $1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}$ and the Avogadro constant is $6.02\times10^{23}/\mathrm{mol}$.

[II] Motion of microscopic particles and long-time averages

Next, we consider the relation between the motion of microscopic particles and the observed quantities obtained as macroscopic physical quantities. Below, the position coordinate, velocity and acceleration of particle $i$ at time $t$ are denoted by $\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)$, $\overrightarrow{v_i}(t)$, $\overrightarrow{a_i}(t)$, respectively. By the equation of motion, the force acting on particle $i$ is $\overrightarrow{F_i}(t)=m\overrightarrow{a_i}(t)$.

When the behaviour of microscopic particles is observed, we consider that the observed macroscopic physical quantity corresponds to the long-time average of the corresponding physical quantity $Q(t)$ of the microscopic particles,

$$\lim_{T_{\mathrm{obs}}\to\infty}\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}Q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=\langle Q\rangle .$$

We therefore consider integrating the physical quantity $Q(t)=\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}(t)$ from time $t=0$ to $t=T_{\mathrm{obs}}$. Here $\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}$ denotes the inner product (scalar product) of the vectors $\overrightarrow{A}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$.

Q5. Show, using the equation of motion, that the relation

$$\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=m\Big[\overrightarrow{r_i}(T_{\mathrm{obs}})\cdot\overrightarrow{v_i}(T_{\mathrm{obs}})-\overrightarrow{r_i}(0)\cdot\overrightarrow{v_i}(0)\Big]-m\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}|\overrightarrow{v_i}(t)|^2\,\mathrm{d}t$$

holds.

Q6. By dividing the result of Q5 by $T_{\mathrm{obs}}$ and then letting the observation time $T_{\mathrm{obs}}$ tend to infinity, we obtain the long-time average of the particle motion $\big\langle\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}\big\rangle$. In this process the first term on the right-hand side of the equation of Q5, $m\Big[\overrightarrow{r_i}(T_{\mathrm{obs}})\cdot\overrightarrow{v_i}(T_{\mathrm{obs}})-\overrightarrow{r_i}(0)\cdot\overrightarrow{v_i}(0)\Big]$, does not contribute to the long-time average; explain the reason. By summing the quantity obtained in this way over all particles, with $K$ as the long-time average of the sum of the kinetic energies of the particles, the relation

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}\right\rangle=\boxed{\mathtt{A}}\times K$$

is obtained. Give the number that goes into $\boxed{\mathtt{A}}$.

Q7. Let us apply this result to the case of free particles. The only forces acting on the particles are the forces that the particles receive from the wall at collisions. If the origin of the position vectors is taken at the centre of the spherical container, a particle receives a force directed towards the centre of the container (in the direction of $-\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)$) when $|\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)|=R$. From this, show that, using the pressure $P$ and the volume of the sphere $V=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}R^3$, one can write

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}\right\rangle=\boxed{\mathtt{B}}\times PV$$

and give the number that goes into $\boxed{\mathtt{B}}$.

The quantity on the left-hand side of the equations of Q6 and Q7 is called the virial, and the equation of Q6, which shows the relation between the sum of the kinetic energies of the particles and the virial, is sometimes called the virial theorem. From the results of Q6 and Q7, the relation (1), which holds for the free particles obtained in [I], is obtained.

[III] Kinetic theory of a gas of interacting particles

Next, consider the case in which, in addition to the forces received from the wall, intermolecular forces (forces received from other molecules) act on the particles. That is, the force $\overrightarrow{F_i}$ acting on particle $i$ is written as

$$\overrightarrow{F_i}(t)=\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{wall}}(t)+\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)$$

where $\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{wall}}(t)$ and $\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)$ are, respectively, the force that particle $i$ receives from the wall and the force that particle $i$ receives from the particles other than $i$. As for the sum $K$ of the kinetic energies on the right-hand side of the equation of Q6, it is known that the relation (2) between the average kinetic energy and the absolute temperature $T$ holds even when intermolecular forces act. Also, since the contribution of the force $\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{wall}}(t)$ received from the wall to the virial is expressed in terms of the pressure by the result of Q7, we obtain

$$PV=Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T+\frac{1}{3}\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}\right\rangle \qquad (3)$$

Here the second term on the right-hand side represents the deviation from an ideal gas; below we estimate this term.

Q8. Considering that the intermolecular forces arise from forces acting between two particles, consider the case in which

$$\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}(t)$$

Here $\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}(t)$ is the force that particle $j$ exerts on particle $i$, and $\overrightarrow{f_{ii}}(t)=0$. Show that in this case

$$\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Big[\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)-\overrightarrow{r_j}(t)\Big]\cdot\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}(t) .$$

Consider the case in which the intermolecular force $\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}(t)$ that particle $j$ exerts on particle $i$ is parallel to the vector $\overrightarrow{r_{ij}}=\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)-\overrightarrow{r_j}(t)$ directed from particle $j$ to particle $i$, and its magnitude depends only on the distance between the particles $r_{ij}=|\overrightarrow{r_{ij}}|$, that is,

$$\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{r_{ij}}}{r_{ij}}\,f(r_{ij}) .$$

Further, suppose that the magnitude of the force $f(r_{ij})$ is expressed, using a certain function $U(r)$, as

$$f(r)=-\frac{\mathrm{d}U(r)}{\mathrm{d}r} .$$

This function $U(r)$ is called the potential energy of the intermolecular force, and can be interpreted as the potential energy of a particle at distance $r$ from the particle under consideration. Then, from Q8, the virial is expressed as

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\langle\sideset{}{'}\sum_{j=1}^{N}r_{ij}\frac{\mathrm{d}U(r_{ij})}{\mathrm{d}r_{ij}}\right\rangle .$$

Here the prime on the sum over $j$ on the right-hand side, $\displaystyle\sideset{}{'}\sum_{j=1}^{N}$, indicates that the sum does not include the term $j=i$.

To obtain the equation of state from equation (3) using this, one has to calculate the long-time average on the right-hand side, which is difficult in general. We therefore assume that, as seen from particle $i$, the other particles are distributed uniformly in the region where the potential energy $U(r)$ is at most of the order of the average kinetic energy of the particles, and we estimate the long-time average approximately by the average over a uniform spatial distribution in the region $U(r)<k_{\mathrm{B}}T$.

$U(r)$ usually has a shape like that in Fig. 2: at small $r$ a large repulsive force acts ($f=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}r}>0$), and outside that a weak attractive force ($f<0$) acts. Let $r_{\mathrm{c}}$ be the distance at which $U(r)=k_{\mathrm{B}}T$, and assume that particles $j$ are uniformly distributed in the region $r_{ij}>r_{\mathrm{c}}$. The average number of particles at distance $r$ from the particle $i$ under consideration is given by the product of the volume $4\pi r^2\mathrm{d}r$ of the region enclosed by the sphere of radius $r$ and the sphere of radius $r+\mathrm{d}r$ (with $\mathrm{d}r$ a small length, a spherical shell of radius $r$ and thickness $\mathrm{d}r$) and the average number density of particles $\rho=\dfrac{N}{V}$, i.e. by $4\pi r^2\rho\,\mathrm{d}r$. From this the virial is expressed as

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{2}N\int_{r_{\mathrm{c}}}^{\infty}r\frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}r}4\pi r^2\rho\,\mathrm{d}r .$$

Here, since the spatial average does not depend on particle $i$, the sum over $i$ has been replaced by the number of particles $N$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Q9. Show that from this expression the virial is given by

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}\right\rangle=-\frac{3V}{2}\left(\frac{N}{V}\right)^2\left[-k_{\mathrm{B}}T\frac{4\pi}{3}r_c^3-4\pi\int_{r_c}^{\infty}r^2U(r)\,\mathrm{d}r\right]$$

where $r^3U(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$.

Q10. For systems with weak intermolecular forces, such as the noble-gas elements, the Lennard-Jones potential

$$U(r)=4\varepsilon\left[\left(\frac{d}{r}\right)^{12}-\left(\frac{d}{r}\right)^{6}\right]$$

is often adopted as the potential of the intermolecular force. Here $\varepsilon$ and $d$ are positive quantities, having the magnitudes of the binding energy of two particles and of the order of the particle diameter, respectively. Using this potential and approximating the lower limit $r_c$ of the integral in the expression obtained in Q9 by $d$, the equation of state obtained from equation (3) can be arranged in the form

$$PV=Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T-V\left(\frac{N}{V}\right)^2(a-bk_{\mathrm{B}}T) \qquad (4)$$

Find the mathematical expressions corresponding to $a$ and $b$.

Q11. For real gases, the equation of state

$$P+a\left(\frac{N}{V}\right)^2=\frac{Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T}{V-Nb} \qquad (5)$$

has been proposed and is called the van der Waals equation of state. Here $a$ and $b$ are constants; the second term on the left-hand side, containing $a$, represents the correction due to the intermolecular attraction, and the term $Nb$ in the denominator on the right-hand side represents the effect of the excluded volume, by which the space in which the gas molecules can move around becomes smaller because of the intermolecular repulsion. Show that when the excluded volume $Nb$ in the van der Waals equation of state is sufficiently small compared with the total volume $V$, that is, when $\dfrac{Nb}{V}\ll1$, the equation of state (5) can be expressed in the form of equation (4). You may use the approximation $(1+x)^{-1}\fallingdotseq1-x$ for $|x|\ll1$.

Q12. For argon atoms, the parameters $\varepsilon$, $d$ of the Lennard-Jones potential are given as

$$\varepsilon=1.725\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J},\qquad d=3.410\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$$

Using these, calculate the values of the van der Waals parameters $a$, $b$. Here you may approximate $r_c$ by $d$. Also, in this case, evaluate, at standard conditions ($1$ atm $=1013\ \mathrm{hPa}$, $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}=273\ \mathrm{K}$), the ratio $\dfrac{a}{P}\left(\dfrac{N}{V}\right)^2$ of the correction term due to the intermolecular attraction to the pressure in the van der Waals equation of state, and the ratio $\dfrac{Nb}{V}$ of the excluded volume to the volume of the gas. The volume of 1 mole of an ideal gas at standard conditions is $22.4\,\mathrm{L}$, and since argon gas is close to an ideal gas, you may use the volume of the ideal gas when calculating the ratios of the corrections.

problems.title: Problem 2: Electrostatic Carnot cycle
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (75 points)

Electrostatic Carnot cycle

A capacitor is a device that stores charge on its positive and negative plates. The stored charge $Q$ and the potential difference $V$ between the plates are related by $Q=CV$. The constant $C$ is determined by the shape of the capacitor plates, their separation, etc., and is called the capacitance. In this problem we investigate the properties of circuits using capacitors.

[I] Electrostatic energy of a capacitor

As in Fig. 1, a battery of emf $V$, a capacitor of capacitance $C$, a resistor of resistance $R$ and two switches SW1, SW2 are connected. Starting from the state in which the charge of the capacitor is 0, SW2 is opened and SW1 is closed to charge the capacitor. After the charging is complete, SW1 is opened, and then SW2 is closed to discharge the capacitor.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Q1. Find the work done by the battery until the charging of the capacitor is complete.

Q2. Let $t=0$ be the time at which SW2 is closed, let $Q(t)$ be the charge of the capacitor at time $t\geqq0$ (the charge of the upper plate in Fig. 1), and let $I(t)$ be the current flowing in the circuit (the arrow in Fig. 1 is the positive direction).

(a) From the condition that the sum of the potential differences around the closed circuit is 0, find the relation satisfied by $Q(t)$ and $I(t)$.

(b) By differentiating the above relation with respect to $t$, derive the differential equation satisfied by $I(t)$, that is, the expression of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}$ in terms of $I(t)$.

(c) Find the current $I(0)$ immediately after SW2 is closed, and find the solution $I(t)$ of the above differential equation.

(d) In the discharging process, by integrating with respect to time the Joule heat generated in the resistor per unit time, $R\big(I(t)\big)^2$, find the Joule heat generated up to time $T(>0)$.

The total Joule heat due to the discharge, obtained by letting $T\to\infty$ in the above result, does not depend on the resistance $R$, and can be understood as the energy of the electric field (electrostatic energy) possessed by the charged capacitor. Then there is a difference between the work done by the battery and the energy possessed by the charged capacitor, and it appears that the law of conservation of energy is violated. This is because, in the process of charging the capacitor, we did not take into account the circuit resistance that is always present in a circuit and the Joule heat generated there.

Let us reconsider the process in which the battery charges the capacitor, using Fig. 2, to which the circuit resistance (resistance $r$) has been added.

Q3. Let $t=0$ be the time at which the switch SW is closed, let $Q(t)$ be the charge of the capacitor at time $t\geqq0$ (the charge of the upper plate in Fig. 2, $Q(0)=0$), and let $I(t)$ be the current flowing in the circuit (the arrow in Fig. 2 is the positive direction).

(a) From the condition that the sum of the potential differences around the closed circuit is 0, find the relation satisfied by $Q(t)$ and $I(t)$.

(b) By differentiating this relation with respect to $t$, derive the differential equation satisfied by $I(t)$.

(c) Find the value of the initial condition $I(0)$, and find the solution $I(t)$ of the above differential equation.

(d) How much Joule heat is generated in the circuit resistance during charging, up to time $T(>0)$?

If we let $T\to\infty$ in the above result, we see that the work done by the battery during charging becomes the Joule heat in the circuit resistance and the energy of the capacitor, and the law of conservation of energy is satisfied. Moreover, since this conclusion does not depend on the circuit resistance $r$, it does not depend on how fast the charging is.

[II] Charge transfer without energy loss

The Joule heat in the circuit resistance generated when a capacitor is charged is an energy loss accompanying the charging. Such losses occur not only in charging but whenever charge is transferred, so we consider a way to eliminate them. Below, the capacitor is a parallel-plate capacitor, and you may use the fact that the electrostatic energy $U$ of the capacitor is $U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\dfrac{1}{2}QV=\dfrac{1}{2}CV^2$, where $C$ is the capacitance, $Q$ the charge and $V$ the potential difference of the capacitor.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

The circuit of Fig. 3 (circuit resistance $r$) is prepared. The left plate of the capacitor is fixed to the apparatus, but the right plate can be moved left and right from outside, changing the plate separation. Let $C(x)$ be the capacitance when the position of the right plate is $x$. With the position of the right plate at $x$, the switch SW is closed, and after a sufficiently long time the charge $Q$ is stored on the right plate.

From this state, SW is opened and the position of the right plate is moved from $x$ by a small amount $\mathrm{d}x$; then the potential difference $V$ of the capacitor (the potential of the right plate relative to the left plate) changed by a small amount $\mathrm{d}V$. In this process the charge of the capacitor does not change, so it is called an isocharge process.

Q4. In this small isocharge process, we calculate the small mechanical work $\mathrm{d}W_Q$ that the capacitor does on the outside through the motion of the right plate.

(a) Express the force $F(x)$ due to the electric field acting on the right plate when the right plate is at position $x$ in a form proportional to $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}C}{\mathrm{d}x}$. The positive direction of the force $F$ is the direction of increasing $x$. (Hint: the force acting on the plate is the rate of change of the energy of the system when the plate is moved, with a minus sign.)

(b) Calculate the small work $\mathrm{d}W_Q$ from $\mathrm{d}W_Q=F(x)\mathrm{d}x$, write it in a form proportional to $\mathrm{d}V$, and express the proportionality coefficient using appropriate ones of $Q$, $V$.

In this isocharge process no current flows and no energy loss due to the circuit resistance $r$ occurs, so the work that the capacitor did on the outside is equal to the decrease of the electrostatic energy of the capacitor.

Next, after returning the plate to position $x$, SW is closed. Closing SW causes no transfer of charge, and the force acting on the plate does not change either. After that, when the plate is moved from position $x$ to $x+\mathrm{d}x$, a small charge $\mathrm{d}Q$ is added to the capacitor, and the charge of the right plate becomes $Q+\mathrm{d}Q$. In this process the potential difference $V$ of the capacitor is fixed, so it is called an isopotential process.

Q5. In this small isopotential process, we calculate the small mechanical work $\mathrm{d}W_V$ that the capacitor does on the outside through the motion of the right plate.

(a) The work $\mathrm{d}W_V=F(x)\mathrm{d}x$ is the same amount as the work $\mathrm{d}W_Q$ found in the previous question. Write the work $\mathrm{d}W_V$ in a form proportional to $\mathrm{d}Q$, and express the proportionality coefficient using appropriate ones of $Q$, $V$.

(b) In this isopotential process, write the work $\mathrm{d}P$ done by the battery and the change $\mathrm{d}U$ of the electrostatic energy of the capacitor in forms proportional to $\mathrm{d}Q$, and express each proportionality coefficient using appropriate ones of $Q$, $V$.

As can be seen from the above results, when the charge is increased or decreased in this isopotential process, there is no Joule heat loss due to the circuit resistance. Since this conclusion is derived from relations between small quantities, the operation of changing the position of the plate (increasing or decreasing the capacitance) must be performed sufficiently slowly. This fact corresponds to the general property that a quasi-static process (a process in which the change of state is performed sufficiently slowly while maintaining equilibrium) is a reversible process (not accompanied by the generation of Joule heat).

[III] Electrostatic Carnot cycle

As in Fig. 4, a capacitor whose capacitance can be changed by moving its right plate and two batteries of emf $V_1$ and $V_2$ ($V_1<V_2$) are connected with two switches SW1, SW2. By repeating isopotential processes and isocharge processes, mechanical and electrical work can be exchanged between the capacitor and the outside. Because of the analogy with a heat engine, in this problem this system is called the electrostatic Carnot cycle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

The state of the capacitor is specified by the two variables: its charge $Q$ (the charge of the right plate) and the potential difference $V$ (the potential of the right plate relative to the left plate). One cycle is performed by carrying out the following four processes in succession. In all the processes, the operation of changing the position of the plate is performed sufficiently slowly.

1) A$\to$B: In state A, SW1 is closed and SW2 is open. The charge of the capacitor is $Q_1$ and the potential difference is $V_1$. SW1 is opened and the plate position is moved so that the potential difference increases to $V_2$.

2) B$\to$C: SW2 is closed and the plate position is moved so that the charge increases to $Q_2$.

3) C$\to$D: SW2 is opened and the plate position is moved so that the potential difference decreases to $V_1$.

4) D$\to$A: SW1 is closed and the plate position is moved so that the charge decreases to $Q_1$, returning to state A.

Q6. On the $Q$-$V$ diagram of the answer sheet, draw the above cycle with a solid line, clearly marking the positions of the states A, B, C, D.

Q7. In a certain change of state, let $\varDelta U$ be the increase of the electrostatic energy of the capacitor, $\varDelta P$ the energy supply (electrical work) from the external system to the capacitor through the circuit, and $\varDelta W$ the mechanical work that the capacitor does on the outside through the right plate. These physical quantities are not small quantities.

(a) Write the relation that holds among the three quantities $\varDelta U$, $\varDelta P$, $\varDelta W$.

(b) For each of the four processes of the cycle, express $\varDelta U$, $\varDelta P$, $\varDelta W$ using appropriate ones of $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $V_1$, $V_2$.

Q8. We examine the transfer of energy in this cycle [A$\to$B$\to$C$\to$D$\to$A].

(a) How much work does the capacitor do on the outside through the right plate in one cycle?

(b) Express in terms of $V_1$, $V_2$ the efficiency of this cycle, that is, the ratio of the work that the capacitor does on the outside to the energy (electrical work) supplied to the capacitor from the high-emf side.

Q9. When the reverse cycle [A$\to$D$\to$C$\to$B$\to$A], in which all the processes are reversed, is run, it operates as a pump carrying charge to the side of higher potential, and works as a device that charges the battery on the high-emf side. In this reverse cycle, let $C_{\min}$ be the minimum value and $C_{\max}$ the maximum value of the capacitance of the capacitor.

(a) In which of the states A, B, C, D is the capacitance minimum, and in which is it maximum? Express the charge transferred to the battery on the high-emf side in one reverse cycle using $V_1$, $V_2$, $C_{\max}$, $C_{\min}$.

(b) This reverse cycle is run at $3.0\times10^2$ Hz while the capacitance of the capacitor is changed by a factor of $5.0\times10^2$. With $V_1=0.60\mathrm{V}$, $V_2=5.0\mathrm{V}$, what is the maximum capacitance $C_{\max}$ of the capacitor needed to fully charge, in 24 hours, a mobile battery ($5.0\mathrm{V}$, $2.0\mathrm{Ah}$) connected on the $V_2$ side with this device, starting from the empty state? Give it to 2 significant figures, and state the unit. Assume that the emf of the mobile battery is constant regardless of the remaining charge. Ah (ampere-hour) is a unit of charge, used to express the capacity of a battery; 1 Ah denotes the capacity to draw a current of 1 A continuously for 1 hour.

[IV] Magnetic energy of a coil

Besides the method using the isopotential process of [II], another way to transfer charge without Joule heat loss is to use the magnetic energy stored in a coil. A coil is a device consisting of a conducting wire wound many times, which produces a magnetic field when a current $I$ flows. By the law of electromagnetic induction, when the current $I$ is changing, an emf $-L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}$ is produced in the direction that opposes the change. The constant $L$ is called the self-inductance and is determined by the shape and the number of turns of the coil.

As in Fig. 5, a battery, a coil of self-inductance $L$, and resistors of resistance $R$ and $r$ are connected. After the switch SW is closed and a sufficiently long time has passed, the current flowing in the coil becomes a constant value $I_0$. After that, SW is opened at time $t=0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig5.png

Fig. 5.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig6.png

Fig. 6.

Q10. We find the Joule heat generated in the resistor after SW is opened.

(a) Let $I(t)$ be the current flowing in the coil at time $t\geqq0$ (the direction of the arrow in Fig. 5 is positive). Derive the differential equation satisfied by $I(t)$, and find the solution satisfying the initial condition $I(0)=I_0$.

(b) By integrating with respect to time the Joule heat generated per unit time in the resistor of resistance $R$, $R\big(I(t)\big)^2$, find the Joule heat generated from time 0 to $T(>0)$.

The total Joule heat obtained by letting $T\to\infty$ in the above result does not depend on $R$, and can be regarded as the energy when the current $I_0$ flows in a coil of self-inductance $L$. This energy can be understood as the energy of the magnetic field produced by the current flowing in the coil.

As in Fig. 6, a circuit connecting two capacitors of capacitance $C_1$, $C_2$ is made. Initially, the charge of the left capacitor was $Q_1$ (on the upper plate), and the charge of the right capacitor was 0. When the switch SW is closed, the charges move and are redistributed so that the sum of the electrostatic energies of the two capacitors becomes minimum.

Q11. Let $U(Q)$ be the sum of the electrostatic energies of the two capacitors when a charge $Q$ has moved in the direction of the arrow in the figure. What is the $Q$ that minimizes $U(Q)$?

As the charge moves, the electrostatic energy decreases and reaches its minimum value. The decrease of the electrostatic energy must have become Joule heat generated by the circuit resistance present in the circuit.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig7.png

Fig. 7.

As in Fig. 7, a coil of self-inductance $L$ and a resistor representing the circuit resistance $r$ are added to the circuit of Fig. 6. Initially the charge of the left capacitor is $Q_1$ (on the upper plate) and the charge of the right capacitor is 0, and the switch SW is closed at time $t=0$. We examine what happens to the electrostatic energy in this circuit.

Let $I(t)$ be the current at time $t$ (the arrow in Fig. 7 is the positive direction), $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}$ the rate of change of the current, $Q(t)$ the charge on the upper plate of the right capacitor, and $K(t)$ the magnetic energy of the coil. Also let $J(t)$ be the amount of Joule heat generated in the circuit resistance $r$ from time 0 to $t$.

Q12. Taking point A of the circuit as the reference point of potential (zero potential), let $V(t)$ be the potential of point B.

(a) Express $V(t)$ using $C_1$, $C_2$, $Q_1$, $Q(t)$.

(b) Express $V(t)$ using $L$, $r$, $I(t)$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}$.

Q13. Suppose that at time $t$, during a small time $\mathrm{d}t$, a small charge $\mathrm{d}Q$ flows in the circuit, and the charge of the right capacitor becomes $Q(t)+\mathrm{d}Q$.

(a) Find the rates of change of each of the following three physical quantities accompanying this transfer of charge $\mathrm{d}Q$.

• The rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}Q}$ of the sum $U$ of the electrostatic energies of the two capacitors

• The rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}Q}$ of the energy $K$ of the magnetic field produced by the current flowing in the coil

• The rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}J}{\mathrm{d}Q}$ of the amount $J$ of Joule heat generated in the circuit resistance

(b) Using the expressions for the potential $V(t)$ found in the previous question, find the relation satisfied by $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}Q}$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}Q}$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}J}{\mathrm{d}Q}$, and state its physical meaning.

(c) When the circuit resistance is $r=0$, what is the maximum value $I_{\max}$ of the current flowing in the circuit?

Even if the circuit resistance $r$ is made to approach 0, the current flowing in the circuit remains finite, so Joule heat generation disappears. This is completely different from the situation calculated in Q3. In the circuit of Fig. 7, the charge at potential $V$ released from the lower plate of the right capacitor has its electrostatic energy converted into magnetic energy by the back emf of the coil, and reaches the lower plate of the left capacitor at potential 0. In this sense, the coil takes on the characteristic of the isopotential process of the previous section, realizing a transfer of charge without Joule heat loss.

problems.title: Problem 3: Optics related to lenses
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (75 points)

Optics related to lenses

[I] Measurement of the refractive index

When designing optical instruments made of glass or resin, the value of the refractive index of the material is needed. For a prism whose two faces have been precisely polished to an apex angle $\alpha$ ($<90^{\circ}$), we want to find the refractive index of the material by measuring the angle $\delta$ (the deviation angle) between the incident ray and the emerging ray.

Q1. Let $\theta_1$ be the angle of incidence on the prism and $\theta_2$ the exit angle from the prism (the angle of refraction of the light going out from the prism side). Express the deviation angle $\delta$ using $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ and the apex angle $\alpha$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1. A prism with apex angle $\alpha$, the angle of incidence $\theta_1$, the exit angle $\theta_2$, and the deviation angle $\delta$, the angle between the incident ray and the emerging ray

Fig. 2 shows the relation between the angle of incidence $\theta_1$ and the deviation angle $\delta$ for $\alpha=60^{\circ}$, $n=1.50$. As can be seen from this figure, for a given apex angle and refractive index the deviation angle has a minimum value.
