Since the light pulse travels a distance $\dfrac{l'}{2} - vt'_{\mathrm{A}}$ at the speed of light $c$,

$$t'_{\mathrm{A}} = \frac{l'}{2(c+v)}$$

Q11 In the $S'$ frame, let $t'_{\mathrm{B}}$ be the time needed for the pulse to reach B from the light source. Express $t'_{\mathrm{B}}$ in terms of $l'$, $c$ and $v$.

In the $S$ frame the pulse reaches A and B at the same time. However, in the $S'$ frame, as is clear from the result of the question above, $t'_{\mathrm{A}} < t'_{\mathrm{B}}$, so the pulse reaches A before arriving at B. In other words, even if events occur simultaneously at two separated points in one inertial frame, in another inertial frame moving in the direction of the mutual displacement of those events, the times at which the two events occur are not the same.

Q12 Derive that the time difference between the two events in the $S'$ frame, $\mathit{\Delta}t' = t'_{\mathrm{B}} - t'_{\mathrm{A}}$, is $\dfrac{\gamma vl}{c^2}$.

3.4 Velocity addition law

Let us continue to consider the setting of Fig. 5 on the previous page. At time $t$ in the $S$ frame, the origin of the $x'$ axis of the $S'$ frame is at distance $vt$ from the origin of the $x$ axis of the $S$ frame. Consider a point located on the $x'$ axis of the $S'$ frame. Seen from the $S'$ frame, the $S$ frame moves with constant speed $v$ in the $-x'$ direction, so the distance between the origin of the $S'$ frame and that point in the $S$ frame differs from the distance in the $S'$ frame. That is, noting the relation obtained in Q10, the coordinate $x$ in the $S$ frame is related to the coordinate $x'$ in the $S'$ frame by $x = vt + \dfrac{x'}{\gamma}$. Rewriting,

$$x' = \gamma(x-vt) \qquad (1)$$

Between the two inertial frames there is no motion in the $y$ and $z$ directions, and there is no contraction of lengths perpendicular to the $x$ axis, so the following hold:

$$y' = y \qquad (2)$$

$$z' = z \qquad (3)$$

By the relation between the rates of time in the $S$ and $S'$ frames obtained in Q7, if the elapsed time in the $S$ frame is $t$, the elapsed time in the $S'$ frame is $\gamma t$. Even for simultaneous events at two separated points in the $S$ frame, there is a time difference in the $S'$ frame, as shown in Q12. That is, the elapsed time $t$ at a point at distance $x$ from the origin on the $x$ axis in the $S$ frame becomes the elapsed time $\gamma t - \dfrac{\gamma vx}{c^2}$ in the $S'$ frame:

$$t' = \gamma\left(t - \frac{vx}{c^2}\right) \qquad (4)$$

Consider a particle moving in the $S$ frame with constant velocity (less than the speed of light) $\overrightarrow{u} = (u_x, u_y, u_z)$. If the particle is at the origin at time $t = 0$, its position at time $t$ is

$$(x,\, y,\, z) = (u_x t,\, u_y t,\, u_z t) \qquad (5)$$

The motion of the same particle is observed in the $S'$ frame. As can be confirmed from equation (4), the particle is at the origin of the $S'$ frame at $t' = 0$. Hence the position of the particle in the $S'$ frame at time $t'$ is

$$(x',\, y',\, z') = (u'_x t',\, u'_y t',\, u'_z t') \qquad (6)$$

Q13 From the relations (1)–(6), express the components $(u'_x, u'_y, u'_z)$ of the velocity $\overrightarrow{u'}$ in the $S'$ frame in terms of the components $(u_x, u_y, u_z)$ of the velocity $\overrightarrow{u}$ in the $S$ frame, $\gamma$, $v$ and $c$ (velocity transformation law).

3.5 Derivation of aberration based on the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light"

Consider light travelling from a star to an observer located at the origin of the inertial frame $S$. Let the velocity of the light be $\overrightarrow{c}$. $|\overrightarrow{c}|$ is the speed of light in vacuum $c$. As shown in the left diagram of Fig. 6 on the next page, $\overrightarrow{c}$ lies in the $x$-$z$ plane, and its direction makes an angle $\theta$ with the $-x$ direction. $c_x = -c\cos\theta$ and $c_z = -c\sin\theta$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-3-fig6.png

Fig. 6. Left: direction from the star to the observer in the $S$ frame. Right: direction from the same star to the observer in the $S'$ frame.

[Labels in Fig. 6: S系 = $S$ frame; S′系 = $S'$ frame.]

Suppose a second observer, moving with velocity $\overrightarrow{v}$ in the $x$ direction relative to the first observer, observes the same star. Let $\overrightarrow{c'}$ be the velocity of the light in the inertial frame $S'$ of the second observer. By the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light", $|\overrightarrow{c'}| = c$. As shown in the right diagram of Fig. 6, $\overrightarrow{c'}$ lies in the $x'$-$z'$ plane, and its direction makes an angle $\theta'$ with the $-x'$ direction. $c'_x = -c\cos\theta'$ and $c'_z = -c\sin\theta'$.

Q14 Using the velocity transformation law derived in Q13, express $\tan\theta'$ in terms of $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$, $\dfrac{v}{c}$ and $\gamma$.

The result derived in Q14 is the aberration formulated on the basis of the "principle of the constancy of the speed of light". However, since the magnitude of the Earth's orbital velocity is $v = 3.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the corresponding value of $\gamma$ differs by only $5\times10^{-9}$ from the value $1.0$ for $v = 0$, and numerically it is practically indistinguishable from the value derived by Bradley. The significance of the treatment here lies in having formulated aberration consistently with the principle of the constancy of the speed of light, a fundamental principle of modern physics.

4 Epilogue: if the motion were fast

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-3-fig7.png

Fig. 7. Comparison of the result of Q2 (left) and the result of Q14 (right) against the angle of incidence $\theta$ in the rest frame.

The left diagram of Fig. 7 shows $\theta'$ found in Q2 (b), and the right diagram shows $\theta'$ found in Q14, against the angle of incidence $\theta$ in the rest frame, with $\dfrac{v}{c}$ as a parameter. According to the principle of the constancy of the speed of light, when $\dfrac{v}{c}$ becomes as large as $0.9$, light in the range $\theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ falls within the range $\theta' < \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and even light from behind ($\theta > \dfrac{\pi}{2}$) appears to the observer as light coming from near straight ahead in the direction of motion. For an observer moving at a speed close to the speed of light through an isotropic radiation field, the radiation appears strongly concentrated in the direction of motion; conversely, even if light (electromagnetic waves) is emitted isotropically from a source moving at a speed close to the speed of light, seen from the rest frame it appears as emission strongly concentrated in the direction of motion.

problems.title: Problem 4: Astronomical X-ray observation with the XRISM satellite
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (75 points)

Astronomical X-ray observation with the XRISM satellite

Astronomy has developed dramatically along with the development of observational techniques. In addition to observations with visible light and radio waves, X-ray observation began in earnest in the 1960s, and celestial objects emitting strong X-rays, such as neutron stars and black holes, as well as the hot ionized gas (plasma) filling clusters of galaxies, were discovered. Since X-rays are strongly absorbed by the Earth's atmosphere, observations must be made using rockets or artificial satellites. Japan has launched X-ray astronomy satellites such as "Hakucho", "Ginga", "Tenma", "Asuka" and "Suzaku", and has contributed greatly to the development of X-ray astronomy.

The Japanese X-ray astronomy satellite XRISM (X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission), launched in 2023, observes X-rays emitted from celestial objects using two X-ray telescopes named Xtend and Resolve. Xtend is an imaging device with an element called a CCD (Charge-Coupled Device) placed at its focal plane. Resolve is a spectroscopic device with a detector capable of precisely measuring the energy of X-ray photons placed at its focal plane. With these it is possible to determine elemental compositions and to determine the velocity of a radiation source from the Doppler shift.

Below we treat the principles of these devices and astronomical X-ray observation using line spectra.

1 X-ray mirror

As in Fig. 1, suppose X-rays are incident at an angle $\alpha$ to the surface on a material with a flat surface placed in vacuum. Let the refractive index of this material be $n$. The refractive index for visible light is larger than 1, but it is known that for X-rays the refractive index is slightly smaller than 1. Since the refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum $c$ to the speed at which a surface of constant phase of the light wave propagates in the material (phase velocity), when the refractive index is smaller than 1 the phase velocity is larger than $c$. However, the speed at which energy and information are actually transmitted is smaller than $c$, and there is no contradiction with relativity. Bragg reflection is not considered.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1

[Label in Fig. 1: X線 = X-rays.]

Q1 Find the condition for X-rays incident at an angle $\alpha$ to the surface to be totally reflected at the surface of this material.

Q2 Let $n = 1-\beta$, with $\beta \ll 1$ and $\alpha > 0$. Using the following approximation, express the maximum value $\alpha_{\max}$ of $\alpha$ for which X-rays are totally reflected, in terms of $\beta$.

For $|x| \ll 1$, $\cos x \fallingdotseq 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}$

A visible-light telescope collects light by combining lenses and mirrors, but for X-rays the reflectivity for light incident on a mirror from the front (normal incidence) is small, and it is hard to focus X-rays by making them incident from the front. Therefore X-ray telescopes adopt a method in which X-rays are made incident obliquely and are collected using total reflection.

The XRISM satellite uses a multilayer mirror in which many thin aluminium mirrors are nested axisymmetrically (concentrically). In each layer, as in Fig. 2, X-rays incident parallel to the central axis are totally reflected twice, by the conical mirror 1 and mirror 2, and are thereby focused at the focal point on the central axis.

As shown in Fig. 3, the angles that the incident X-rays make with the surfaces of mirror 1 and mirror 2 are equal, both being $\alpha$. The central axis is taken as the $x$ axis and the focal point as the origin. Let the $x$ coordinate of the first reflection point be $x_1$ and its distance from the axis $r_1$, and the $x$ coordinate of the second reflection point be $x_1 - d$ and its distance from the axis $r_2$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3

[Labels in Figs. 2 and 3: ミラー1 = mirror 1; ミラー2 = mirror 2; X線 = X-rays; 内側の層のミラー = mirror of the inner layer; 焦点 = focal point; 焦点O = focal point O.]

Q3 Express $r_2$ in terms of $r_1$, $d$ and $\alpha$.

Q4 Express $x_1$ in terms of $r_1$, $d$ and $\alpha$. For $0 < \alpha \ll 1$, use the approximations $\sin\alpha \fallingdotseq \alpha$, $\cos\alpha \fallingdotseq 1$, $\tan\alpha \fallingdotseq \alpha$.

Q5 In the XRISM satellite, $d = 0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ and $x_1 = 5.6\,\mathrm{m}$, and the distance from the central axis of the reflection point of the outer mirror 1 is $r_1 = 0.22\,\mathrm{m}$. Find $\alpha$ of the outer mirror in degrees ($^\circ$).

Here we found $\alpha$ for the outer mirror, but for the inner mirrors too the value of $\alpha$ can be determined so that X-rays totally reflected twice are collected at the focal point.

2 X-ray imaging device Xtend

A device that images, with a CCD, the X-rays collected by the X-ray mirror. When an X-ray is absorbed in the CCD, an electron is ejected, and a hole is created at the place where this electron was. This set of an electron and a hole is called an electron–hole pair. For each photon of energy $E$ [eV] absorbed in the CCD, $N = \dfrac{E}{3.65\,\mathrm{eV}}$ electron–hole pairs are produced, and this number $N$ is counted.

Q6 The energy of the incident photon can be estimated from the count of electron–hole pairs, but the number of electron–hole pairs produced has an uncertainty of about $\sqrt{N}$. For $E = 10\,\mathrm{keV}$, find the uncertainty in energy due to this uncertainty, in units of eV.

3 High-resolution X-ray spectrometer Resolve

As the X-ray spectrometer, a microcalorimeter of 36 pixels $(6\times6)$ is used. A microcalorimeter is a device that measures the energy of an incident photon by detecting the slight temperature rise caused by absorbing an X-ray. Each pixel consists of a mercury telluride (HgTe) absorber with a square base of side $820\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ and thickness $10\,\mathrm{\mu m}$, as in Fig. 4, and a thermometer using a silicon semiconductor element (thermistor) whose electrical resistance changes greatly when the temperature changes, and it is connected by thin silicon wires to a low-temperature heat reservoir kept at $50\,\mathrm{mK}$. When an X-ray photon is absorbed, the temperature of the absorber rises, but after a sufficiently long time the absorber is cooled down to the temperature of the low-temperature heat reservoir.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig4.png

Fig. 4

[Labels in Fig. 4: X線 = X-rays; 吸収体 (HgTe) = absorber (HgTe); シリコン 半導体温度計 = silicon semiconductor thermometer; 50mKに保たれた熱源 = heat reservoir kept at 50 mK.]

Q7 Let the density of HgTe be $\rho$, the volume per pixel $V$, and the specific heat $C$. Find the temperature rise $\mathit{\Delta}T$ when one photon of energy $E$ is absorbed in the absorber. Heat conduction through the wires connecting the pixel to the heat reservoir kept at $50\,\mathrm{mK}$ and heat transport to the thermometer can be neglected.

Q8 For $C = 2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$ and $\rho = 8.1\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, find the temperature rise of the HgTe due to the absorption of a photon of $E = 10\ \mathrm{keV}$, in units of mK, to 2 significant figures. $1\mathrm{eV} = 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Q9 Ion-implanted silicon is used as the thermometer. Since its resistance changes greatly with temperature at low temperatures, this material is sensitive to temperature changes, and temperature differences down to $5.0\ \mathrm{\mu K}$ can be measured. This measurable temperature difference is called the precision of the temperature measurement. If the ability to separate and measure energies (energy resolution) is determined by this precision of the temperature measurement, find the energy resolution at $E = 10\ \mathrm{keV}$ in units of eV, to 2 significant figures.

4 Energy of iron emission lines

By observing the line spectra emitted by ionized elements such as iron and nickel, the XRISM satellite can measure the temperature and velocity of astrophysical plasmas emitting X-rays. A state in which ionization has advanced and only one electron orbits the nucleus can be treated, using the Bohr model, in the same way as the hydrogen atom.

Q10 Suppose an electron of mass $m_{\mathrm{e}}$ and charge $-e$ $(e > 0)$ moves in uniform circular motion with orbital radius $r$ and speed $v$ around a nucleus of positive charge $Q$. In the Bohr model it is assumed that the electron takes only circular orbits satisfying the following condition:

$$m_{\mathrm{e}}vr = n\frac{h}{2\pi}$$

Here $h$ is the Planck constant and $n$ is a positive integer. Taking the permittivity of vacuum as $\epsilon_0$, express the orbital radius $r_n$ of the electron in the $n$-th state in terms of $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, $Q$, $e$, $\epsilon_0$, $h$, $n$.

Q11 Express the energy $E_n$ of the electron in the $n$-th state in terms of $m_{\mathrm{e}}$, $Q$, $e$, $\epsilon_0$, $h$, $n$.

Q12 When an iron atom (atomic number 26) has been ionized 25 times so that only one electron remains around the nucleus, find the ratio of the energy $E_{21}$ of the light emitted when this electron makes a transition from the $n = 2$ to the $n = 1$ state to the absolute value $|E_{\mathrm{H0}}|$ of the energy of the ground state of the hydrogen atom ($Q = e$, $n = 1$).

Q13 Express $E_{21}$ in units of keV. If necessary, use the following values: $h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$, $m_{\mathrm{e}} = 9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $e = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, $\epsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$.

The line spectra observed by the XRISM satellite include, besides the above emission lines emitted from hot regions of high ionization, fluorescent iron lines emitted when a non-ionized iron atom absorbs an X-ray and emits an electron, and another electron makes a transition into the energy level that this electron occupied. By precisely measuring the energies of these spectral lines, it has become possible to measure the velocity of the emitting matter more accurately from the wavelength shift due to the Doppler effect.

5 Formation of disk winds

From observations of iron emission lines and absorption lines by the XRISM satellite, the velocity of hot outflows ejected from the central region (nucleus) of a galaxy, which is thought to have a supermassive black hole at its centre, has been measured when the luminosity (energy radiated per unit time) of this region increased.

As in Fig. 5, let the mass of the galactic central region, shown as a small circle centred on the origin O, be $M$, its luminosity $L$, and the gravitational constant $G$, and assume that the radiation from the nucleus is spherically symmetric. At time $t = 0$ a spherical absorber of cross-sectional area $\sigma$ and mass $m$ is at rest at distance $R_0$ from the origin. The radius of the absorber is sufficiently small, and $m \ll M$. Radiation incident on this absorber is completely absorbed. The absorber does not deform when it absorbs radiation, and its cross-sectional area does not change. Outside the absorber is vacuum.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig5.png

Fig. 5

[Labels in Fig. 5: 吸収体 = absorber; 中心核 = nucleus; 光度 $L$ = luminosity $L$.]

Q14 Suppose the frequency of the photons emitted from the nucleus is constant, equal to $\nu$. Express the number $N_\nu$ of photons passing per unit time through unit area at distance $R_0$ from the origin in terms of $L$, $R_0$, $h$, $\nu$.

Q15 Express the momentum $p$ transferred from the photon to the absorber when one photon of frequency $\nu$ is absorbed by the absorber, in terms of $h$, $\nu$, $c$.

Q16 Express the momentum $P_0$ transferred per unit time from the radiation of the nucleus to the absorber at distance $R_0$ from the origin, in terms of $\sigma$, $c$, $L$, $R_0$. The change of frequency due to gravity can be neglected.

Q17 Let the direction joining the origin and the centre of the absorber be the $R$ direction, and let the velocity of the absorber in this direction be $v$. Write the equation of motion of the absorber. Assume $|v| \ll c$.

Q18 For the absorber to be accelerated outward in the $R$ direction, the luminosity of the nucleus must be larger than $L_{\mathrm{E}}$. Find $L_{\mathrm{E}}$.

Q19 When the above condition is satisfied, express the velocity $v_\infty$ as $R \to \infty$ in terms of $G$, $L$, $L_{\mathrm{E}}$, $M$, $R_0$.

Next, as in Fig. 6, consider the case where the absorber floats above a disk centred on the origin and rotating counterclockwise about the $z$ axis. Let the coordinates of the centre of the absorber at time $t = 0$ be $(r, z) = (r_0, z_0)$ and its distance from the origin $R_0$, and suppose the absorber moves with an initial velocity of magnitude $u_0$ in the direction perpendicular to the $rz$ plane (the direction from the front of the page to the back). The absorption and scattering of radiation by the rotating disk and radiation from the rotating disk are ignored. The gravity exerted by the rotating disk on the absorber can also be neglected. The speed $u$ of the absorber satisfies $u \ll c$, and the resistive force that the absorber receives, opposite to its direction of motion, through interaction with the radiation (radiation drag) is ignored.

Q20 For $L > L_{\mathrm{E}}$, express the speed $u_\infty$ of the absorber as $t \to \infty$ in terms of $G$, $u_0$, $L$, $L_{\mathrm{E}}$, $M$, $R_0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-4-fig6.png

Fig. 6

[Labels in Fig. 6: 吸収体 = absorber; 回転円盤 = rotating disk; 中心核 = nucleus; 光度 $L$ = luminosity $L$.]

Here the frequency of the photons emitted from the nucleus was taken to be constant, but even when photons of various frequencies are emitted, the same relations are obtained provided all of those photons are absorbed by the absorber.

Q21 Suppose the absorber is formed near the surface of the rotating disk, with $z_0 = 0.1r_0$, $u_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r_0}}$, $L = 1.5L_{\mathrm{E}}$. If the absorber has been accelerated by the radiation from the nucleus up to $u_\infty = 0.05c$, find $\dfrac{r_0}{r_{\mathrm{S}}}$ using the radius of a non-rotating black hole (the radius of the event horizon)

$$r_{\mathrm{S}} = \frac{2GM}{c^2}$$

This value shows how far from the black hole the region is in which the absorber is formed.

In the vicinity of the nuclei of active galaxies, absorbers are ionized by strong X-rays and no longer emit visible line spectra, so understanding had not progressed with conventional visible-light observations. X-ray observations by the XRISM satellite have made it possible to observe in detail the distribution and velocities of absorbers in such regions, and research on the activity of galactic nuclei is progressing rapidly.
